Stage II; FDL transfer with medializing calcaneal osteotomy

Stage II is tibialis posterior dysfunction with a flexible flatfoot. Stage I is tenosynovitis without deformity, stage III a rigid deformity usually treated with triple arthrodesis, and stage IV adds valgus tilt of the talus in the ankle mortise.
A 50-year-old has pain and stiffness of the first MTP joint with a dorsal osteophyte. Pain occurs only at the end of dorsiflexion and the joint space is preserved. Best surgical option:

This is early hallux rigidus. Cheilectomy removes the dorsal osteophyte and part of the dorsal metatarsal head to restore dorsiflexion. Arthrodesis is the standard for advanced disease with mid-range pain; chevron osteotomy treats hallux valgus.
A woman has burning forefoot pain radiating to the third and fourth toes. Squeezing the metatarsal heads together while pressing the third web space produces a painful click. Diagnosis:

Morton's neuroma is perineural fibrosis of the common digital nerve, most often in the third web space; the click is Mulder's sign. Treatment starts with wide shoes, a metatarsal pad and injection, with excision for persistent symptoms.
A 30-year-old has burning pain and paraesthesia over the sole, worse with standing, and Tinel's sign is positive behind the medial malleolus. The nerve is compressed beneath the:

This is tarsal tunnel syndrome, compression of the tibial nerve or its branches. Causes include ganglia, varicosities, accessory muscles and hindfoot valgus. Anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome is compression of the deep peroneal nerve under the inferior extensor retinaculum.
A man has a cavovarus foot. Standing on a block under the lateral forefoot and heel, so the first ray drops off the edge, his heel varus corrects. This means:
The hindfoot varus is rigid and needs calcaneal osteotomy
The deformity is forefoot-driven, from a plantarflexed first ray
The cause is a tarsal coalition

In the Coleman block test, correction of the heel shows a flexible hindfoot whose varus is driven by the plantarflexed first ray, so a dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal may be enough. A cavovarus foot, especially when bilateral, should prompt assessment for Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease.
When a constant load is applied to a viscoelastic tissue such as tendon, its continued deformation over time is called:

Creep is increasing deformation under a constant load. Stress relaxation is the fall in stress under a constant deformation, and hysteresis is the energy lost between the loading and unloading curves. Viscoelastic tissues are also stiffer at higher loading rates.
Cortical bone is strongest when loaded in:
Bone is anisotropic and strongest in compression, weaker in tension and weakest in shear. Its properties also depend on the direction of loading relative to the osteons.
Increased compression across a physis slows its growth, while reduced compression accelerates it
Bone remodels according to the loads placed on it
Fracture healing depends on interfragmentary strain
Tendon strength increases with cyclic loading
This explains progressive deformities such as Blount disease and scoliosis and is the basis of guided growth. Wolff's law describes bone remodelling in response to load.
Most physeal fractures, and the slip in SCFE, pass through which zone of the physis?

The hypertrophic zone, especially near the zone of provisional calcification, is weakest because its enlarged cells have little matrix and it is not yet calcified. Germinal cells in the reserve and proliferative zones are often spared, which is why most physeal fractures grow normally.
Inhibiting farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteoclasts
Acting as a soluble decoy receptor that binds RANKL

Osteoblasts and stromal cells produce RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their formation and activity, and also OPG, which neutralises RANKL. The RANKL/OPG balance controls resorption. Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase.
Sclerostin, the target of romosozumab, is secreted mainly by:

Sclerostin from osteocytes binds LRP5/6 and inhibits Wnt signalling, reducing bone formation; mechanical loading lowers sclerostin. Loss-of-function mutations in its gene (SOST) cause sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease, with high bone mass.
Compared with normal aged cartilage, cartilage in early osteoarthritis typically shows:
Increased water content with reduced proteoglycan content and stiffness
Decreased water content and increased stiffness
Replacement of all collagen by type I collagen
In OA, damage to the collagen network lets the tissue swell, so water rises while proteoglycans fall and the modulus decreases. Ageing alone lowers water content.
In the superficial (tangential) zone of articular cartilage, collagen fibres are oriented:

The superficial zone has fibres parallel to the surface, the highest water content and the lowest proteoglycan content, and resists shear. The middle zone is oblique and the deep zone perpendicular, crossing the tidemark into calcified cartilage.
The circumferential collagen fibres of the meniscus mainly serve to:
Carry the blood supply to the inner third
Resist shear between the femur and tibia
Resist hoop stresses generated by axial load
Anchor the meniscus to the capsule

Axial load pushes the meniscus outwards, and the circumferential type I collagen fibres, anchored at the roots, convert this into hoop tension; radial fibres act as ties. A complete radial or root tear disrupts hoop function and behaves biomechanically like a meniscectomy.
In a Sunderland grade 3 nerve injury, which structures are disrupted?
Axon only, with all connective tissue intact
Axon, endoneurium and perineurium, with the epineurium intact
Axon and endoneurium, with the perineurium intact

Grade 1 is neuropraxia, grade 2 axonotmesis with intact endoneurium (good recovery), grade 3 adds endoneurial disruption (incomplete recovery from misdirected regeneration), grade 4 adds perineurium, and grade 5 is complete transection.
After a nerve injury, fibrillation potentials on EMG first appear in the denervated muscle at about:

Denervation potentials (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) need Wallerian degeneration, which takes about 2–3 weeks depending on the distance to the muscle. Earlier studies can miss axonal injury, so EMG is usually done 3–4 weeks after injury.
Which bone graft property is lacking in a fresh-frozen cortical allograft but present in autograft?

Only autograft (and bone marrow aspirate) supplies living osteoprogenitor cells, which is osteogenesis. Allograft is mainly osteoconductive with weak osteoinductive capacity, and demineralised bone matrix is osteoconductive and variably osteoinductive.
The bending and torsional strength of a bone screw depends mainly on its:
Resistance to breakage depends on the core diameter, rising with the cube of the core radius. Pull-out strength depends mainly on the outer diameter, thread depth and bone quality.
Doubling the thickness of a plate of the same width and material increases its bending stiffness by a factor of about:

Bending stiffness of a rectangular plate is proportional to the cube of its thickness (area moment of inertia = width × thickness³ / 12). For a solid rod, stiffness rises with the fourth power of the radius.
A key biological advantage of a locked plate used in bridging mode over a conventional compression plate is that it:
Does not rely on friction between plate and bone, so periosteal blood supply is better preserved
Allows fewer screws in osteoporotic bone without any risk

Locked screws form a fixed-angle construct that acts as an internal fixator, so the plate need not be pressed onto the bone. This helps in osteoporotic bone and metaphyseal comminution. Conventional plates gain stability from plate–bone friction, which can compromise periosteal perfusion.
In the diaphysis of a long bone, the inner two-thirds of the cortex is normally supplied by:
The nutrient (endosteal) artery, with centrifugal flow

Blood normally flows centrifugally from the medullary nutrient system outwards, and periosteal vessels supply the outer third. Reamed nailing temporarily disrupts the endosteal supply and the periosteal supply compensates, so periosteal stripping should be avoided.
A 14-year-old has an ankle fracture that looks like a Salter–Harris III on the AP view and a Salter–Harris II on the lateral view. Diagnosis and best imaging:
Juvenile Tillaux fracture; no further imaging
Triplane fracture; CT to assess articular displacement

A triplane fracture has sagittal (epiphyseal), axial (physeal) and coronal (metaphyseal) components, so it looks like a type III on the AP and a type II on the lateral, and is a type IV injury overall. It occurs in the transitional period of physeal closure. CT guides treatment; articular displacement over 2 mm usually needs reduction and fixation.
Which physeal fracture carries the highest rate of growth disturbance, even when it is a Salter–Harris type II injury?

The distal femoral physis is large and undulating, so fractures often cross its germinal layer, and growth arrest or angular deformity follows in a substantial proportion. These injuries need anatomical reduction and follow-up for leg-length discrepancy. Distal radius and proximal humerus physeal fractures remodel well.
A 10-year-old has a displaced tibial spine (eminence) fracture that will not reduce with knee extension. The structure most commonly blocking reduction is the:
Anterior horn of the medial meniscus or the intermeniscal ligament

Soft tissue entrapped under the fragment, usually the anterior horn of the medial meniscus or the intermeniscal ligament, prevents closed reduction of displaced (Meyers–McKeever type II–III) fractures. These are treated by arthroscopic or open reduction and fixation with sutures or screws.
A 14-year-old boy has a displaced tibial tubercle avulsion fracture after a jump. Which complication must be specifically watched for?
Peroneal nerve palsy from the fragment
Anterior compartment syndrome from bleeding of the anterior tibial recurrent artery
Avascular necrosis of the tibial plateau

The anterior tibial recurrent artery runs near the tubercle and can bleed into the anterior compartment. Displaced fractures are treated with ORIF, and some surgeons add prophylactic anterior fasciotomy. Osgood–Schlatter disease is a risk factor.
A 6-year-old has a lateral condyle fracture of the humerus displaced by 4 mm. Why is ORIF preferred over casting?
The fracture is extra-articular and remodels poorly
It always injures the radial nerve
The fracture is intra-articular and pulled by the extensor origin, with a high risk of non-union and malunion

Lateral condyle fractures displaced more than about 2 mm are fixed because the fragment carries the common extensor origin, is bathed in synovial fluid and tends to displace. Non-union leads to cubitus valgus and tardy ulnar nerve palsy. Undisplaced fractures can be casted with close radiographic follow-up.
After a reduced elbow dislocation in a 12-year-old, radiographs show the medial epicondyle fragment lying within the joint. Management:
Excision of the fragment only if symptoms persist at 6 months
Open reduction of the fragment out of the joint and fixation

An incarcerated medial epicondyle fragment is an absolute indication for surgery because it blocks concentric reduction and threatens the ulnar nerve. Indications for fixation of an extra-articular displaced fragment remain debated.
A 3-year-old will not use her arm after being lifted by the hand. She holds it slightly flexed and pronated, radiographs are normal, and there is no swelling. The lesion and treatment are:
Subluxation of the radial head through the annular ligament; reduction by supination and flexion or by hyperpronation
Supracondylar fracture; closed reduction and pinning

Nursemaid's elbow is common between about 1 and 4 years. A palpable click usually accompanies reduction and the child resumes use within minutes. Hyperpronation is slightly more successful than supination-flexion. Radiographs are not needed with a classic history and examination.
A child with a Gartland type III supracondylar fracture has no palpable radial pulse but a warm, pink, well-perfused hand after closed reduction and pinning. The most appropriate next step is:
Admit and monitor perfusion and neurology closely

A pink, perfused but pulseless hand after adequate reduction is usually observed in hospital, because collateral circulation around the elbow is good and many pulses return. Exploration is needed if the hand is or becomes poorly perfused, or if a compartment syndrome or worsening nerve deficit develops.
A 2-year-old has started limping without clear trauma. Radiographs show an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft with an intact fibula. Most likely diagnosis and treatment:
Non-accidental injury; skeletal survey in every case
Toddler's fracture; immobilisation for a few weeks

Toddler's fractures occur in newly walking children from a twisting fall. They may be visible only on oblique views or later as periosteal reaction. Immobilisation in a boot or cast is enough. A spiral fracture in a non-ambulant infant should raise concern for abuse.
Which radiographic finding is most specific for non-accidental injury in an infant?
Classic metaphyseal lesion (corner or bucket-handle fracture)

Classic metaphyseal lesions and posterior rib fractures are highly specific because they need shearing or squeezing forces. Clavicle, supracondylar and simple linear skull fractures are common accidental injuries. Suspicion requires a skeletal survey and multidisciplinary safeguarding assessment.
An otherwise healthy 3-year-old has an isolated closed femoral shaft fracture with 1 cm of shortening. Usual treatment:

Between about 6 months and 5 years, early hip spica casting is standard, accepting some shortening because of overgrowth. Flexible nails are typical for children aged about 5–11 years, and a Pavlik harness is used in infants under 6 months. Unexplained femoral fractures in non-walking children need assessment for abuse.
For hip surveillance in children with cerebral palsy, Reimers' migration percentage measures:
The proportion of the femoral head width lying lateral to Perkins' line

The migration percentage is the width of femoral head lateral to Perkins' line divided by total head width. It increases with GMFCS level, and rising values above about 30–40% prompt soft-tissue release or reconstructive osteotomy to prevent painful dislocation.
A child has a short neck, low posterior hairline and restricted neck movement. Radiographs show congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae. Which investigation is most important to arrange?

Klippel–Feil syndrome is associated with renal anomalies (including unilateral agenesis), scoliosis, Sprengel deformity, hearing loss and congenital heart disease. Renal ultrasound is routine. Fused segments put adjacent levels at risk of instability, so collision sports may be restricted.
An infant has anterolateral bowing of the tibia. Which association should be sought, given the risk of progression to pseudarthrosis?

Anterolateral bowing is linked to congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia and NF1. It is protected in a brace to delay fracture, and established pseudarthrosis is treated with resection, fixation and graft or Ilizarov techniques. Posteromedial bowing is benign and usually corrects, but leaves leg-length discrepancy.
A 7-year-old boy has lateral elbow pain. Radiographs show fragmentation and irregularity of the whole capitellar ossific nucleus. Diagnosis and management:
Osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum; arthroscopic fixation

Panner disease is osteochondrosis of the whole capitellum in children under about 10 and usually resolves with rest. Osteochondritis dissecans affects a focal area in adolescent throwers and gymnasts and may need surgery if unstable.
A child with fibular hemimelia (the most common congenital long-bone deficiency) is most likely to also have:
Lateral ray deficiency, tarsal coalition and a ball-and-socket ankle

Fibular hemimelia comes with anterior tibial bowing, a short femur, ACL deficiency, genu valgum, missing lateral rays, tarsal coalition and a ball-and-socket ankle. Treatment depends on predicted leg-length discrepancy and foot function, ranging from lengthening to Syme or Boyd amputation.
In infantile idiopathic scoliosis, which measurement best predicts curve progression?

An RVAD over 20°, or a phase 2 rib head overlapping the apical vertebra, predicts progression. Most curves with low RVAD resolve. Progressive curves are treated with Mehta serial casting. Infantile curves warrant MRI to exclude neural axis abnormalities.
After an inversion ankle sprain, which ligament is most commonly injured, and which test assesses it?
Anterior talofibular ligament; anterior drawer test

The ATFL is the weakest lateral ligament and is injured first in plantarflexion and inversion; the anterior drawer tests it. The calcaneofibular ligament is tested with talar tilt in neutral. Most sprains respond to functional rehabilitation; chronic instability is treated with a Broström repair.
An athlete feels a snap behind the lateral malleolus during forced dorsiflexion. Radiographs show a small cortical avulsion from the lateral rim of the distal fibula. The injury is:
Peroneal tendon dislocation from superior peroneal retinaculum avulsion

Sudden dorsiflexion with eversion and peroneal contraction avulses the superior peroneal retinaculum, sometimes with a rim fragment, letting the tendons dislocate anteriorly. Recurrent dislocation is treated with retinacular repair, with groove deepening if needed.
A ballet dancer has posterior ankle pain on full plantarflexion (en pointe), and pain with resisted great toe flexion. Most likely diagnosis:
Posterior impingement from an os trigonum, with FHL tenosynovitis

The os trigonum (or a Stieda process) is compressed between the tibia and calcaneus in plantarflexion. FHL runs between the medial and lateral tubercles, so it is often involved. Treatment is rest and injection, then arthroscopic or open excision.
A footballer hyperextends his great toe on artificial turf and has pain and swelling of the plantar first MTP joint. The structure injured is the:
Plantar plate of the first MTP joint

Turf toe is a sprain or tear of the plantar plate and capsuloligamentous complex. Proximal migration of the sesamoids on radiographs suggests a complete tear, which often needs repair. Most lower-grade injuries settle with taping and a stiff-soled shoe.
A sprinter has vague dorsal midfoot pain and tenderness over the 'N spot'. CT confirms an incomplete fracture of the navicular body. Standard initial treatment:
Continue training in a stiff shoe

Navicular stress fractures are high-risk because of a relatively avascular central third. Strict non-weight-bearing in a cast for about 6 weeks gives good results for incomplete fractures; displaced, complete or non-united fractures usually need screw fixation, with or without graft.
Compared with lateral talar dome osteochondral lesions, medial lesions are typically:
Posterior, deeper, cup-shaped and often without a clear injury

Lateral lesions are usually anterolateral, thin and wafer-like, and follow inversion-dorsiflexion trauma. Medial lesions are posteromedial, deeper and more often atraumatic. Small symptomatic lesions are commonly treated with arthroscopic debridement and microfracture.
The optimal position for ankle arthrodesis is:
Neutral dorsiflexion, 0–5° hindfoot valgus, and external rotation matching the other side (about 5–10°)

Neutral flexion with slight valgus and slight external rotation gives the best gait. Equinus causes back-knee thrust, and varus locks the transverse tarsal joints and overloads the lateral foot. Slight posterior translation of the talus also eases toe-off.
Flexion of the DIP joint only
Flexion of the PIP joint with a neutral or extended MTP and DIP joint
Hyperextension of the MTP joint with flexion of the PIP and DIP joints

Mallet toe is DIP flexion alone, and hammer toe is mainly PIP flexion. Claw toes are often multiple and suggest neuromuscular disease (such as CMT or diabetic neuropathy) or inflammatory arthritis, from imbalance between intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
A diabetic patient has a deep plantar ulcer with an underlying abscess and probe-to-bone osteomyelitis, without gangrene. What is the Wagner grade?

Wagner grade 0 is an at-risk foot without ulcer, 1 a superficial ulcer, 2 a deep ulcer reaching tendon, capsule or bone, 3 a deep ulcer with abscess or osteomyelitis, 4 forefoot or localised gangrene, and 5 gangrene of the whole foot.
A 14-year-old girl has forefoot pain. Radiographs show flattening and sclerosis of the second metatarsal head. Diagnosis:

Freiberg infraction is osteonecrosis of a lesser metatarsal head, usually the second, most common in adolescent girls. A long second metatarsal may contribute. Treatment starts with offloading; dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy or debridement is used for persistent pain.
A 5-year-old boy limps with medial midfoot pain. Radiographs show a flattened, sclerotic, fragmented tarsal navicular. Prognosis:
Usually self-limiting, with reconstitution of the navicular
High risk of tarsal coalition later

Köhler disease is osteochondrosis of the navicular, typically in boys aged about 4–7. Symptoms settle with activity modification or a short-leg cast, and the bone reconstitutes without long-term problems.
A 45-year-old has sharp heel pain on the first steps in the morning, with tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle. Recommended first-line treatment:
Plantar fascia–specific and calf stretching with supportive footwear

Plantar fasciitis settles in most patients within a year with stretching, heel cushions, night splints and footwear change. Corticosteroid injections give short-term relief but risk fascial rupture and fat pad atrophy. A heel spur is a common incidental finding and is not the cause of pain.
A 40-year-old has pain and a tender bony prominence at the posterosuperior calcaneus, worse with rigid heel counters, with a retrocalcaneal bursitis. This is:

Haglund deformity (the 'pump bump') causes retrocalcaneal bursitis and may accompany insertional Achilles tendinopathy. Treatment is footwear change and heel lifts, then excision of the prominence and bursa with debridement of the tendon if needed. Sever disease is calcaneal apophysitis in children.
After correction of the metatarsophalangeal deformity in hallux valgus, residual valgus at the interphalangeal level of the great toe is best treated with:
Akin osteotomy (medial closing-wedge of the proximal phalanx)
The Akin osteotomy corrects hallux valgus interphalangeus and is commonly added to metatarsal osteotomies. Cheilectomy and Keller resection are procedures for hallux rigidus.
Chopart's (transverse tarsal) joint consists of the:

The talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints lock when the hindfoot is in varus, making the foot rigid for push-off, and unlock in valgus for shock absorption. Lisfranc's joint is the tarsometatarsal articulation.
A crush injury of the foot has led to compartment syndrome. Which late deformity results if it is not decompressed?
Claw toes from intrinsic muscle contracture

The foot has multiple compartments, including the calcaneal compartment containing quadratus plantae. Necrosis and fibrosis of the intrinsic muscles cause claw toes, stiffness and neuropathic pain. Decompression is through two dorsal and one medial incision.
Young's modulus of a material is the:
Slope of the linear elastic portion of the stress–strain curve
Stress at which plastic deformation begins
Young's modulus reflects stiffness. The yield point is where plastic deformation begins, ultimate strength is the maximum stress, and the area under the curve is the energy absorbed (toughness).
In a clinical trial, a type I (alpha) error means:
Failing to detect a real difference
Concluding there is a difference when none exists (a false positive)
Alpha is usually set at 0.05. A type II (beta) error is missing a real difference, and power is 1 − beta, usually set at 0.8 or more. Larger samples reduce type II error.
The sensitivity of a diagnostic test is the:
Proportion of people with the disease who test positive
Proportion of people without the disease who test negative
Proportion of positive tests that are true positives
Proportion of negative tests that are true negatives

Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives). Specificity is the proportion of people without disease who test negative. Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do not.
In a trial, infection occurs in 20% of controls and 10% of treated patients. The number needed to treat to prevent one infection is:
Absolute risk reduction = 20% − 10% = 10% (0.1), and NNT = 1/ARR = 10. The relative risk reduction is 50%, which sounds larger and can exaggerate the benefit.
A well-designed randomised controlled trial with narrow confidence intervals is level of evidence:

Level I is high-quality RCTs (or systematic reviews of them). Level II includes lesser-quality RCTs and prospective cohort studies, level III includes case–control and retrospective cohort studies, and level IV is case series.
Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement is strongest when loaded in:

PMMA is a grout rather than an adhesive: strong in compression and weak in tension and shear. Porosity reduction (vacuum mixing) and an even cement mantle of about 2 mm improve fatigue life. Polymerisation is exothermic.
Which implant combination is most likely to cause galvanic corrosion?
Titanium alloy screws with a titanium alloy plate
Cobalt–chromium head on a cobalt–chromium stem
316L stainless steel screws with a cobalt–chromium plate
Ceramic head on a polyethylene liner

Galvanic corrosion occurs when dissimilar metals with different electrochemical potentials are in contact in body fluid. Stainless steel is the most vulnerable. Titanium and cobalt–chromium are relatively compatible because both form stable passive oxide layers.
When placing a lag screw by technique across an oblique fracture, the near cortex is drilled to:
The core diameter of the screw
A smaller diameter than the core
No drilling, using a self-tapping screw
The outer (thread) diameter of the screw, making a gliding hole

The gliding hole lets the threads engage only the far cortex, so tightening compresses the fragments. Ideally the screw is perpendicular to the fracture plane. A partially threaded screw achieves the same with threads only in the far fragment.
Placing a screw eccentrically (away from the fracture) in the hole of a dynamic compression plate produces compression because:
The sloped hole drives the screw head, and the bone, towards the centre of the hole as it is tightened
The screw locks into the plate
The screw head slides down the inclined hole as it is tightened, moving the bone fragment about 1 mm towards the fracture. Pre-bending the plate slightly avoids gapping of the far cortex.
In the normal walking gait cycle, stance phase occupies about:
Stance is about 60% and swing about 40% of the cycle, with two periods of double-limb support. As walking speed increases, stance shortens; running has no double support but a flight phase.
A patient with an arthritic right hip uses a walking stick. It is most effective in reducing the hip joint reaction force when held:
In the right hand with a shortened stick

In single-leg stance the abductors must balance body weight acting through a long lever arm, producing a joint reaction force of about 3 times body weight. A stick in the opposite hand provides a counter-moment with a long lever arm, greatly reducing the abductor force needed.
Lubricin (proteoglycan 4), produced by superficial chondrocytes and synoviocytes, contributes mainly to:

Lubricin coats the cartilage surface and reduces friction when surfaces are in contact (boundary lubrication). Fluid film mechanisms, including weeping and boosted lubrication, act at higher loads and speeds. Joint friction is extremely low.
The key transcription factor needed for mesenchymal cells to differentiate into osteoblasts is:
RUNX2 (with osterix downstream) drives osteoblast differentiation; its haploinsufficiency causes cleidocranial dysplasia. SOX9 drives chondrogenesis, PPAR-gamma adipogenesis and MyoD myogenesis.
Type I (slow-twitch) muscle fibres are characterised by:
Oxidative metabolism, many mitochondria and fatigue resistance

Type I fibres are red, aerobic and postural, and are recruited first. Type II fibres are fast-twitch: type IIa is oxidative-glycolytic and IIb (IIx) glycolytic and fatigue quickly. Immobilisation causes early atrophy of type I fibres.
A direct ligament or tendon insertion into bone, such as the ACL femoral attachment, consists of:
Sharpey fibres blending into the periosteum only
Four zones: ligament, unmineralised fibrocartilage, mineralised fibrocartilage and bone

Direct insertions have a graded fibrocartilaginous transition with a tidemark between unmineralised and mineralised zones. Indirect insertions, such as the superficial MCL on the tibia, attach through Sharpey fibres into periosteum. Tendon grafts in bone tunnels heal by forming Sharpey-like fibres rather than recreating the four zones.
After axonotmesis, the regenerating axon advances at roughly:

Regeneration of about 1 mm per day (about an inch per month) allows prediction of recovery; an advancing Tinel sign tracks it. Motor end plates degenerate after about 12–18 months, so distal muscles may not recover after long proximal injuries, which drives early nerve transfer.
Compared with stainless steel, titanium alloy implants are more notch sensitive. In practice this means that:
They corrode more readily in body fluid
They are more likely to cause allergy
Scratches or notches on the surface markedly reduce their fatigue life
They cannot be used with locking screws

Notch sensitivity means surface defects act as stress risers that start fatigue cracks, so titanium plates should not be repeatedly bent back and forth or scratched. Titanium has excellent corrosion resistance and biocompatibility and a lower modulus than steel, but lower wear resistance as a bearing surface.
In the Cierny–Mader classification of osteomyelitis, a full-thickness, well-demarcated cortical sequestrum that can be excised without making the bone mechanically unstable is anatomical type:

Type III (localised) involves the full cortical thickness but the bone stays stable after debridement. Type IV (diffuse) is unstable before or after debridement and needs stabilisation. Host class A is a normal host, B has local or systemic compromise, and C is a patient for whom treatment would be worse than the disease.

An 11-year-old has had several weeks of mild aching near the ankle, no fever and a normal white cell count. Radiographs show a well-defined lucency in the distal tibial metaphysis with a thick sclerotic rim and a serpiginous tract towards the physis. On T1 MRI the cavity has a thin rim brighter than the abscess (penumbra sign). Most likely diagnosis:

Brodie abscess is subacute osteomyelitis, usually from S. aureus, where host defences and organism virulence are balanced so systemic signs are mild. The tract to the physis and the penumbra sign (a lining of granulation tissue) favour it over osteoid osteoma. Treatment is curettage with culture, followed by antibiotics.

A 22-year-old sexually active woman develops migratory joint pains, tenosynovitis of the wrist extensors and a few painless pustules on her limbs, followed by a knee effusion. The most likely organism is:

Disseminated gonococcal infection presents with the triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and polyarthralgia, or with a purulent monoarthritis. Synovial cultures are often negative, so test urethral, cervical, pharyngeal and rectal sites (culture or NAAT). It responds well to ceftriaxone and needs surgical drainage less often than staphylococcal septic arthritis.
In a suspected native-joint bacterial septic arthritis, which synovial fluid finding is most suggestive?
White cell count of about 2,000 cells/µL with 25% neutrophils
White cell count above 50,000 cells/µL with neutrophil predominance

Counts above about 50,000 cells/µL with more than 75–90% neutrophils strongly suggest infection, although lower counts do not exclude it (early, gonococcal or immunosuppressed cases). Crystals do not exclude infection because the two can coexist. Thresholds for periprosthetic infection are much lower.
Joint aspirate shows rhomboid crystals that are weakly positively birefringent under polarised light. These are:

CPPD crystals cause pseudogout and chondrocalcinosis, typically of the knee menisci, triangular fibrocartilage and symphysis pubis. Monosodium urate (gout) crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent. Hydroxyapatite crystals are not birefringent and need alizarin red staining or electron microscopy.

A 50-year-old diabetic has rapidly worsening thigh pain out of proportion to a small abrasion, tachycardia, tense oedema extending beyond the erythema and crepitus on palpation. The best next step is:
Urgent radical surgical debridement with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
MRI of the thigh before deciding on surgery
Intravenous antibiotics with observation for 48 hours
Needle aspiration for culture and Gram stain

Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency, and delay to debridement is the main determinant of mortality. At surgery there is grey 'dishwater' fluid, non-bleeding fascia, and tissue planes that separate easily on finger dissection. Imaging and the LRINEC score are supportive only and must not delay surgery.
The main toxin responsible for the rapid myonecrosis of gas gangrene after a contaminated crush wound is:
Alpha toxin (phospholipase C) of Clostridium perfringens

Alpha toxin is a lecithinase that destroys cell membranes, causing myonecrosis, haemolysis and shock, with gas in the tissue planes on radiographs. Treatment is urgent radical debridement or amputation, high-dose penicillin with clindamycin, and hyperbaric oxygen as an adjunct where available. Panton–Valentine leukocidin is linked with severe S. aureus osteomyelitis and necrotising pneumonia.

A 3-year-old has bowed legs, short stature and dental abscesses. Serum phosphate is low, calcium normal, ALP raised, PTH normal and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D inappropriately normal, with high urinary phosphate loss. The underlying defect is:

This is X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets, the most common heritable rickets. Excess FGF23 causes renal phosphate wasting and suppresses 1α-hydroxylase. Treatment is oral phosphate with calcitriol or the anti-FGF23 antibody burosumab. Nutritional rickets has raised PTH and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and vitamin D receptor defects often come with alopecia.
Which biochemical profile is typical of nutritional vitamin D–deficiency rickets?
Normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D, low PTH, low ALP, high phosphate
Low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, raised PTH, raised ALP, low phosphate
Low ALP, normal PTH, high calcium
High calcium, high PTH, normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D

Secondary hyperparathyroidism keeps serum calcium near normal at the expense of phosphate, because PTH increases urinary phosphate loss. ALP is raised from increased osteoblast activity. A low ALP points to hypophosphatasia, and high calcium with high PTH to primary hyperparathyroidism.
The earliest radiographic change of rickets at a growing physis is:
Widening of the physis with loss of the zone of provisional calcification

Failure to mineralise the zone of provisional calcification lets hypertrophic chondrocytes pile up, so the physis widens. Metaphyseal cupping, fraying and splaying, a rachitic rosary and limb bowing follow. Fast-growing sites such as the wrist and knee show changes first. Looser zones are typical of adult osteomalacia.

An adult with diffuse bone pain, low phosphate and raised ALP has bilateral, symmetrical lucent bands running perpendicular to the cortex on the medial side of both femoral necks and in the pubic rami. These are:
Fatigue stress fractures of a runner

Looser zones are bands of unmineralised osteoid at sites of stress, typically the medial femoral neck (compression side), pubic rami, lateral border of the scapula and ribs, often bilateral and symmetrical. Atypical femoral fractures start in the lateral (tension) cortex of the subtrochanteric region or shaft.
The most specific radiographic sign of hyperparathyroidism is:
Subperiosteal resorption along the radial margins of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers

Other signs are tuft resorption, a 'salt-and-pepper' skull, resorption of the distal clavicle and brown tumours (osteitis fibrosa cystica). Brown tumours resemble giant cell tumour histologically, so check calcium and PTH in any patient with multifocal 'giant cell' lesions.

A 68-year-old has bone pain and bowing of the tibia. ALP is raised with normal calcium and phosphate, and radiographs show cortical thickening with coarse trabeculae. The treatment of choice for symptomatic disease is:
A single intravenous infusion of zoledronic acid

Zoledronic acid gives the most sustained remission of Paget's disease. Treatment is indicated for bone pain, before elective surgery on pagetic bone (to reduce bleeding) and for active disease at sites at risk of complications. Teriparatide is contraindicated because of the osteosarcoma risk.
A radiograph of the tibia shows a sharply demarcated, V-shaped lytic front advancing from one end of the bone along the diaphysis ('blade of grass' appearance). Most likely diagnosis:
Paget's disease in the lytic phase

Paget's disease starts at one end of a long bone and advances along it; the skull equivalent is osteoporosis circumscripta. Mixed and sclerotic phases follow, with cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae and bone enlargement. Sarcomatous change, most often osteosarcoma, occurs in under 1% and is suggested by new pain and lytic destruction.
The WHO densitometric definition of osteoporosis in a postmenopausal woman is:

The T-score compares BMD with the young adult mean: −1.0 to −2.5 is osteopenia and −2.5 or lower is osteoporosis, called severe or established if a fragility fracture is present. Z-scores (age-matched) are used in children and premenopausal adults. A fragility hip or vertebral fracture justifies treatment regardless of BMD.
A woman who has had denosumab for 5 years wants to stop it. What is the recommended approach to avoid rebound vertebral fractures?

Denosumab's effect is reversible: after stopping, bone turnover surges and BMD falls rapidly, with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures. Unlike bisphosphonates, it should not be given a 'drug holiday'; transition to a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid or alendronate.
A child with premature loss of deciduous teeth (with intact roots), rickets-like changes and recurrent fractures has a persistently low serum ALP. Diagnosis:

Hypophosphatasia is caused by ALPL mutations that reduce tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, so its substrates (pyrophosphate and pyridoxal-5'-phosphate) accumulate and inhibit mineralisation. Enzyme replacement with asfotase alfa is available. Bisphosphonates are avoided because they are pyrophosphate analogues and may worsen mineralisation.

An irritable 10-month-old on a restricted diet refuses to move his legs. Radiographs show generalised osteopenia, a dense metaphyseal line with a lucent band beneath it, a sclerotic ring around the epiphyses and subperiosteal haemorrhage. The underlying defect is:
Defective mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency
Defective hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen from vitamin C deficiency

Scurvy gives the white line of Frankel, the lucent Trümmerfeld zone beneath it, the Wimberger ring around the epiphysis and painful subperiosteal haemorrhages causing pseudoparalysis. Vitamin C is a cofactor for collagen hydroxylation. Lead lines are dense metaphyseal bands without these other features.
Which of the following is NOT part of Phemister's triad of tuberculous arthritis?
Gradual narrowing of the joint space
Early, marked loss of joint space with subchondral sclerosis

Cartilage is preserved for a relatively long time in tuberculous arthritis because mycobacteria lack the proteolytic enzymes of pyogenic organisms, which destroy cartilage and narrow the joint quickly. Synovial biopsy for histology, culture and molecular testing gives the highest diagnostic yield.

A 4-year-old has a painless swelling of a proximal phalanx. Radiographs show an expanded diaphysis with a thin, ballooned cortex and a cyst-like interior. In an endemic area, the most likely diagnosis is:

Spina ventosa is tuberculous infection of a short tubular bone in children, with granulation tissue expanding the bone like a balloon. It responds to antitubercular treatment. Sickle cell dactylitis (hand–foot syndrome) is acute and painful in infants, and enchondroma is uncommon at this age and rarely so expansile.
A man with a chronic osteomyelitis sinus of the tibia for 25 years notices increasing foul discharge, bleeding and heaped-up, everted wound edges. The most likely diagnosis is:

Malignant change in a long-standing sinus is usually a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma arising decades after the infection began. Biopsy the margin of the sinus. Treatment is usually amputation or wide excision, with assessment of regional lymph nodes.

A 10-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of bone pain at different sites, including the medial clavicle and distal tibial metaphysis. MRI shows multifocal marrow oedema, and biopsies and cultures are sterile. The usual first-line treatment is:

Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis) is an autoinflammatory diagnosis of exclusion in children, classically affecting the clavicle and metaphyses, and associated with palmoplantar pustulosis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease. NSAIDs are first line, with bisphosphonates or TNF inhibitors for refractory or spinal disease. Prolonged antibiotics do not help.

A patient has a painless, grossly swollen and unstable shoulder with destruction of the humeral head, and loss of pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and upper limbs in a cape distribution. The underlying cause is most likely:

Neuropathic (Charcot) joints of the upper limb are most often caused by syringomyelia, which damages the crossing spinothalamic fibres first. Diabetes typically affects the foot and ankle, and tabes dorsalis the knee, hip and spine. Arrange MRI of the cervical spine and brainstem.

A 45-year-old from an area with high groundwater fluoride has mottled teeth, a stiff spine and dense bones. Radiographs show calcification of the forearm interosseous membrane and the sacrotuberous ligaments. Diagnosis:

Chronic fluoride excess, endemic in parts of India, causes osteosclerosis and ossification of ligaments and interosseous membranes, which is a strong pointer. Ossified ligaments can compress the spinal cord and nerve roots. Dental mottling reflects exposure during childhood.
Excess osteoblast activity driven by PTH

Mutations in genes such as carbonic anhydrase II, CLCN7 and TCIRG1 impair osteoclast acidification and resorption, so bone is dense but brittle (chalk-stick fractures). Marrow crowding causes anaemia and extramedullary haematopoiesis, and foraminal narrowing causes cranial nerve palsies. The severe infantile form is treated with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, since osteoclasts derive from the monocyte–macrophage lineage.
A 40-year-old has a closed tendinous mallet finger with a 40° extensor lag at the DIP joint, 2 days after injury. Radiographs show no fracture. Best treatment:
Continuous DIP extension splinting for about 6–8 weeks, leaving the PIP joint free
Splint the DIP and PIP joints in flexion for 3 weeks

The DIP joint must stay continuously in extension; letting it flex during treatment restarts the clock. Splinting works even when presentation is delayed by several weeks. Surgery is considered for bony mallets with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx or a large articular fragment.
Which of the following is a recognised cause of swan-neck deformity of a finger?

In a chronic mallet finger, extensor force is concentrated on the central slip, hyperextending the PIP joint while the lateral bands sublux dorsally. Other causes are volar plate laxity at the PIP joint (as in rheumatoid arthritis) and intrinsic tightness. Central slip rupture causes the opposite deformity, boutonnière.
Flexor tendon zone II extends from the:
A1 pulley (distal palmar crease) to the FDS insertion
Distal edge of the carpal tunnel to the A1 pulley
Musculotendinous junction to the carpal tunnel

Zone II, once called 'no man's land', contains both FDS and FDP in a tight fibro-osseous sheath. Zone I is distal to the FDS insertion, zone III is the palm, zone IV the carpal tunnel and zone V the forearm. Modern repairs use a multistrand core suture of at least four strands with early active motion.
Which flexor pulleys are most important to preserve to prevent bowstringing of the flexor tendons?

A2 (over the proximal phalanx) and A4 (over the middle phalanx) are the largest annular pulleys and the most important biomechanically. The odd-numbered pulleys lie over joints: A1 at the MCP, A3 at the PIP and A5 at the DIP joint. A1 is released for trigger finger, and A2 rupture is a classic rock-climbing injury.
Which of the following is NOT one of Kanavel's signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis?
Fusiform swelling of the whole finger
Tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath
Tense, tender swelling confined to the fingertip pulp

Kanavel's four signs are a flexed posture, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the sheath and pain on passive extension, which is often the earliest. A tense, tender pulp is a felon. Flexor sheath infection needs urgent intravenous antibiotics and usually surgical irrigation of the sheath.
A 'horseshoe' abscess of the hand typically links the flexor sheaths of the:

The FPL sheath continues proximally as the radial bursa and the little finger sheath as the ulnar bursa. These often communicate in Parona's space, deep to the flexor tendons and superficial to pronator quadratus, so infection can spread from one to the other. The index, middle and ring finger sheaths usually end near the A1 pulley.
A man has a small wound over the third MCP joint after punching someone in the mouth. Which organism is characteristic of this injury, and what is the key management step?
Eikenella corrodens; surgical exploration and washout of the joint with antibiotics

A 'fight bite' over the MCP joint is assumed to have entered the joint, and the tendon laceration retracts away from the skin wound when the hand opens. Eikenella is sensitive to amoxicillin–clavulanate but resistant to clindamycin. Pasteurella is typical of cat and dog bites.

A man who cleans fish tanks has a slowly progressive, painless nodular swelling along the dorsum of a finger with a chronic tenosynovitis that has not responded to standard antibiotics. The likely organism and laboratory requirement are:
Mycobacterium marinum; culture at about 30–32 °C with prolonged incubation

M. marinum grows best at lower temperatures, so the laboratory must be told to incubate at about 30–32 °C, often for weeks. Tissue biopsy for histology and culture is key. Treatment is months of combination antibiotics, often with surgical debridement. Sporothrix causes lymphocutaneous nodules after rose-thorn injuries.
In carpal tunnel syndrome, sensation over the thenar eminence is usually preserved because:
The thenar skin is supplied by the radial nerve
The recurrent motor branch carries the sensory fibres
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the wrist and passes superficial to the transverse carpal ligament
The ulnar nerve supplies the thenar skin
Thenar sensory loss suggests a more proximal median nerve lesion, such as pronator syndrome. The palmar cutaneous branch is at risk if the carpal tunnel release incision is placed too far radially.
In ulnar nerve palsy, the Wartenberg sign (persistent abduction of the little finger) is caused by:
Unopposed pull of extensor digiti minimi with a weak third palmar interosseous

The radially innervated extensor digiti minimi has an abducting vector that the paralysed third palmar interosseous can no longer resist. It differs from Wartenberg syndrome, which is entrapment of the superficial radial nerve (cheiralgia paraesthetica).
A cyclist has weakness of the interossei and adductor pollicis but normal sensation of the little and ring fingers and the dorsal ulnar hand. The ulnar nerve lesion is most likely in:

Zone 1 lies proximal to the bifurcation (mixed motor and sensory loss), zone 2 surrounds the deep motor branch (pure motor) and zone 3 the superficial sensory branch (pure sensory). A cubital tunnel lesion would also reduce sensation over the dorsal ulnar hand and weaken FCU and FDP to the ring and little fingers. Causes include ganglia, hook of hamate fractures and repetitive pressure.
A patient cannot extend the fingers or thumb at the MCP joints. The wrist extends but deviates radially, and sensation is normal. The most common site of nerve compression is the:

This is posterior interosseous nerve palsy: ECRL is supplied by the radial nerve before the PIN branches, while ECU is supplied by the PIN, so the wrist deviates radially. The arcade of Frohse is the proximal edge of supinator. Struthers' ligament and the lacertus fibrosus compress the median nerve, and Osborne's ligament the ulnar nerve.

A woman has aching in the volar forearm and paraesthesia in the thumb, index and middle fingers, including the thenar eminence, worse with repetitive forearm rotation and without night symptoms. Resisted pronation reproduces the symptoms. Diagnosis:

Pronator syndrome compresses the median nerve at the elbow (lacertus fibrosus, pronator teres or FDS arch), so the palmar cutaneous branch is affected and thenar sensation is reduced. AIN syndrome is purely motor (FPL, FDP to index and middle, pronator quadratus). Nerve conduction studies are often normal.
Which Dupuytren cord most endangers the digital neurovascular bundle by displacing it towards the midline and superficially?

The spiral cord forms from the pretendinous band, spiral band, lateral digital sheet and Grayson's ligament, and wraps around the bundle, pulling it centrally, proximally and superficially. It typically causes PIP contracture. Cleland's ligaments, dorsal to the bundle, are not involved. The key cell is the myofibroblast.
In Dupuytren disease, surgical treatment is generally indicated for:
MCP flexion contracture of about 30° or more, or any PIP contracture

A positive Hueston tabletop test (the hand cannot lie flat) is a practical guide. PIP contractures correct less completely and recur more often, so they are treated earlier. Options include limited fasciectomy, needle fasciotomy, collagenase where available, and dermofasciectomy for recurrent or aggressive disease.
In de Quervain tenosynovitis, failure of steroid injection and persistent symptoms after surgical release are often due to:
A separate fibro-osseous subcompartment for EPB within the first dorsal compartment
Involvement of EPL in the third compartment

The first dorsal compartment contains APL (often several slips) and EPB, and a septum separating EPB is common. The surgeon must look for and release it. During release, protect the branches of the superficial radial nerve and release on the dorsal side to avoid volar subluxation of the tendons.
A rower has pain, swelling and crepitus on the dorsoradial forearm about 4–8 cm proximal to the wrist. Diagnosis:

Intersection syndrome occurs where the first-compartment muscles (APL and EPB) cross over the second-compartment tendons (ECRL and ECRB), proximal to the de Quervain site. It usually settles with rest, splinting and injection, with release of the second compartment for resistant cases.
Six weeks after an undisplaced distal radius fracture, a patient suddenly cannot extend the thumb IP joint. The usual reconstruction is:
Extensor indicis proprius transfer to EPL

EPL rupture after distal radius fracture is attritional or ischaemic, at Lister's tubercle in the third compartment, and is more common after undisplaced fractures. The frayed ends rarely allow direct repair, so EIP transfer is standard. It can also follow prominent dorsal screw tips after volar plating.
After a fall on the outstretched hand, the lateral wrist radiograph shows the lunate tilted dorsally with a scapholunate angle of 80°, and the PA view shows a 5 mm scapholunate gap. The pattern is:

A normal scapholunate angle is 30–60°. Scapholunate ligament disruption lets the scaphoid flex and the lunate extend with the triquetrum (DISI), with the Terry Thomas gap and cortical ring sign on the PA view. VISI goes with lunotriquetral injury. Untreated, DISI progresses to SLAC wrist.

After a high-energy wrist injury, the lateral radiograph shows the lunate rotated volarly and displaced in front of the radius ('spilled teacup'), with the capitate in line with the radius. The patient has numbness in the median nerve distribution. Diagnosis and priority:
Perilunate dislocation (Mayfield III); elective repair at 2 weeks
Lunate dislocation (Mayfield IV); urgent reduction to relieve median nerve compression

In Mayfield's progression, stage I disrupts the scapholunate ligament, II the lunocapitate joint, III the lunotriquetral ligament (perilunate dislocation), and IV the dorsal radiocarpal ligament, so the lunate dislocates volarly into the carpal tunnel. Urgent closed reduction is followed by open reduction and ligament repair.
In scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) wrist, which joint is characteristically preserved even in late stages?

Arthritis progresses from the radial styloid and scaphoid (stage I), to the whole radioscaphoid joint (II), then the capitolunate joint (III). The radiolunate joint is spared because the lunate fossa loads the lunate concentrically, which allows scaphoid excision with four-corner fusion, or proximal row carpectomy if the capitate head is preserved.
A patient has anatomical snuffbox tenderness after a fall but normal scaphoid radiographs. Which investigation is most accurate for confirming or excluding a scaphoid fracture early?
Repeat radiographs at 2 weeks as the definitive test

MRI is highly sensitive and specific and also shows other carpal or distal radius fractures. CT is an alternative when MRI is not available. Bone scans are sensitive but non-specific and need about 72 hours to become positive. Immobilise the wrist until a fracture is excluded.
In a Bennett fracture, the main deforming force displacing the thumb metacarpal shaft proximally and radially is:

The small volar-ulnar fragment stays attached to the anterior oblique (beak) ligament, while APL pulls the shaft proximally, dorsally and radially and adductor pollicis adducts it. Treatment is closed reduction and percutaneous pinning or ORIF to restore the CMC joint. A Rolando fracture is a comminuted Y- or T-shaped intra-articular fracture.
A skier has a complete rupture of the thumb MCP ulnar collateral ligament, with no firm end point on stress testing in 30° of flexion. Why is surgical repair usually advised?
The volar plate is always entrapped
The FPL tendon is usually interposed
The adductor pollicis aponeurosis often lies between the torn ligament and its insertion (Stener lesion)
A sesamoid fracture always accompanies it

In a Stener lesion the retracted ligament lies superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, so it cannot heal back to the proximal phalanx. Laxity of more than about 30–35°, or 15° more than the other side, without an end point suggests a complete tear. 'Skier's thumb' is the acute injury and 'gamekeeper's thumb' the chronic attritional form.

A child crushes a fingertip in a door. The distal phalanx is flexed, the nail plate lies on top of the eponychial fold with blood at the nail fold, and radiographs show a Salter–Harris I fracture of the distal phalanx. Appropriate management:
Treat as a closed mallet finger in an extension splint
Buddy strapping and review in 2 weeks
Treat as an open fracture: antibiotics, nail plate removal, washout, extraction of the trapped nail bed, reduction and nail bed repair

This Seymour fracture is an open physeal fracture with the germinal matrix trapped in the fracture. It looks like a mallet finger because FDP flexes the distal fragment while the extensor holds the epiphysis. If missed, it leads to osteomyelitis, physeal arrest and nail deformity.
A man with haemophilia A and end-stage haemophilic arthropathy of the knee is listed for TKA. The key perioperative measure is:
Tranexamic acid alone, without factor replacement
Factor VIII replacement to near-normal levels before surgery and through rehabilitation, planned with a haematologist, after screening for inhibitors

The knee is the joint most often affected, followed by the elbow and ankle. Factor levels must be kept up during surgery and the early rehabilitation period, and inhibitors (antibodies to factor VIII) change the replacement strategy completely. These knees are often stiff, with flexion contracture and poor bone stock.

A lateral lumbar radiograph shows dense, wafer-like calcification of multiple intervertebral discs with disc space narrowing. The patient's urine darkens on standing and the ear cartilage is bluish-black. Diagnosis:

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase. Homogentisic acid polymerises in connective tissue, causing pigmentation, multilevel disc calcification and early degeneration of large joints. Nitisinone reduces homogentisic acid production.
A young adult with Gaucher disease has bone crises, femoral head AVN and an Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femora. The enzyme deficiency is:

Glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages (Gaucher cells) that infiltrate the marrow, causing marrow expansion, infarcts, osteonecrosis and fractures. Enzyme replacement therapy or substrate reduction therapy is used. Hexosaminidase A deficiency is Tay–Sachs disease, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency Fabry disease and sphingomyelinase deficiency Niemann–Pick disease.
The final activation step of vitamin D occurs in the:
Kidney proximal tubule, by 1α-hydroxylation, stimulated by PTH and low phosphate and inhibited by FGF23
Kidney, by 24-hydroxylation, stimulated by low calcium

Cholecalciferol from skin or diet is 25-hydroxylated in the liver (serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D reflects body stores), then 1α-hydroxylated in the kidney to active calcitriol. 24-hydroxylation produces inactive metabolites and is favoured when calcitriol or FGF23 is high.

Radiographs of the first MTP joint show well-defined, 'punched-out' juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges, a soft-tissue mass and relatively preserved joint space. Most likely diagnosis:

The overhanging edge (Martel sign) results from bone remodelling around a tophus. Joint space is preserved until late, and periarticular osteopenia is absent, unlike rheumatoid arthritis. Psoriatic arthritis gives 'pencil-in-cup' erosions with new bone formation.

A farmer who drinks unpasteurised milk has low back pain and fever. Imaging shows an erosion of the anterosuperior corner of L4 with preserved vertebral height and a small paravertebral soft-tissue reaction. The most likely organism is:

Brucellar spondylitis favours the lower lumbar spine and characteristically erodes the anterosuperior end plate (Pedro Pons sign), with relatively little vertebral collapse, kyphosis or abscess formation compared with tuberculosis. Diagnosis is by serology and blood culture; treatment is a prolonged course of combination antibiotics such as doxycycline with rifampicin or an aminoglycoside.

A previously healthy 6-year-old has uncomplicated acute haematogenous osteomyelitis of the distal femur caused by meticillin-sensitive S. aureus, and is improving clinically with a falling CRP. Current evidence supports:
A short intravenous course followed by oral antibiotics, for a total of about 3–4 weeks
Six weeks of intravenous antibiotics in every case
Surgical drilling of the metaphysis in every case
Stopping antibiotics as soon as the fever settles

Randomised trials in children showed that a few days of intravenous treatment followed by high-dose oral antibiotics is as effective as prolonged intravenous therapy for uncomplicated disease. Surgery is reserved for abscesses, sequestra, failure to respond or adjacent septic arthritis.
A labourer has a painless, slowly enlarging swelling of the foot with multiple sinuses discharging grains. Why is it essential to determine whether the mycetoma is eumycotic or actinomycotic?
Eumycetoma always responds to a short course of penicillin
Actinomycetoma usually responds to prolonged antibiotic combinations, whereas eumycetoma needs long-term antifungals combined with surgery
Both are treated by primary amputation

Mycetoma is a chronic granulomatous infection after implantation of organisms through the skin, common in tropical regions. Grain colour, histology and culture distinguish fungal (eumycetoma, e.g. Madurella, often black grains) from bacterial (actinomycetoma, e.g. Nocardia, Actinomadura) disease. Bone involvement makes treatment harder.
The FRAX tool estimates a patient's:
10-year probability of hip fracture and of a major osteoporotic fracture

FRAX combines age, sex, BMI, previous fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, alcohol, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis and, optionally, femoral neck BMD. Country-specific thresholds guide treatment decisions.
Romosozumab, a monoclonal antibody against sclerostin, should be avoided in a patient with:
Myocardial infarction or stroke within the past year

Romosozumab increases bone formation and decreases resorption, giving rapid BMD gains, but trials showed a signal for cardiovascular events. It is given monthly for 12 months and must be followed by an antiresorptive drug to keep the gains. Previous fracture identifies exactly the high-risk patients it is designed for.
Which of the following amputations is the strongest indication for replantation?
Isolated index finger amputation proximal to the FDS insertion in an adult
Segmental, multilevel crush of a single finger
Thumb amputation through the proximal phalanx
Severe ring-avulsion injury of a single finger with long warm ischaemia

Strong indications are the thumb, multiple digits, partial hand, wrist or forearm amputations, any level in a child, and a single digit distal to the FDS insertion. A single digit amputated proximal to the FDS insertion in an adult often ends with a stiff finger that impairs the hand. Severe crush, multilevel injury and long warm ischaemia are relative contraindications.
During digital replantation, the structure usually repaired first is:

Bone shortening and stable fixation come first, allowing tension-free vessel and nerve repair. The usual sequence is then extensor tendons, flexor tendons, arteries, nerves and veins (some surgeons repair veins before arteries). The amputated part is wrapped in moist gauze in a sealed bag placed on ice, never directly on ice.

A 35-year-old has ulnar-sided wrist pain worse with grip and ulnar deviation. Radiographs show positive ulnar variance, and MRI shows oedema in the ulnar side of the lunate and the ulnar head. If non-operative treatment fails, the procedure that best addresses the cause is:
Darrach excision of the distal ulna

Ulnar impaction syndrome results from excessive load transfer through the ulnocarpal joint, often with a degenerative central TFCC tear. Ulnar shortening unloads the ulnocarpal joint and tightens the ulnocarpal ligaments; arthroscopic wafer resection is an alternative for small degrees of positive variance. Darrach excision is usually reserved for low-demand elderly patients.
Which part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex has the best healing potential after a tear?
The radial attachment at the sigmoid notch

The peripheral 10–40% of the TFCC is vascularised, so peripheral tears (Palmer class 1B) can be repaired arthroscopically or openly. The central disc is avascular, so central tears (1A) are debrided. A foveal detachment can cause DRUJ instability.
In Madelung deformity, the abnormal structure tethering the volar-ulnar part of the distal radial physis is:

Vickers' ligament is an abnormal thick radiolunate ligament that tethers the volar-ulnar physis, causing increased radial inclination, volar tilt and a prominent ulnar head. Madelung deformity is associated with SHOX deficiency (Léri–Weill dyschondrosteosis), and is most common in adolescent girls. Release of the ligament with physiolysis can prevent progression in the growing child.
An infant has radial longitudinal deficiency (radial club hand) with a hypoplastic thumb. Which investigation must be arranged because marrow failure may only appear later?
Chromosomal breakage test for Fanconi anaemia

Fanconi anaemia can present with radial deficiency years before aplastic anaemia appears, and early diagnosis allows planned stem cell transplantation. Other associations are TAR syndrome (thrombocytopenia with absent radius but thumbs present), Holt–Oram syndrome (cardiac septal defects) and VACTERL association.
A motorcyclist has a flail arm after a brachial plexus injury, with ptosis and miosis on the same side. This most strongly suggests:
Postganglionic rupture of C5 and C6
Preganglionic avulsion of the C8 and T1 roots

Horner syndrome reflects injury to the sympathetic fibres leaving at T1, close to the cord, so a root avulsion is likely. Other signs of preganglionic injury are scapular winging, rhomboid paralysis, a raised hemidiaphragm, pseudomeningocele on imaging, and preserved sensory nerve action potentials in an insensate limb. Avulsions cannot be repaired directly and are treated with nerve transfers.
When a patient pushes against a wall, the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall and the scapula moves towards the midline. The nerve injured is the:

Long thoracic nerve palsy paralyses serratus anterior, causing medial winging. Spinal accessory nerve palsy (trapezius) causes lateral winging with shoulder droop and is often iatrogenic after lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck. Most long thoracic nerve palsies from traction or viral neuritis recover over 1–2 years.
Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) mainly involves the origin of:

Histology shows angiofibroblastic hyperplasia, a degenerative tendinosis rather than inflammation. Most cases settle within about a year with activity modification and eccentric exercise. Steroid injections give short-term relief but higher recurrence at longer follow-up.
A painter injects paint into his index fingertip with a high-pressure spray gun. There is a tiny entry wound and only mild pain. The correct management is:
Elevation, oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
Digital block and local steroid injection
Urgent surgical exploration and thorough debridement
Observation, as the small wound indicates minimal injury

High-pressure injection injuries spread material along tissue planes far beyond the entry wound, and paints and solvents cause chemical necrosis and severe inflammation. Amputation rates are high, especially with oil-based paint and delayed treatment. Early wide debridement improves outcome.
Which clinical test is most sensitive for an acute ACL tear in an awake patient?
Anterior drawer test at 90° of flexion

The Lachman test is the most sensitive examination for ACL tear. The pivot shift is highly specific but often cannot be elicited in an awake, guarding patient. The anterior drawer at 90° is less sensitive acutely because of hamstring spasm, haemarthrosis and the posterior horn of the medial meniscus acting as a doorstop.
After ACL reconstruction, a femoral tunnel placed too far anteriorly typically causes:
A graft that is tight in flexion, limiting flexion or stretching out
A graft that is tight in extension, limiting extension
Persistent rotational instability with a good Lachman test

An anterior femoral tunnel increases graft length as the knee flexes, so the graft becomes tight in flexion. An anterior tibial tunnel causes roof impingement and loss of extension. A vertical ('high noon') femoral tunnel may control anteroposterior translation but leaves a residual pivot shift.

Four months after ACL reconstruction, a patient has lost the last 10° of extension with a painful clunk when straightening the knee. MRI shows a nodular fibrous mass anterior to the graft in the intercondylar notch. Diagnosis and treatment:

A cyclops lesion is a fibroproliferative nodule from graft or ACL stump debris that impinges in the notch in extension. Arthroscopic excision restores extension. Risk factors include an anterior tibial tunnel and failure to regain extension early after surgery.
Compared with a hamstring autograft, a bone–patellar tendon–bone autograft for ACL reconstruction has a higher rate of:
Weakness of deep knee flexion and internal rotation
Slow tendon-to-bone incorporation in the tunnels
Saphenous nerve sartorial branch injury from graft harvest
Anterior knee pain and pain on kneeling

BPTB grafts heal bone-to-bone in the tunnels within about 6 weeks, but harvest morbidity includes anterior knee and kneeling pain, and rarely patellar fracture or tendon rupture. Hamstring harvest weakens deep flexion and internal rotation, and its tendon-to-bone healing is slower. Both incisions can injure the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve.
On posterior drawer testing at 90° of flexion, the anterior tibial plateau falls behind the front of the femoral condyles (grade III). This most suggests:
Combined PCL and other ligament injury, most often the posterolateral corner
A normal finding in hyperlax patients

Normally the medial tibial plateau lies about 1 cm anterior to the medial femoral condyle. Grade I keeps the plateau anterior to the condyles, grade II brings it flush and grade III takes it behind. Isolated grade I–II PCL injuries usually do well with quadriceps-focused rehabilitation; combined injuries are usually reconstructed.
A displaced bony avulsion of the PCL from its tibial insertion is best treated by:
Early reduction and fixation through a posterior approach
Delayed PCL reconstruction with a tendon graft

Bony avulsions unite reliably when reduced and fixed with a screw or sutures, with good functional results, unlike mid-substance tears. The posteromedial approach of Burks and Schaffer uses the interval between the medial head of gastrocnemius and semimembranosus, retracting the gastrocnemius laterally to protect the popliteal vessels.
An isolated grade III MCL injury of the knee, with no cruciate or other ligament injury, is usually treated with:
Cast in full extension for 6 weeks
A hinged brace with early range of motion and weight-bearing as comfort allows

The MCL heals well because of its rich blood supply. Surgery is considered for combined injuries with persistent valgus laxity, a distal tibial avulsion with the pes anserinus trapped beneath it (a 'Stener-like' lesion), or chronic symptomatic instability. Immobilisation in extension leads to stiffness.
After a reduced knee dislocation, the distal pulses are palpable. What is the most appropriate vascular assessment?
No further assessment because palpable pulses exclude arterial injury
Ankle–brachial index, with CT angiography if it is below 0.9
Routine angiography in every case regardless of findings
Duplex ultrasound only if the foot becomes cold

The popliteal artery is tethered at the adductor hiatus and the soleus arch, so it is injured in a significant proportion of knee dislocations. Normal pulses do not exclude an intimal tear. An ABI of 0.9 or more has a high negative predictive value with serial examination, and ischaemia beyond about 6–8 hours sharply increases amputation risk.
In a patient with recurrent lateral patellar dislocation, which finding most supports adding a tibial tubercle medialising osteotomy to MPFL reconstruction?
TT–TG distance of about 20 mm or more

The TT–TG distance measures how lateral the tibial tubercle is relative to the trochlear groove on CT or MRI; normal is about 10–15 mm. A Fulkerson anteromedialisation also unloads distal and lateral patellar cartilage. Distalisation is added for significant patella alta.
The Insall–Salvati ratio (patellar tendon length divided by patellar length) indicates patella alta when it is:
Greater than 1.2 on the AP view only

It is measured on a lateral radiograph with the knee in about 30° of flexion; a ratio below 0.8 indicates patella baja. Patella alta delays engagement of the patella in the trochlea and predisposes to instability. The Caton–Deschamps index is an alternative that relates the patella to the tibial joint line.
On a true lateral knee radiograph, the line of the trochlear floor crosses the anterior outline of the femoral condyles. This is the:

The crossing sign means the trochlea becomes flat at that level. Dejour classifies trochlear dysplasia from A to D using the crossing sign, the supratrochlear spur and the double contour. A sulcus angle greater than about 145° on axial views also indicates a shallow trochlea. Severe dysplasia with high-grade instability may need trochleoplasty.
In the Watanabe classification of discoid lateral meniscus, the type most associated with 'snapping knee syndrome' in a child is the:

The Wrisberg type lacks the posterior meniscotibial (coronary) attachment, being held only by the meniscofemoral ligament of Wrisberg, so the posterior horn is hypermobile. Treatment is saucerisation with repair to stabilise the posterior horn. Asymptomatic complete or incomplete discoid menisci are left alone.
Which coronal MRI finding is most associated with a posterior root tear of the medial meniscus?
Medial meniscal body extruding more than 3 mm beyond the tibial margin
Absent bow-tie sign on two consecutive sagittal slices

A root tear disrupts hoop tension, so the meniscus extrudes and loses its load-sharing function, accelerating arthritis and subchondral insufficiency fracture. The sagittal 'ghost sign' (missing posterior horn) is also seen. Root repair is considered in patients without advanced arthritis.
The classic location of osteochondritis dissecans of the knee is the:
Lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle
Weight-bearing surface of the lateral femoral condyle

Juvenile OCD with open physes and a stable lesion usually heals with activity modification. Lesions that are unstable on MRI (a high-signal rim or fluid behind the fragment, or cysts) or loose need fixation, drilling or cartilage restoration. Wilson's test reproduces pain with internal tibial rotation as the knee extends, relieved by external rotation.
After a posterior shoulder dislocation during a seizure, the humeral head impaction defect (reverse Hill–Sachs lesion) lies:

The posterior glenoid rim impacts the anteromedial head. Posterior dislocations are easily missed on AP views (lightbulb and rim signs), so an axillary view or CT is essential. Large defects are treated with a McLaughlin procedure (subscapularis or lesser tuberosity transfer into the defect) or grafting.
In the glenoid track concept, a Hill–Sachs lesion whose interval is wider than the glenoid track is:
On-track, so Bankart repair alone is adequate
Off-track (engaging), so Bankart repair alone has a high failure rate
On-track but needs a Latarjet in every case

The glenoid track is about 83% of the intact glenoid width minus the width of glenoid bone loss. Off-track lesions engage the glenoid rim in abduction and external rotation and need remplissage with Bankart repair, or a bony procedure when glenoid bone loss is significant.
On MR arthrography after a shoulder dislocation, the inferior glenohumeral ligament has a J shape instead of the normal U-shaped axillary pouch. This indicates:

Humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament detaches the IGHL from the humeral neck. A missed HAGL is a recognised cause of failed Bankart repair. ALPSA is a medially displaced labroligamentous sleeve, GLAD a labral tear with glenoid cartilage injury, and Perthes a labral avulsion with intact but stripped periosteum.
A patient cannot hold the arm in external rotation with the shoulder abducted to 90°, and raises the elbow when bringing the hand to the mouth. The muscle that is deficient is:

This is the hornblower's sign. The external rotation lag sign with the arm at the side tests infraspinatus, the belly-press and lift-off tests test subscapularis, and the drop-arm sign suggests a large supraspinatus tear. Teres minor loss in a massive cuff tear affects decisions about tendon transfer and reverse arthroplasty.
In a chronic rotator cuff tear, which finding predicts poor tendon healing after repair?
Goutallier grade 3 or 4 fatty infiltration (as much or more fat than muscle)
Tendon retraction to the level of the greater tuberosity

Fatty infiltration is largely irreversible and predicts re-tear and poor function. A positive tangent sign on MRI (supraspinatus not crossing the line joining the coracoid and the scapular spine) indicates significant atrophy. Patte grading describes tendon retraction.
A volleyball player has isolated weakness of external rotation and infraspinatus wasting, with normal supraspinatus bulk. MRI shows a paralabral cyst. The nerve is compressed at the:

At the spinoglenoid notch the suprascapular nerve has already given off its supraspinatus branch, so only infraspinatus is affected. Compression at the suprascapular notch, beneath the transverse scapular ligament, affects both muscles. Paralabral cysts usually arise from labral tears and are treated by arthroscopic decompression and labral repair.
An overhead athlete has poorly localised posterior shoulder pain and paraesthesia over the lateral arm. MRI shows isolated atrophy of teres minor. Which structures are compressed?
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery

Quadrilateral space syndrome involves the space bounded by teres minor above, teres major below, the long head of triceps medially and the humeral shaft laterally. Symptoms worsen with abduction and external rotation, and fibrous bands are the usual cause. The triangular interval below it transmits the radial nerve and profunda brachii.
In the Rockwood classification of acromioclavicular injuries, posterior displacement of the clavicle into or through trapezius, best seen on an axillary view, is:

Type III has torn AC and coracoclavicular ligaments with 25–100% increase in CC distance, and its management is debated. Types IV (posterior), V (100–300% increase in CC distance with deltotrapezial fascia stripped) and VI (inferior, subacromial or subcoracoid) are usually treated surgically.
A 52-year-old diabetic woman has a painful, stiff shoulder with normal radiographs. Which movement is typically lost first and most markedly in adhesive capsulitis?
Passive external rotation with the arm at the side
Active abduction only, with full passive range
Forward flexion with preserved passive range
