Adhesive capsulitis causes global loss of active and passive motion, especially external rotation, from contracture of the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament. A cuff tear limits active motion with passive motion preserved. Radiographs are needed to exclude glenohumeral arthritis and a missed posterior dislocation, which also restrict external rotation.
In calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff, the most painful stage is the:

Calcium hydroxyapatite is deposited, most often in supraspinatus. In the resorptive phase the deposit becomes soft and toothpaste-like, with vascular invasion and intense pain, and may rupture into the bursa. Treatment includes NSAIDs, physiotherapy, ultrasound-guided barbotage, shock-wave therapy and arthroscopic removal for refractory cases.

A baseball pitcher has posterior shoulder pain in late cocking. Arthroscopy shows undersurface fraying of the posterosuperior cuff and a posterosuperior labral tear, and he has marked loss of internal rotation compared with the other side. First-line management is:
Posterior capsular stretching (sleeper stretch) and scapular stabilisation

Internal impingement occurs in abduction and external rotation, when the articular side of the cuff is pinched between the greater tuberosity and the posterosuperior glenoid. Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit from posterior capsular tightness is a key contributor. Most athletes improve with stretching and rehabilitation.
A pitcher has posteromedial elbow pain at ball release, and CT shows an osteophyte on the posteromedial olecranon. When excising it, what must be assessed?

In valgus extension overload, repeated valgus and extension forces drive the posteromedial olecranon into its fossa. Excessive removal of the osteophyte can unmask ulnar collateral ligament insufficiency. The anterior bundle of the UCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress at about 20–120° of flexion.
On a well-centred AP pelvic radiograph, the line of the anterior acetabular wall crosses the line of the posterior wall before reaching the lateral edge of the acetabulum. This indicates:
A cam deformity of the femoral head–neck junction

The crossover sign, the posterior wall sign and the prominent ischial spine sign indicate retroversion. Pelvic tilt must be neutral, because anterior tilt produces a false crossover sign. A cam deformity is assessed with the alpha angle on lateral views or radial MRI.
Which proximal hamstring injury is the clearest indication for early surgical repair in an active adult?
Grade 1 strain of the biceps femoris muscle belly
Partial avulsion of one tendon without retraction
Complete avulsion of all three tendons with more than 2 cm of retraction

Early repair of complete avulsions with significant retraction gives better strength and function than late repair. Delay makes mobilisation harder and allows scar to tether the nearby sciatic nerve. Most muscle-belly strains are managed with rehabilitation.
Which structures are most at risk when creating a posteromedial knee arthroscopy portal?
Saphenous nerve and great saphenous vein

The posteromedial portal is made under direct vision with transillumination, in the soft spot above the joint line behind the MCL. The posterolateral portal risks the common peroneal nerve, which lies behind biceps femoris, so that portal is placed anterior to the biceps tendon.
After a first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, the factor most strongly associated with recurrence is:
Age under 20 at the first dislocation

Young patients, especially males in contact or overhead sports, have very high recurrence rates, which supports early stabilisation in high-risk athletes. Patients over 40 dislocate again less often but more often have associated rotator cuff tears and axillary nerve injuries, so weakness after reduction in older patients needs imaging.
At revision THA, the hip centre has migrated more than 3 cm superiorly. Which finding classifies the acetabular defect as Paprosky type IIIB rather than IIIA?
An intact Köhler's line with mild ischial lysis
Disruption of Köhler's line with severe ischial lysis and loss of the teardrop (superomedial migration)
An intact rim with a contained cavitary defect

Type III defects have more than 3 cm of superior migration and an unsupportive rim. IIIA is 'up and out' with Köhler's line intact and moderate ischial lysis; IIIB is 'up and in' with Köhler's line broken, severe ischial and teardrop lysis and a strong association with pelvic discontinuity. IIIB defects usually need augments, a cup–cage or a custom triflange component.
A periprosthetic femoral fracture occurs well distal to the tip of a well-fixed THA stem. In the Vancouver classification this is type C, managed by:
Fixing the fracture independently of the prosthesis, with a plate that overlaps the stem to avoid a stress riser

Type A involves the trochanters, type B is around or just below the stem (B1 stable, B2 loose, B3 loose with poor bone) and type C is well below the stem. Because the stem is unaffected in type C, the fracture is treated on its own merits, but the construct should span the stem to avoid a gap between implants.
On an AP radiograph of a femoral stem, Gruen zone 7 corresponds to the:

The seven AP Gruen zones run from zone 1 (greater trochanter) down the lateral side (zones 2–3) to the tip (zone 4) and back up the medial side (zones 5–6) to the calcar (zone 7); zones 8–14 are on the lateral view. Acetabular radiolucencies are described in the three DeLee–Charnley zones. Calcar bone loss in zone 7 commonly reflects stress shielding or osteolysis.

Two years after shoulder arthroplasty, a patient has stiffness and mild pain, with normal inflammatory markers. Low-grade infection is suspected. Which organism is most likely, and what must the laboratory do?
Cutibacterium acnes; hold tissue cultures for about 14 days

C. acnes lives in the sebaceous glands of the shoulder skin and is the leading cause of shoulder periprosthetic infection, typically indolent with normal CRP and ESR. It grows slowly, so several tissue samples are taken and cultures are held for about 2 weeks. Male sex and revision surgery are risk factors.
The Grammont reverse shoulder arthroplasty restores elevation in a cuff-deficient shoulder mainly by:
Lateralising the centre of rotation to tension the remaining cuff
Medialising and distalising the centre of rotation, which lengthens the deltoid lever arm and tensions the deltoid
Increasing glenoid offset to reduce deltoid load

A medialised, fixed centre of rotation reduces shear forces on the glenoid baseplate, and lowering the humerus tensions the deltoid so it can elevate the arm without a functioning cuff. The trade-offs are scapular notching and weaker rotation; many modern designs add some lateralisation. A working deltoid and axillary nerve are essential.
Why is anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty avoided in a patient with glenohumeral arthritis and a massive irreparable rotator cuff tear?
Superior migration of the humeral head loads the glenoid eccentrically, causing 'rocking-horse' loosening of the glenoid component
The humeral stem cannot be cemented

Without a cuff to centre the head, the deltoid pulls the humerus upwards, so the glenoid component is loaded on its superior edge and tilts and loosens. Reverse shoulder arthroplasty is the standard option for cuff tear arthropathy, while anatomic TSA needs an intact or reparable cuff.
Which patient is the best candidate for metal-on-metal hip resurfacing?
A 50-year-old woman with a small femoral head
A 45-year-old active man with a large femoral head and good bone stock
A 55-year-old man with chronic kidney disease

Results are best in young, active men with large femoral heads and good bone. Women, small component sizes, osteoporosis, large femoral head cysts and renal impairment (which impairs clearance of metal ions) increase the risks of failure, femoral neck fracture and adverse reaction to metal debris.
In revision THA, an extended trochanteric osteotomy is mainly used to:
Give safe access for removing a well-fixed stem or cement and allow correction of proximal femoral deformity

A controlled osteotomy of the lateral part of the proximal femur is lifted as a single fragment with gluteus medius and vastus lateralis attached. Its length is planned so that enough intact diaphysis remains for distal fixation of the revision stem. It is closed with cerclage wires or cables and has a high union rate.
Charnley chose a small (22.225 mm) femoral head for his low-friction arthroplasty mainly to:
Lower the frictional torque transmitted to the cup–cement interface
Reduce linear wear of the polyethylene

A small head has a short moment arm for friction, so less torque loosens the cemented cup. The penalties are higher linear penetration of the polyethylene, a smaller head–neck ratio and a shorter jump distance, so instability is more likely than with larger heads.
With a conventional polyethylene liner and the same linear penetration rate, increasing femoral head size from 28 mm to 36 mm will:

Volumetric wear is roughly proportional to the square of the head radius multiplied by linear wear, so larger heads generate a greater volume of debris and more osteolysis. Highly crosslinked polyethylene has reduced wear enough that larger heads, which improve stability, are now widely used.
Which stem feature most increases proximal femoral stress shielding after uncemented THA?
A large-diameter, extensively porous-coated cobalt–chromium stem

Engh showed that stiffer stems (larger diameter, stiffer metal) and extensive distal coating transfer load distally and bypass the proximal femur, causing calcar and proximal bone loss. Poor preoperative bone quality also increases it. Stress shielding is mainly a radiographic finding and rarely causes loosening, but it complicates revision.
Which radiographic finding indicates stable bone ingrowth into an uncemented porous-coated femoral stem?
A radiolucent line around the entire porous surface
Endosteal 'spot welds' at the porous coating with no reactive lines around the porous section
A distal pedestal with progressive migration of the stem

Engh's signs of ingrowth include spot welds of new bone bridging to the porous surface, absence of reactive lines next to the coating and proximal stress shielding. Fibrous (unstable) fixation shows parallel reactive lines around the porous section, progressive subsidence, a distal pedestal and bead shedding.
On the immediate postoperative radiograph of a cemented femoral stem, Barrack grade A cementing means:
Complete filling of the canal with a 'white-out' at the cement–bone interface
Slight radiolucency at the cement–bone interface
Radiolucency over 50–99% of the interface or a defective mantle
Complete radiolucency or no cement below the stem tip

Barrack grades A and B are good cementing; grade C (radiolucency over 50–99% or a thin or incomplete mantle) and grade D (100% radiolucency or no cement beyond the tip) are linked to earlier aseptic loosening. A continuous mantle of about 2 mm or more around the stem is the aim.
Notching of the anterior femoral cortex during TKA matters mainly because it:
Increases the risk of a supracondylar periprosthetic femoral fracture
Prevents use of a posterior-stabilised design

A notch creates a stress riser and reduces the bending and torsional strength of the distal femur, especially in osteoporotic bone. It arises from an undersized or posteriorly placed femoral component or an overly deep anterior cut. Anterior referencing systems and careful sizing help avoid it.
In revision TKA, failing to augment distal femoral bone loss and filling the extension gap with a thick insert raises the joint line. The typical consequence is:
Patella baja with mid-flexion instability and poor function

Joint line elevation lowers the patella relative to the joint (pseudo-patella baja), alters collateral ligament kinematics and causes mid-flexion instability and anterior knee pain. Restore the joint line with distal femoral augments, using landmarks such as the epicondyles, the fibular head and the old meniscal scar.
A patient with a posterior-stabilised TKA has the femoral cam dislocate over the tibial post. This most often occurs:
In full extension with a tight extension gap
In deep flexion, when the flexion gap is loose relative to the extension gap
During stair descent with a tight flexion gap

A loose flexion gap, from an undersized femoral component or excessive posterior condylar resection, lets the femur ride over the post in flexion, especially with varus or valgus stress and rotation. It is treated by closed reduction and revision to balance the gaps, sometimes with a more constrained insert.
In balancing a valgus knee during TKA, which lateral structure is tight mainly in flexion?

The iliotibial band and posterolateral capsule are tight mainly in extension, the popliteus mainly in flexion, and the lateral collateral ligament affects both. Releases are performed in a stepwise fashion, guided by whether the knee is tight laterally in flexion, extension or both.
During TKA, the flexion gap is balanced but the knee will not fully extend with the trial components (tight extension gap). Most appropriate correction:
Resect more distal femur, or release the posterior capsule and remove posterior osteophytes

A problem in extension only is corrected on the distal femur or at the posterior capsule. Changing the insert or tibial cut affects both gaps, and downsizing the femur affects only the flexion gap. Posterior osteophytes tent the capsule and should be removed first.
Compared with lateral closing-wedge high tibial osteotomy, medial opening-wedge HTO tends to:
Decrease the posterior tibial slope and cause patella alta
Increase the posterior tibial slope and lower the patella (patella baja)

Opening the wedge equally from front to back tilts the plateau and increases the slope, so the gap should be narrower anteriorly than posteriorly; distal advancement of the tubercle lowers the patella. Closing-wedge HTO reduces the slope, needs a fibular osteotomy or proximal tibiofibular release, risks the peroneal nerve and slightly shortens the limb.
In HTO for varus medial compartment arthritis, the corrected mechanical axis is commonly aimed through a point about what percentage of the tibial plateau width from its medial edge?

Fujisawa's point, at about 62% of the width (just lateral to the lateral tibial spine), gives mild valgus overcorrection that unloads the medial compartment. Too much correction overloads the lateral compartment and causes a cosmetically unacceptable valgus.
Which of the following is a contraindication to high tibial osteotomy?
A 45-year-old labourer with isolated medial compartment arthritis

Inflammatory arthritis affects all compartments, so redirecting load does not help. Other contraindications include significant lateral or patellofemoral disease, flexion contracture over about 10–15°, flexion under about 90° and marked instability; smoking and obesity reduce success. Young, active patients with isolated medial disease are ideal.
At revision for a fractured ceramic femoral head, which bearing should be avoided?
A ceramic head with a titanium sleeve on a new ceramic liner
A ceramic head with a titanium sleeve on a new highly crosslinked polyethylene liner
A cobalt–chromium head on a new polyethylene liner
A ceramic head with a titanium sleeve after exchange of both components

Ceramic fragments left in the joint embed in polyethylene and cause catastrophic third-body wear of a metal head, with metallosis and early failure. Revision involves thorough synovectomy, exchanging the liner and using a new ceramic head with a titanium sleeve to sit on the damaged trunnion.
The Exeter femoral stem (polished, collarless, double-tapered) achieves stable cemented fixation by:
Bonding firmly to the cement as a composite beam
Taper-slip: small controlled subsidence within the cement mantle that loads the cement in compression
A collar transferring load to the calcar

The polished taper behaves like a wedge, and slight subsidence through viscoelastic creep of the cement generates radial compressive stresses and hoop stresses that the cement tolerates well. Composite-beam (shape-closed) stems are roughened and rely on a strong cement–stem bond; when they debond they generate abrasive debris.
During TKA through a medial parapatellar arthrotomy, an additional lateral retinacular release endangers which vessel, increasing the risk of patellar osteonecrosis?

The arthrotomy divides the medial genicular supply and fat pad excision damages the inferior supply, so the superior lateral geniculate artery may be the patella's main remaining source. Preserving it during lateral release reduces the risk of osteonecrosis and patellar fracture.
A patient with several old longitudinal scars over the knee needs TKA. Which incision is generally preferred?
A new midline incision between the scars, regardless of skin bridge width
The most lateral usable longitudinal scar

The skin's blood supply comes mainly from the medial side through a plexus just above the deep fascia, so using the most lateral scar avoids leaving an ischaemic lateral flap. Keep wide skin bridges, raise full-thickness flaps without undermining, and cross old transverse scars at a right angle.
In adults, the most common primary malignant tumour arising in bone is:

Myeloma, a plasma cell neoplasm of the marrow, is the most common primary bone malignancy, typically after 50 years. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone sarcoma, mostly in adolescents, and chondrosarcoma predominates among sarcomas of older adults. Metastases are far more common than any primary bone tumour.
Before limb-salvage surgery for a distal femoral osteosarcoma, MRI of the entire femur is obtained mainly to:
Detect skip metastases in the same bone

Skip lesions are separate tumour foci in the same bone or across the adjacent joint. They are uncommon but worsen prognosis and change the level of resection. Staging also includes chest CT and a bone scan or PET-CT.
A 15-year-old has osteosarcoma. His mother had breast cancer at 30 and his brother a brain tumour. The most likely germline mutation is in:

Li–Fraumeni syndrome (TP53) causes sarcomas, early breast cancer, brain tumours, adrenocortical carcinoma and leukaemia. Hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1) also predisposes to osteosarcoma, particularly after radiotherapy. EXT1 mutations cause multiple hereditary exostoses, and APC mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis with osteomas and desmoids in Gardner syndrome.

A 17-year-old has a surface lesion on the tibial diaphysis with saucerisation of the cortex, perpendicular 'hair-on-end' periosteal spiculation and a predominantly chondroblastic histology. Most likely diagnosis:

Periosteal osteosarcoma is an intermediate-grade surface tumour of the tibial or femoral diaphysis in adolescents and is treated by wide resection. Parosteal osteosarcoma is low grade, densely ossified and typical of the posterior distal femur. A periosteal chondroma gives a well-defined saucerised defect with buttressing but no spiculated reaction.
Biopsy of a permeative femoral diaphyseal lesion in a 12-year-old shows a small round blue cell tumour with strong membranous CD99 staining. Together with an EWSR1 rearrangement, this confirms:

CD99 is sensitive but not specific for Ewing sarcoma, as it also stains lymphoblastic lymphoma and other tumours, so molecular confirmation of an EWSR1 fusion (most often with FLI1) is standard; NKX2.2 is a supportive nuclear marker. Neuroblastoma metastases occur in younger children and raise urinary catecholamines.
A 16-year-old has dull back pain and a painful scoliosis. CT shows a 3 cm expansile, partly mineralised lesion of the L2 lamina and pedicle, and NSAIDs help little. Most likely diagnosis:

Osteoblastoma is larger than about 2 cm, favours the posterior elements of the spine, responds poorly to NSAIDs and can be locally aggressive, so it is treated by curettage or en bloc excision. Osteoid osteoma is smaller and NSAID-responsive; both can cause painful scoliosis with the lesion on the concave side. Chordoma is a midline sacral or clival tumour of older adults.

A 20-year-old has an eccentric, lobulated lytic lesion with a sclerotic, scalloped margin in the proximal tibial metaphysis. Biopsy shows lobules of stellate cells in a chondroid and myxoid matrix. Diagnosis:

Chondromyxoid fibroma is a rare benign cartilage tumour of young adults, most often in the proximal tibia, and carries GRM1 rearrangements. It is treated by curettage and grafting and can recur. Chondroblastoma is epiphyseal, and enchondromas are central with chondroid calcification.
A child has multiple non-ossifying fibromas of the long bones and café-au-lait spots. This combination is called:

Non-ossifying fibromas are eccentric, cortically based metaphyseal lesions with a scalloped sclerotic rim that usually heal spontaneously by ossifying at skeletal maturity; large lesions involving more than about half the diameter risk fracture. Many patients with Jaffe–Campanacci syndrome have NF1 mutations. Mazabraud syndrome is fibrous dysplasia with intramuscular myxomas.
A 25-year-old has a progressive varus 'shepherd's crook' deformity of the proximal femur. Radiographs show an expansile intramedullary lesion with a ground-glass matrix. Diagnosis:

Fibrous dysplasia (activating GNAS mutation) replaces bone with fibrous tissue and woven bone trabeculae ('Chinese letters') lacking osteoblastic rimming. Symptomatic proximal femoral lesions are best treated with intramedullary fixation, because curettage and cancellous graft alone tend to be resorbed. Bisphosphonates can help bone pain.
Immunostaining for which mutant protein helps distinguish giant cell tumour of bone from other giant cell–rich lesions?

Most GCTs carry an H3F3A G34W mutation in the neoplastic stromal cells. Chondroblastoma carries H3F3B K36M, aneurysmal bone cyst has USP6 rearrangements and enchondromas have IDH1 or IDH2 mutations. Brown tumours lack these mutations and are excluded with calcium and PTH.
A patient treated for giant cell tumour of the distal radius later develops lung nodules with the same benign histology as the primary. The best description is:
Benign pulmonary implants ('benign metastasising' GCT) that often behave indolently

A small percentage of GCTs produce lung nodules, more often after local recurrence and in the distal radius. They are histologically benign, often grow slowly or stabilise, and are managed by observation, resection or denosumab, with good survival. True malignant GCT is rare.
Histology of a destructive femoral lesion in a 65-year-old shows low-grade cartilage abruptly adjacent to a high-grade non-cartilaginous sarcoma. Diagnosis and prognosis:

Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma is bimorphic, and radiographs may show a calcified cartilage lesion with an aggressive lytic component. Survival is poor despite wide resection, and the benefit of chemotherapy is uncertain. Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma consists of small round cells with islands of cartilage and affects younger patients.
A 28-year-old has a slowly growing, painful soft-tissue mass near the knee with small calcifications on radiographs. Molecular testing shows an SS18–SSX fusion. Diagnosis:

Synovial sarcoma, t(X;18), occurs in young adults close to but rarely inside joints, and may grow slowly enough to be mistaken for a benign lesion. Calcification is seen in about a third. Treatment is wide excision with radiotherapy; it is relatively chemosensitive and can spread to lymph nodes.
A 60-year-old has a large, deep thigh mass that is mostly fat on MRI but contains thick septa and nodular non-fatty areas. Which test best distinguishes atypical lipomatous tumour from a lipoma?

Atypical lipomatous tumour (well-differentiated liposarcoma) has amplification of MDM2 and CDK4 on chromosome 12q. In the limbs it is treated by marginal excision, recurs locally and rarely dedifferentiates or metastasises; in the retroperitoneum the same tumour behaves more aggressively.
Which primary tumour most typically produces purely osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases in men?

Prostate cancer metastases are classically sclerotic, mediated partly by endothelin-1 driving osteoblast activity; breast cancer is often mixed. Renal cell and thyroid metastases are purely lytic and highly vascular, so they may be cold on bone scan and bleed heavily at surgery.
A 68-year-old with metastatic breast cancer has a pathological fracture of the femoral shaft and an expected survival of many months. The best management is:
A plate spanning only the fracture
A short antegrade nail with no further treatment
A long cephalomedullary nail protecting the femoral neck and whole femur, followed by radiotherapy to the operative field

Metastatic lesions are often multiple and pathological fractures heal poorly, so fixation should protect the whole bone and allow immediate weight-bearing, often with cement augmentation. Postoperative radiotherapy reduces local progression and implant failure. Lesions of the femoral head or neck are better treated by arthroplasty.
A patient with myeloma becomes confused and dehydrated, with a corrected calcium of 3.6 mmol/L. Initial treatment is:
Intravenous normal saline rehydration followed by an intravenous bisphosphonate

Rehydration restores volume and promotes renal calcium excretion, and zoledronic acid or pamidronate lowers calcium over 2–4 days. Calcitonin acts quickly but briefly, and denosumab is used when bisphosphonates fail or kidney function is poor. Loop diuretics are only used after rehydration, and thiazides raise calcium.
Which criterion is part of the definition of a radiation-associated bone sarcoma?
It arises outside the radiation field
It has the same histology as the original tumour
It appears within 6 months of radiotherapy
It arises within the irradiated field after a latent period of several years and differs histologically from the original lesion

Cahan's criteria require the sarcoma to arise in the field in previously normal bone, after a latent period of years, with different histology. Osteosarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma are the most common types, and the prognosis is poorer than for primary sarcomas of the same type.
A lytic lesion with a permeative pattern (many small holes and a wide, indistinct zone of transition) in a child's diaphysis most suggests:
A slow-growing benign lesion such as a non-ossifying fibroma
A rapidly growing, aggressive process such as Ewing sarcoma, lymphoma or osteomyelitis

In the Lodwick system, a geographic lesion with a sclerotic margin (IA) is the slowest growing, a moth-eaten pattern is more aggressive and a permeative pattern the most aggressive. The width of the zone of transition is one of the most useful features for judging how aggressive a bone lesion is.
A unicameral (simple) bone cyst is described as 'active' when it:
Lies within about 1 cm of the physis, with higher recurrence after treatment

Active cysts abut the physis, occur in younger children and recur more often after treatment, which also risks damaging the growth plate. Latent cysts have moved away from the physis with growth. Fluid–fluid levels are typical of aneurysmal bone cyst, although they can appear in a simple cyst after fracture.

A 50-year-old has a permeative lesion of the femoral diaphysis with extensive marrow replacement and a large soft-tissue mass on MRI but little cortical destruction. Biopsy shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The mainstay of treatment is:
Systemic chemoimmunotherapy, often combined with radiotherapy

Primary lymphoma of bone is usually diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and has a relatively good prognosis with R-CHOP-based chemotherapy, with or without radiotherapy. Surgery is reserved for biopsy and for fixing actual or impending pathological fractures.

A 55-year-old has a single lytic lesion of T10 confirmed as a plasmacytoma, with no other lesions on whole-body imaging, a normal marrow biopsy and no end-organ damage. Treatment of choice and main long-term concern:

Solitary bone plasmacytoma is highly radiosensitive and local radiotherapy is the standard treatment. A large proportion progress to multiple myeloma over the following years, so long-term monitoring is needed. Surgery is added for instability or cord compression.
A 30-year-old woman has a firm, deep thigh mass. Biopsy shows desmoid-type fibromatosis with a CTNNB1 mutation. For an asymptomatic, stable tumour, the usual initial management is:

Desmoid tumours are locally aggressive but do not metastasise, and many stabilise or regress spontaneously, while surgery has high recurrence rates. Progressive or symptomatic tumours are treated with systemic therapy (such as tyrosine kinase or gamma-secretase inhibitors), radiotherapy or surgery in selected cases. APC mutations (Gardner syndrome) are linked to intra-abdominal desmoids.

A 70-year-old manual worker has a firm mass beneath the inferior angle of the scapula that becomes prominent when the arm is flexed forwards. MRI shows a lens-shaped mass of fibrous tissue interlaced with fat between the chest wall and scapula. Diagnosis:

Elastofibroma dorsi is a benign pseudotumour of abnormal elastic fibres, often bilateral, in older people who do repetitive shoulder work. The location and MRI appearance are characteristic, so biopsy is often unnecessary. It is observed or excised if symptomatic.

MRI of a mass along the tibial nerve shows a well-encapsulated fusiform lesion lying eccentric to the nerve, with a T2 'target sign'. Biopsy confirms a schwannoma. At surgery the lesion can usually be:
Removed only by resecting the nerve segment with cable grafting
Shelled out from the nerve, preserving the fascicles
Left alone because it always becomes malignant

Schwannomas are encapsulated and displace the fascicles, so careful enucleation preserves nerve function. Neurofibromas grow among the fascicles, are often central or plexiform (especially in NF1) and carry a risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour. Both can show a target sign and a positive Tinel sign over the mass.
A young manual labourer with a painful, post-traumatic hip is having a hip arthrodesis. The recommended position is:
Neutral flexion, 20° abduction and 20° internal rotation
10° extension, neutral adduction and 30° external rotation

This position allows sitting and walking with the least strain on adjacent joints. Abduction causes pelvic obliquity and back pain, and malposition speeds degeneration of the lumbar spine, ipsilateral knee and contralateral hip. Preserving the abductors makes later conversion to THA possible.
For bone ingrowth into a porous-coated implant, the optimal pore size is about:

Pores of roughly 50–400 µm allow bone to grow in, with porosity of about 30–40% or more and gaps between implant and bone under about 50 µm. Ingrowth also needs intimate contact and initial stability; much smaller pores allow only fibrous ingrowth, and much larger pores weaken the coating.
Above about what level of micromotion at the implant–bone interface does an uncemented implant tend to become fixed by fibrous tissue rather than bone?
Micromotion does not matter if the implant is hydroxyapatite-coated

Micromotion under about 20–50 µm allows bone ingrowth, while motion of about 150 µm or more leads to a fibrous interface and unstable fixation. This is why press-fit and initial mechanical stability are essential, whatever the surface coating.
For isolated lateral compartment arthritis, why is a fixed-bearing unicompartmental knee arthroplasty usually preferred over a mobile-bearing design?
The lateral tibial plateau is too small for a mobile bearing
Fixed bearings produce less polyethylene wear in the lateral compartment
The lateral compartment is lax in flexion, so mobile bearings have a high dislocation rate
Mobile bearings cannot be cemented laterally

The lateral collateral ligament and lateral structures allow much more movement in flexion than the medial side, so a mobile bearing can spin out or dislocate. Domed mobile-bearing designs reduced but did not remove this problem, so fixed-bearing implants are generally used for lateral UKA.
Which finding is an absolute contraindication to reverse shoulder arthroplasty for cuff tear arthropathy?
Permanent axillary nerve palsy with a non-functioning deltoid

A reverse prosthesis relies entirely on the deltoid to elevate the arm, so a deltoid without function leaves an unstable, useless shoulder. Other contraindications include active infection and inadequate glenoid bone stock for baseplate fixation. Age, massive cuff tears and pseudoparalysis are typical indications.
Scapular notching after reverse shoulder arthroplasty is caused by impingement of the humeral component on the inferior scapular neck in adduction. It is reduced by:
Placing the baseplate high on the glenoid with superior tilt
Placing the baseplate low on the glenoid, with an inferiorly offset or lateralised glenosphere
Using a smaller glenosphere placed centrally

Inferior positioning, inferior tilt, larger or eccentric glenospheres, glenoid lateralisation and a lower neck–shaft angle all increase the clearance between the humeral cup and the scapular neck. Notching is common with the original medialised Grammont design and can progress to polyethylene wear and osteolysis.
A 45-year-old has a high (Crowe IV) developmental dislocation of the hip and needs THA. The usual technique is to:
Place the cup at the true acetabulum and add a subtrochanteric femoral shortening osteotomy
Place the cup in the false acetabulum
Lengthen the limb by 6 cm or more without osteotomy

Crowe grades proximal migration of the femoral head as a percentage of femoral head height: I under 50%, II 50–75%, III 75–100% and IV over 100%. Placing the cup at the anatomical hip centre restores biomechanics, and shortening the femur prevents sciatic nerve stretch and allows reduction. A small, straight or modular stem suits the narrow, anteverted femur.
In revision TKA there is complete loss of the medial collateral ligament and a large flexion–extension gap mismatch. The appropriate level of constraint is a:

A constrained condylar (varus–valgus constrained) design suits partial collateral insufficiency with gaps that can be balanced. Global instability, complete collateral loss or a gap mismatch that cannot be corrected needs a hinge. Highly constrained implants transfer more stress to fixation, so stems are used.
A commonly used landmark for setting rotational alignment of the tibial component in TKA is:
The posterior border of the tibial plateau
The medial third of the tibial tubercle
The lateral border of the tibial tubercle

Aligning the tibial tray towards the junction of the medial and middle thirds of the tubercle (or Akagi's line, from the PCL attachment to the medial border of the patellar tendon) avoids internal rotation. Internal rotation of the tibial component causes patellar maltracking and pain; the posterior plateau border is unreliable because of its asymmetry.
During insertion of an uncemented femoral stem, an undisplaced crack appears in the calcar. The best management is to:
Ignore it and allow full weight-bearing
Remove the stem, place a cerclage wire or cable around the femur below the crack, and reinsert the stem

Calcar cracks are common with press-fit stems, especially in patients with poor bone. If left, the crack can propagate and the stem can subside. A cerclage restores hoop stresses so the stem can be reseated with stable fixation; distal propagation needs a longer stem.
After THA through the direct anterior approach, the nerve most commonly injured is the:

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve runs near the interval between tensor fasciae latae and sartorius and is injured in a substantial proportion of patients, causing numbness or meralgia paraesthetica over the lateral thigh. Most symptoms improve with time. Placing the incision lateral, over the tensor muscle, reduces the risk.
A woman has exquisite pinpoint pain under her fingernail, worse in the cold. Pain is reproduced by pressing a pinhead on one spot and relieved after inflating a tourniquet on the arm. Diagnosis:

The triad of pain, cold intolerance and point tenderness (Love's pin test) with relief after a tourniquet (Hildreth's test) is typical. MRI shows a small T2-bright enhancing lesion, and there may be bone erosion of the distal phalanx. Complete excision through the nail bed is curative.
A child receiving high-dose methotrexate for osteosarcoma needs which accompanying measures to prevent toxicity?
Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue with hydration and urinary alkalinisation

Leucovorin bypasses the folate block in normal cells, and hydration with alkalinisation prevents methotrexate precipitation in the kidney; serum levels are monitored. Mesna protects the bladder from ifosfamide, and dexrazoxane is used to reduce doxorubicin cardiotoxicity.
Which toxicity of cisplatin, part of standard osteosarcoma chemotherapy, needs monitoring with serial audiometry?

Cisplatin causes high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, nephrotoxicity with magnesium wasting, and neuropathy. Doxorubicin causes dose-dependent cardiomyopathy, ifosfamide haemorrhagic cystitis, and bleomycin pulmonary fibrosis.
For conventional chondrosarcoma of bone, the most important predictor of metastasis and survival is:

Grade 1 tumours of the long bones (atypical cartilaginous tumours) rarely metastasise, while grade 3 tumours metastasise frequently. Adequate surgical margins also matter for local control, since chondrosarcoma responds poorly to chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
A 65-year-old has a destructive lytic lesion of a distal phalanx of the hand. Which primary tumour most often causes such acral (distal to the elbow or knee) metastases?

Metastases to the hands and feet are rare, and lung cancer is the most common source. They can mimic infection, so biopsy any destructive lesion of a digit in an older patient. Acral metastases usually indicate widespread disease and a poor prognosis.

A young adult has a rapidly growing bony mass on the surface of a proximal phalanx. Radiographs show a mineralised mass attached to the cortex without continuity of the cortex or medullary canal with the host bone. Most likely diagnosis:

The Nora lesion is a benign surface proliferation in the hands and feet with a bizarre but benign histology that can be mistaken for sarcoma. Unlike an osteochondroma, it has no corticomedullary continuity. It is excised, but recurs often.
A 30-year-old has a slowly growing mass attached to the tendons near the ankle. Biopsy shows a tumour positive for S-100 and HMB-45 with an EWSR1–ATF1 fusion. Diagnosis:
Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath

Clear cell sarcoma ('melanoma of soft parts') arises from tendons and aponeuroses, often in the foot and ankle of young adults. It shares melanocytic markers with melanoma but carries the EWSR1–ATF1 fusion and has no skin primary. It spreads to lymph nodes and is treated with wide excision.
The most common soft-tissue sarcoma of childhood is:

Rhabdomyosarcoma is mainly a tumour of young children, with embryonal and alveolar subtypes; alveolar tumours carry PAX3- or PAX7–FOXO1 fusions and have a worse prognosis. Treatment is multimodal, with chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy.

An incidental 1 cm sclerotic focus in the femoral neck has a 'brush border' of radiating bony spicules blending with the surrounding trabeculae, and shows little or no uptake on bone scan. Most likely diagnosis:

Bone islands are foci of compact bone within cancellous bone and are usually stable. Thorny margins, low attenuation on CT compared with metastases and lack of marked uptake help distinguish them. Lesions that are large, growing or hot on bone scan need further work-up.
In Ewing sarcoma, the strongest adverse prognostic factor is:

Metastases at presentation, especially to bone or marrow rather than the lungs alone, have the greatest impact. Other adverse factors are a large tumour volume, pelvic location, older age and a poor histological response to chemotherapy. Local control uses surgery, radiotherapy or both.
A closed tibial fracture has subcutaneous degloving, extensive muscle crush and an established compartment syndrome. Tscherne grade:

Tscherne grades closed fractures by soft-tissue injury: grade 0 negligible, grade 1 superficial abrasion or contusion from within, grade 2 deep contaminated abrasion with local skin or muscle contusion, and grade 3 extensive contusion or crush, degloving, muscle destruction, compartment syndrome or major vascular injury. Higher grades predict wound complications and infection.
Which of the following is NOT a component of the Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS)?

MESS scores skeletal and soft-tissue injury, limb ischaemia (doubled after more than 6 hours), shock and age; scores of 7 or more were associated with amputation. The LEAP study showed that absent plantar sensation at presentation did not predict a poor outcome after limb salvage, and no score should decide amputation alone.
According to BOAST guidance on open fractures, a fracture grossly contaminated with marine, agricultural or sewage material should be debrided:

Other high-energy open fractures are debrided within 12 hours and low-energy ones within 24 hours, by senior orthopaedic and plastic surgeons together. Definitive soft-tissue cover should be achieved within 72 hours if it cannot be done at the first debridement.
In a subtrochanteric femoral fracture, the proximal fragment is typically displaced into:

Iliopsoas flexes the fragment, gluteus medius and minimus abduct it and the short external rotators rotate it externally, while the adductors pull the shaft medially. Reduction aids and a correct, often slightly medial, trochanteric entry point are needed to avoid nailing the fracture in varus and flexion.
Rüedi and Allgöwer's four classical principles of pilon fracture fixation, in order, are:
Buttress the medial tibia, graft, reconstruct the joint, then fix the fibula
Restore fibular length, reconstruct the articular surface, bone graft the metaphyseal defect, then buttress the medial tibia
Reconstruct the joint, fix the fibula, apply an external fixator, then graft
Fix the fibula and treat the tibia in a cast

Fixing the fibula first restores length and helps reduce the lateral (Chaput) fragment, then the joint is rebuilt, the metaphyseal void grafted and the tibia buttressed. Modern practice adds staged management with temporary spanning external fixation until the soft tissues recover.
A pelvic injury from a side impact shows horizontally oriented superior and inferior pubic rami fractures with an ipsilateral impaction (buckle) fracture of the anterior sacrum. Young–Burgess type:
Lateral compression type II with a crescent fracture

LC injuries rotate the hemipelvis internally, producing horizontal or coronal rami fractures and sacral impaction; LC I is usually stable. LC II adds a posterior iliac crescent fracture or posterior SI disruption, and LC III adds an open-book injury of the other side ('windswept pelvis'). APC injuries have vertical rami fractures or symphyseal diastasis.
In a pelvic fracture, an avulsion fracture of the L5 transverse process suggests:

The iliolumbar ligament attaches the L5 transverse process to the iliac crest, so its avulsion implies a vertically unstable posterior ring injury such as vertical shear. Other signs of vertical instability include cranial displacement of the hemipelvis and posterior SI gapping. Vertical shear injuries need skeletal traction and posterior fixation.
A pelvic binder for a suspected unstable pelvic ring injury should be centred over the:

Compression at the level of the trochanters closes the pelvic ring most effectively; binders placed over the iliac crests are less effective and can worsen some injuries. Pressure sores can develop if binders are left on for long periods, so definitive stabilisation should follow early.
In a haemodynamically unstable patient with a pelvic ring fracture, most of the bleeding usually comes from:
The presacral venous plexus and the cancellous fracture surfaces

Venous and bony bleeding responds to pelvic stabilisation and pre-peritoneal packing. Arterial bleeding occurs in a minority and is treated by angioembolisation; the superior gluteal artery is the most common arterial source, especially with posterior ring injuries. Always exclude other sources of bleeding.
The 'corona mortis', at risk in the ilioinguinal and intrapelvic (Stoppa) approaches, is a vascular connection between the:
Obturator vessels and the external iliac or inferior epigastric vessels

This anastomosis crosses the superior pubic ramus about 5–7 cm from the symphysis. Either an arterial or venous connection is common, and if cut it retracts into the obturator foramen and bleeds heavily, so it should be identified and ligated.
Using Matta's roof arc angles, an acetabular fracture may be treated non-operatively if the fracture line spares the weight-bearing dome, shown by roof arc angles of:
More than 45° on the AP and both Judet views
Less than 20° on the AP view only
Any value, as long as the femoral head is congruent on traction
More than 10° on the obturator oblique view only

The roof arc angle is measured between a vertical line through the centre of the femoral head and a line to where the fracture enters the joint. Angles over 45° on all three views indicate an intact dome, provided the head stays congruent with the roof out of traction. Both-column fractures with secondary congruence can also be managed without surgery in selected patients.
Using the Denis classification of sacral fractures, which zone carries the highest rate of neurological injury?
Zone I, lateral to the foramina
Zone III, medial to the foramina involving the central canal

Zone I injuries rarely cause deficit (occasionally L5 root), zone II injuries commonly cause sacral root injuries, and zone III injuries affect around half of patients, often with bowel, bladder and sexual dysfunction. Transverse zone III fractures and U-shaped fractures (spinopelvic dissociation) are particularly associated with deficits.

A 78-year-old independent woman has a displaced four-part proximal humerus fracture with tuberosity comminution and an intact rotator cuff before injury. If surgery is chosen, which option gives the most predictable function?
Intramedullary nail with suture tension band

Hemiarthroplasty depends on anatomical tuberosity healing, which often fails in older patients and leaves poor elevation. Reverse arthroplasty uses the deltoid, so function is more reliable even if the tuberosities do not heal. Non-operative treatment remains a reasonable option for many low-demand patients.
A humeral shaft fracture treated in a functional brace is generally acceptable if alignment is within:
20° anterior angulation, 30° varus and 3 cm shortening
5° in any plane and no shortening

The shoulder and elbow's wide range of motion compensates for this degree of deformity with little functional or cosmetic loss, as shown by Klenerman and Sarmiento. Union rates with functional bracing are high, although non-union is more frequent with proximal-third transverse fractures.
A 78-year-old low-demand woman with osteoporosis has a comminuted intra-articular distal humerus fracture that cannot be stably fixed. Best treatment:

In older patients with poor bone, a linked total elbow arthroplasty gives good early function and avoids fixation failure, although lifelong lifting restrictions apply (about 5 kg repeated, less for a single lift). Younger patients are treated with ORIF using two plates, often through an olecranon osteotomy.
After a fall onto an outstretched hand with varus stress, CT shows a fracture of the anteromedial facet of the coronoid process and the LCL is torn. This pattern produces:

Anteromedial facet fractures (O'Driscoll type 2) combined with lateral collateral ligament injury allow the ulna to rotate into varus and posteromedially, leading to rapid arthritis if untreated. Treatment is buttress fixation of the anteromedial facet and LCL repair. Small tip fractures with a radial head fracture form part of the terrible triad.
In O'Driscoll's model of a posterolateral elbow dislocation (the Horii circle), soft-tissue disruption begins with the:
Anterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament
Posterior bundle of the medial collateral ligament

Disruption progresses from lateral to medial in three stages: the LUCL first (posterolateral rotatory subluxation), then the anterior and posterior capsule (perched dislocation), and finally the medial collateral ligament, with the anterior bundle failing last. A dislocation can occur with the anterior bundle intact.
A 30-year-old has displaced fractures of both radius and ulna shafts. The treatment that best restores forearm rotation is:
Compression plating with anatomical reduction, restoring the radial bow

Forearm rotation depends on the length, alignment and curvature of both bones, so adult shaft fractures are treated as articular injuries with open reduction and compression plating. Loss of the radial bow reduces pronation and supination. Children tolerate closed treatment or flexible nails because of remodelling.
The normal radiographic parameters of the adult distal radius are approximately:
Radial inclination 22°, radial height 11 mm and volar tilt 11°
Radial inclination 10°, radial height 20 mm and dorsal tilt 10°
Radial inclination 35°, radial height 5 mm and volar tilt 25°
Radial inclination 22°, radial height 11 mm and dorsal tilt 11°

These values guide reduction. Commonly accepted limits for an active patient include dorsal tilt under about 10°, radial shortening under about 3 mm and articular step-off under 2 mm. Ulnar variance should be compared with the uninjured side.
Several months after volar locking plate fixation of a distal radius fracture, a patient suddenly cannot flex the thumb IP joint. The main risk factor is:
A plate placed proximal to the pronator quadratus
A plate placed distal to the watershed line (Soong grade 2)
Use of a radial styloid screw

The watershed line is the most volar ridge of the distal radius, where FPL lies directly on the bone. A plate placed on or beyond it, or prominent from inadequate fracture reduction, rubs on FPL and causes attrition rupture. Prominent plates should be removed once the fracture has healed. Dorsal screw tips instead threaten EPL.

After closed reduction of a displaced distal radius fracture, a patient has worsening numbness in the median nerve distribution and increasing pain despite elevation and loosening of the cast. Best management:
Urgent carpal tunnel release with stabilisation of the fracture
Steroid injection into the carpal tunnel

Acute carpal tunnel syndrome, with progressive symptoms, needs urgent decompression to prevent permanent nerve damage, along with fracture fixation. Symptoms from initial contusion or traction that are stable or improving after reduction can be observed. Avoid immobilising the wrist in extreme flexion (Cotton–Loder position).
In acute compartment syndrome of the forearm, the muscles usually most affected are those of the:

The deep flexors lie against the interosseous membrane and bones, where pressure is highest. Untreated, necrosis and fibrosis lead to Volkmann ischaemic contracture. Decompression is through a curvilinear volar incision that also releases the carpal tunnel and lacertus fibrosus, with a dorsal incision if needed.
In the Masquelet (induced membrane) technique for a segmental bone defect, the second stage involves:
Removing the cement spacer while preserving the induced membrane and filling the cavity with cancellous autograft
Removing both the spacer and the membrane

In the first stage, debridement and stabilisation are followed by a PMMA spacer that induces a vascular membrane. At about 4–8 weeks, the spacer is removed and the membrane, which secretes growth factors and prevents graft resorption, is filled with autograft. It is widely used for defects after infection or trauma.
In Ilizarov distraction osteogenesis, the standard protocol after corticotomy is:
A latency of about 5–7 days, then distraction of about 1 mm per day in about four increments
No latency, then 3 mm per day in one step
A latency of 6 weeks, then 1 mm per week
An immediate acute lengthening of 1 cm

A low-energy corticotomy preserves the periosteum and blood supply. Too fast a rate risks poor regenerate and nerve stretch, while too slow a rate risks premature consolidation. The consolidation phase usually takes longer than distraction, often about twice as long.
After a road accident, a 30-year-old has medial clavicle pain, difficulty swallowing and a hoarse voice. Imaging shows a posterior sternoclavicular dislocation. Best management:
Immediate closed reduction in the emergency department without further imaging
CT angiography, then reduction in theatre with a cardiothoracic surgeon available

The displaced clavicle can compress the trachea, oesophagus and great vessels. CT defines the injury and nearby structures, and closed reduction (abduction-traction with a towel clip) or open reduction is done in theatre. In patients under about 25 the injury is often a medial physeal fracture.
In the Garden classification of femoral neck fractures, type I is:

Garden I and II are often grouped as undisplaced and are treated with internal fixation, while III and IV are displaced and in older patients are usually treated with arthroplasty. Interobserver agreement is poor for separating the individual grades, so the undisplaced versus displaced distinction is used in practice.

A 35-year-old has a radial head fracture: a single fragment of about 40% of the head, displaced 3 mm, with a mechanical block to forearm rotation after aspiration and local anaesthetic. Best treatment:
Open reduction and internal fixation with screws

Aspirating the haemarthrosis and injecting local anaesthetic helps separate a true mechanical block from pain. Undisplaced or minimally displaced fractures without a block are treated with early motion, while comminuted fractures that cannot be fixed are replaced. Excision is avoided when there is associated elbow or forearm instability.
A 60-year-old has a basicervical femoral neck fracture. The most appropriate fixation is:
A sliding hip screw with an antirotation screw, or a cephalomedullary nail

Basicervical fractures lie at the junction of the neck and intertrochanteric region and behave biomechanically like extracapsular fractures, with high failure rates when treated with cannulated screws alone. A fixed-angle device with an antirotation screw resists rotation of the head fragment.
After surgery for an acetabular fracture, the approach associated with the highest rate of heterotopic ossification is the:

Extensive stripping of the outer table of the ilium and the abductors causes the highest rates, followed by the Kocher–Langenbeck approach; anterior intrapelvic approaches have the lowest. Head injury and male sex also increase the risk. Prophylaxis includes indomethacin or a single dose of radiotherapy.

A 62-year-old has clumsy hands and an unsteady gait. Tapping the distal radius produces finger flexion while the brachioradialis reflex itself is reduced (inverted supinator sign). The level of cord compression is most likely:

The inverted supinator sign combines a lower motor neuron lesion at C5–C6 (reduced brachioradialis reflex) with upper motor neuron release below it (brisk finger flexors). Hoffmann's sign, a wide-based gait and loss of hand dexterity are other features of cervical spondylotic myelopathy. Compression at C3–C4 tends to make all the upper limb reflexes brisk.
The Nurick grading of cervical spondylotic myelopathy is based mainly on:
Severity of gait disturbance and its effect on employment
MRI signal change in the cord

Nurick grades 0–5 range from root signs only to being chair-bound or bedridden, according to difficulty walking. The modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score assesses upper and lower limb motor function, sensation and bladder function. Moderate, severe or progressive myelopathy is generally treated surgically.

A 58-year-old has progressive spastic paraparesis with normal arm function. MRI shows posterior compression of the cord by thickened, ossified ligamentum flavum. The most common site of this condition is the:

Ossification of the ligamentum flavum mainly affects the lower thoracic spine, especially in East Asian populations, and often coexists with OPLL or DISH. It causes thoracic myelopathy and is treated with posterior laminectomy and excision of the ossified ligament; associated dural ossification increases the risk of dural tear.
Which radiographic feature best distinguishes diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) from ankylosing spondylitis?
Sacroiliac joints without erosion or fusion

Resnick's criteria for DISH are flowing ossification along the anterolateral aspect of at least four contiguous vertebral bodies, relatively preserved disc height, and no facet ankylosis or sacroiliac erosion or fusion. In the thoracic spine it is typically right-sided, away from the pulsating aorta. AS produces thin marginal syndesmophytes and sacroiliitis; both predispose to unstable fractures after minor trauma.
A 30-year-old with low back pain has an enlarged L5 transverse process forming a pseudarthrosis with the sacral ala on one side. This is:
Bertolotti syndrome (Castellvi type IIa transitional vertebra)

Castellvi type I is an enlarged transverse process, type II a pseudarthrosis with the sacrum, type III complete fusion and type IV mixed, with a and b denoting unilateral and bilateral. Transitional anatomy is a common cause of wrong-level surgery, so levels must be counted carefully. Baastrup disease is contact ('kissing') of adjacent spinous processes.
Which spinopelvic parameter is a fixed morphological value that does not change with posture once growth is complete?

Pelvic incidence equals pelvic tilt plus sacral slope. When sagittal balance is lost, the pelvis retroverts to compensate, so pelvic tilt rises and sacral slope falls while pelvic incidence stays the same. A high pelvic incidence needs more lumbar lordosis, and a lordosis within about 10° of the pelvic incidence is a common surgical target.
In adult spinal deformity, which value on a standing full-length lateral radiograph indicates sagittal malalignment linked to worse health-related quality of life?
Sagittal vertical axis of more than 5 cm
Pelvic incidence minus lumbar lordosis of 5°

The sagittal vertical axis is the horizontal distance between a plumb line from the C7 centroid and the posterosuperior corner of S1. Disability rises with an SVA over about 4–5 cm, a pelvic tilt over about 20° and a PI–LL mismatch over about 10° (SRS–Schwab modifiers). A pelvic tilt of 10° and a kyphosis of 30° are normal.
A single-level lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy typically gives about how much sagittal correction?
10°, the same as a Smith-Petersen osteotomy

A PSO removes the posterior elements, both pedicles and a wedge of the vertebral body, closing on an anterior hinge to give about 30–35° of lordosis through all three columns. A Smith-Petersen (posterior column) osteotomy gives about 1° per mm of bone removed, roughly 10° per level, and needs a mobile disc in front. Vertebral column resection is used for larger or multiplanar corrections.
During L4 pedicle screw insertion, a breach of the medial and inferior wall of the pedicle most endangers the:

Each lumbar root exits below its own pedicle, so the L4 root lies just inferior and medial to the L4 pedicle. Lateral breaches are relatively safer for the roots, and anterior perforation of the vertebral body endangers the great vessels. A low triggered EMG threshold during screw stimulation suggests a breach.

When inserting a subaxial cervical lateral mass screw by the Magerl technique, the screw is aimed upwards parallel to the facet joint and about 25° laterally. The lateral angulation mainly protects the:

The vertebral artery lies anterior to the junction of the lateral mass and the lamina, so lateral angulation keeps the screw tip away from it, and the cranial angulation keeps it away from the exiting root below. Subaxial cervical pedicle screws carry more risk to the artery and are mainly used at C7 or in specific situations.
In rheumatoid atlantoaxial instability, which measurement best predicts paralysis and the need for surgery?
Posterior atlanto-dens interval (space available for the cord) of less than 14 mm

Boden showed that a posterior atlanto-dens interval under about 14 mm predicts neurological deficit better than the anterior interval, which is distorted by odontoid erosion. Other indications for fusion include neurological deficit, intractable pain, cranial settling and subaxial subluxation.
Chamberlain's line, used to assess basilar invagination, is drawn from the:
Tip of the dens to the basion
Hard palate to the lowest point of the occiput

The dens tip normally lies no more than about 3 mm above Chamberlain's line. McGregor's line runs from the hard palate to the lowest point of the occipital squama, and McRae's line joins the basion and opisthion across the foramen magnum. In rheumatoid arthritis, erosion of the dens makes the Ranawat and Redlund-Johnell methods more reliable.
Two days after posterior cervical laminoplasty for multilevel myelopathy, a patient develops new deltoid and biceps weakness, with no worsening of myelopathy. Most likely diagnosis:

C5 palsy follows anterior or posterior cervical decompression in a few percent of patients, possibly from root tethering as the cord drifts back; the short C5 root sits at the apex of the lordosis. Most recover over months. An epidural haematoma causes increasing pain and worsening myelopathy and needs urgent evacuation.
A left-sided anterior approach to the lower cervical spine is often preferred because:
The thoracic duct is on the right
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve has a longer and more predictable course
The carotid sheath is absent on the left
The oesophagus lies to the right

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch and ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove, while the right nerve loops under the subclavian artery and crosses the field more obliquely. Low left-sided exposures near C7–T1 risk the thoracic duct. Dysphagia is the most common complaint after anterior cervical surgery.
A diabetic intravenous drug user has severe thoracic back pain, fever and new leg weakness. MRI shows a dorsal epidural collection compressing the cord. Best management:
Intravenous antibiotics alone, with MRI repeated in 2 weeks
Urgent surgical decompression and drainage with intravenous antibiotics

Spinal epidural abscess is most often caused by S. aureus. Back pain, fever and neurological deficit form the classic triad, though all three are often absent early. Patients with a deficit need urgent decompression; selected patients without a deficit can be treated with antibiotics under close observation, because deterioration can be sudden.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis most commonly occurs at:

Facet arthritis with sagittally oriented facets lets L4 slip forward on L5 with an intact pars, causing central and lateral recess stenosis that usually compresses the traversing L5 roots. Slips rarely exceed Meyerding grade II. Isthmic spondylolisthesis, from a pars defect, is most common at L5–S1.
The Pfirrmann classification grades lumbar disc degeneration using:
Signal, structure and height of the disc on T2-weighted MRI

Grade I is a bright, homogeneous disc and grade V a collapsed, black disc. Modic changes describe the adjacent end plates, and a high-intensity zone is a bright focus in the posterior annulus that may reflect an annular fissure.

A 17-year-old pivoting athlete with generalised ligamentous laxity and a grade 3 pivot shift is having a hamstring ACL reconstruction. Which addition has been shown to reduce graft failure in this high-risk group?

In young, high-risk patients, adding a lateral extra-articular tenodesis (such as a modified Lemaire procedure with a strip of iliotibial band) reduces rotational laxity and graft rupture. Anterolateral ligament reconstruction targets the same structures. A graft diameter under about 8 mm is linked to higher failure.
In an ACL-deficient knee, a tear at the meniscocapsular junction of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus is easily missed through standard anterior portals. It is called a:

Ramp lesions are best seen by passing the arthroscope through the notch between the PCL and medial femoral condyle, or through a posteromedial portal. They increase anterior tibial translation and external rotation, so they are repaired at the time of ACL reconstruction. MRI often misses them.
After ACL reconstruction with a tendon autograft, the graft is mechanically weakest at about:

Ligamentisation proceeds through graft necrosis, revascularisation and cellular repopulation, then remodelling over many months. Rehabilitation in this period protects the graft while restoring extension and quadriceps control. The graft never fully reproduces native ACL structure.
After ACL reconstruction, which approach has been shown to reduce the risk of reinjury on returning to pivoting sport?
Delaying return until at least 9 months and regaining symmetrical quadriceps strength
Using a functional brace instead of rehabilitation

Each month of delay up to about 9 months lowers the reinjury rate, and passing objective criteria (such as quadriceps strength and hop tests with a limb symmetry index of 90% or more) lowers it further. Both graft rupture and contralateral ACL injury are common in young athletes.
Pain deep in the shoulder on resisted forward flexion with the arm at 90°, adducted 10–15° and fully internally rotated, which is relieved when the test is repeated in external rotation, suggests:

This is O'Brien's active compression test. Pain deep in the joint suggests a SLAP lesion, while pain on top of the shoulder suggests AC joint pathology. Clinical tests for SLAP lesions are of limited accuracy, so MR arthrography or arthroscopy is often needed.
The most reliable way to quantify anteroinferior glenoid bone loss before shoulder stabilisation is:
Three-dimensional CT en face view of the glenoid with a best-fit circle

A circle is fitted to the inferior glenoid and the missing width or area is expressed as a percentage. Loss above about 20% (less in contact athletes, and even subcritical loss of about 13–15% worsens outcomes after Bankart repair) favours a bony procedure. MRI-based measurement is improving, but CT remains the reference.
Arthroscopic remplissage treats a Hill–Sachs lesion by:
Grafting the humeral defect with allograft
Transferring the coracoid to the glenoid
Tenodesing the infraspinatus tendon and posterior capsule into the defect

Filling the defect with infraspinatus makes it extra-articular, so it can no longer engage the glenoid rim. It is combined with Bankart repair for off-track lesions with little glenoid bone loss. A small loss of external rotation may follow.
The 'sling effect' that contributes to stability after a Latarjet procedure is provided by the:
Conjoint tendon crossing the lower subscapularis in abduction and external rotation
Coracoacromial ligament repaired to the capsule

The triple blocking effect is the bone block extending the glenoid arc, the conjoint tendon acting as a sling over the lower subscapularis, and the capsule repaired to the coracoacromial ligament stump. The musculocutaneous nerve, which enters coracobrachialis a few centimetres below the coracoid, is at risk during the transfer.
The most common site of non-union in an os acromiale, best seen on an axillary radiograph, is between the:

The acromion forms from several ossification centres that normally fuse by about 25 years. Failure at the meso–meta junction is most common. An unstable os acromiale can cause pain and contribute to impingement, and matters when planning reverse shoulder arthroplasty.
On a supraspinatus outlet view, a hooked acromion is Bigliani:

Type I is flat, type II curved and type III hooked; type III has been associated with rotator cuff tears. The importance of acromial shape is debated, and subacromial decompression alone has not been shown to beat placebo surgery for subacromial pain.
On axial MRI of the shoulder, the long head of biceps tendon lies medial to the bicipital groove. This should prompt a search for a tear of the:

The biceps pulley (superior glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments with the upper subscapularis) holds the tendon in the groove, so medial dislocation usually means an upper subscapularis tear. Lift-off and belly-press tests assess subscapularis. Biceps tenotomy or tenodesis usually accompanies subscapularis repair.
A weightlifter feels a pop in the front of the elbow while lowering a heavy weight. Which examination is most sensitive and specific for a complete distal biceps tendon rupture?
Popeye sign in the upper arm

In O'Driscoll's hook test, the examiner cannot hook a finger under the lateral edge of the biceps tendon with the elbow flexed 90° and supinated. Speed's and Yergason's tests assess the proximal biceps, and a Popeye bulge suggests proximal long head rupture. Early anatomical repair restores supination strength; the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve is the nerve most often affected after repair.
A man feels a tearing sensation in the axilla during a bench press, with bruising of the upper arm and loss of the anterior axillary fold. The most common site of injury is the:
Muscle belly of the clavicular head
Tendinous insertion of the sternal head on the humerus

Pectoralis major ruptures typically occur with eccentric loading during bench press, most often avulsing the sternal head at or near the humeral insertion. Complete tendinous tears in active patients are usually repaired early to restore adduction and internal rotation strength.
A volleyball player has pain at the inferior pole of the patella on jumping, with tenderness of the proximal patellar tendon. First-line treatment is:
Progressive tendon loading, such as eccentric decline squats or heavy slow resistance

Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee) is a degenerative tendinopathy of the proximal posterior fibres. Load-based exercise is the mainstay, and steroid injection into the tendon risks rupture. Surgery is reserved for persistent symptoms after prolonged rehabilitation.
On a true lateral fluoroscopic view, the femoral attachment for MPFL reconstruction (Schöttle's point) lies:
At the origin of the medial head of gastrocnemius
At the centre of the medial epicondyle on the AP view only
Just anterior to the line of the posterior femoral cortex, between the posterior origin of the medial condyle and the posterior end of Blumensaat's line

Schöttle's point gives a reproducible radiographic landmark for the femoral tunnel. A tunnel placed too proximally makes the graft tight in flexion, causing pain, stiffness or excessive medial pressure on the patella.
The medial patellofemoral ligament is the primary soft-tissue restraint to lateral patellar translation:
In early flexion, from about 0° to 30°
Only when the trochlea is dysplastic

The MPFL provides about half to two-thirds of the medial restraining force near extension; once the patella engages the trochlea beyond about 30° of flexion, the bony groove dominates. It is torn in nearly all lateral patellar dislocations.
In femoroacetabular impingement, a cam morphology is commonly diagnosed when the alpha angle on a lateral radiograph or radial MRI exceeds about:

The alpha angle is measured between the femoral neck axis and a line from the head centre to where the head–neck contour leaves the circle of the head. A cam lesion jams into the acetabulum in flexion and internal rotation, damaging the chondrolabral junction, and the FADIR test reproduces the pain.
Which sesamoid of the great toe is more often bipartite, a finding that can be confused with a fracture?
Neither; bipartite sesamoids do not occur

A bipartite tibial sesamoid has smooth, rounded, corticated edges and is often bilateral, so comparison views help; an acute fracture has sharp, irregular edges. The tibial sesamoid carries more load and is more often injured.
A 40-year-old woman has hallux valgus with an intermetatarsal angle of 16° and clinical hypermobility of the first tarsometatarsal joint. Which procedure addresses both problems?

The Lapidus procedure fuses the first TMT joint in a corrected position, reducing the intermetatarsal angle and removing hypermobility. A distal chevron osteotomy suits mild to moderate deformity, and Keller resection is reserved for low-demand elderly patients.
After hallux valgus surgery that included excision of the fibular sesamoid and tight medial capsular plication, the great toe drifts into varus. Most likely cause:
Overcorrection, with loss of the lateral restraint from fibular sesamoid excision

Iatrogenic hallux varus results from overcorrection: excessive medial eminence resection, an overtightened medial capsule, fibular sesamoid excision, excessive lateral release or a negative intermetatarsal angle. Flexible deformities can be corrected with tendon transfer or soft-tissue reconstruction, and rigid ones with first MTP arthrodesis.
A 45-year-old runner has a painful fusiform swelling of the Achilles tendon about 4 cm above its insertion. First-line treatment is:

Midportion Achilles tendinopathy responds to progressive eccentric or heavy slow loading in most patients. Steroid injection into or around the tendon risks rupture. Insertional tendinopathy responds less well to full-range eccentric exercise, so loading avoids dropping the heel into dorsiflexion.
A 60-year-old presents 3 months after an untreated Achilles rupture, with a 6 cm gap after debridement. Which reconstruction is commonly used?
Peroneus longus tenodesis to the tibia
Flexor hallucis longus tendon transfer, with or without a turndown or V–Y advancement

FHL fires in phase with gastrocnemius–soleus, lies next to the tendon and brings a blood supply from its low muscle belly. Small gaps can be repaired directly and intermediate ones with V–Y advancement or a turndown flap. The sural nerve lies lateral to the tendon and is at risk during exposure.
On MRI, a peroneus brevis tendon behind the fibula is C-shaped and split longitudinally, with peroneus longus lying in the cleft. This typically results from:
Compression against the posterior edge of the fibula, often with a lax superior peroneal retinaculum

Split tears occur where brevis is squeezed between peroneus longus and the posterior fibular ridge, often with chronic lateral ankle instability, a low-lying brevis muscle belly or a peroneus quartus. Treatment is debridement and tubularisation, with tenodesis to peroneus longus when much of the tendon is unusable.
In the 2020 consensus terminology, adult acquired flatfoot deformity was renamed:

The new term recognises that the deformity involves the hindfoot, midfoot, forefoot and sometimes the ankle, not just the tibialis posterior tendon. The classification records hindfoot valgus, midfoot or forefoot abduction, forefoot varus, peritalar subluxation and ankle valgus, and whether each is flexible or rigid.
The superomedial part of the spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament mainly supports the:

The spring ligament forms a sling beneath and medial to the talar head, from the sustentaculum tali to the navicular. In progressive collapsing foot deformity it attenuates or tears along with the tibialis posterior tendon, so the talar head drops and the forefoot abducts; it may need repair or reconstruction.
The main blood supply to the body of the talus comes from the:
Artery of the tarsal sinus alone
Dorsalis pedis through the talar head
Artery of the tarsal canal, a branch of the posterior tibial artery
Peroneal artery through the posterior process

The artery of the tarsal canal anastomoses with the artery of the tarsal sinus (from the peroneal and dorsalis pedis systems) to form a sling beneath the talar neck. The deltoid branch supplies the medial body and may be its only remaining supply after a displaced neck fracture, so the deltoid ligament should be preserved.
The Canale view, used to judge varus malalignment of a talar neck fracture, is taken with the:
Foot dorsiflexed and the beam horizontal from the lateral side
Foot in maximum equinus and 15° pronation, with the beam angled 75° from the horizontal

This projection shows the talar neck in profile. Varus malunion shortens the medial column and locks the hindfoot in varus, overloading the lateral foot. Anatomical reduction often needs both medial and lateral approaches to judge comminution.
On coronal CT, a calcaneal fracture splits the posterior facet into four or more fragments. Sanders type and a commonly considered treatment:
Type IV; ORIF with primary subtalar arthrodesis

Sanders types are based on the number of posterior facet fragments on the widest coronal cut: type I undisplaced, II two-part, III three-part and IV four or more parts. Type IV fractures do poorly with fixation alone, so primary subtalar fusion, with restoration of calcaneal height and width, is often considered.
A rider's foot is forced into abduction. CT shows a crushed cuboid with shortening of the lateral column. Best management:
Open reduction restoring lateral column length, with bone graft and a plate or external fixator
Primary calcaneocuboid fusion in every case

A nutcracker fracture crushes the cuboid between the calcaneus and the bases of the fourth and fifth metatarsals. Uncorrected shortening leaves a painful planovalgus foot with forefoot abduction. Look for associated Lisfranc and navicular injuries.
A lateral subtalar dislocation cannot be reduced by closed means. The structure most often blocking reduction is the:

Medial subtalar dislocations are more common and are blocked by extensor digitorum brevis, the peroneal tendons or the talonavicular capsule. Lateral dislocations are higher energy, more often open, and are blocked by tibialis posterior wrapping around the talar head. CT after reduction looks for associated fractures.

A footballer has pain above the ankle after an external rotation injury. Externally rotating the foot with the knee flexed 90° and the ankle neutral reproduces pain over the anterior tibiofibular ligament. This test indicates:

The external rotation (Kleiger) test and the squeeze test suggest a syndesmotic injury, which takes longer to recover than a lateral sprain. Unstable injuries, shown by diastasis on weight-bearing radiographs, CT or arthroscopy, are fixed with screws or suture-button devices; flexible fixation has lower rates of malreduction.
In Brodsky's anatomical classification of Charcot neuroarthropathy of the foot, the most common site (type 1) is the:

Type 1 midfoot disease often collapses into a rocker-bottom foot with plantar ulceration. Type 2 involves the hindfoot (subtalar, talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints), type 3A the ankle and 3B the calcaneal tuberosity. Hindfoot and ankle disease are less common but more unstable.
A patient has limited ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended that improves markedly when the knee is flexed. This indicates:
Contracture of both gastrocnemius and soleus
