They occur only in the lateral meniscus
They are best treated with partial meniscectomy

Loss of the root disrupts hoop tension, raising contact pressure and accelerating arthritis. Root repair is recommended in suitable patients without advanced arthritis; lateral root tears often accompany ACL tears.
Which ligament connects the atlas directly to the occiput?

The anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes join C1 to the skull. Alar and apical ligaments run from the dens to the occiput, and the tectorial membrane continues the PLL from C2 to the clivus.
The WOMAC score is a patient-reported outcome measure for:
WOMAC covers pain, stiffness and physical function. The Oswestry Disability Index is used for the back and DASH for the upper limb.
Daily protein intake recommended for most high-performance athletes is about:
The general adult requirement is about 0.8 g/kg/day; athletes need more, spread through the day (about 0.3 g/kg per meal) and soon after training. Higher intakes add little benefit.
A trekker on rapid ascent develops breathlessness at rest, cough and pink frothy sputum. The first and most important step is:

High-altitude pulmonary oedema is treated by descent and oxygen; nifedipine (a pulmonary vasodilator) is an adjunct. A portable hyperbaric bag is used if descent is impossible. Dexamethasone treats cerebral oedema.
The best single test of iron stores in a female athlete is:
Ferritin falls before anaemia develops, identifying iron deficiency without anaemia, which can still impair performance. Ferritin rises with inflammation, so interpret it with CRP.
VO2 max is best measured during:
Incremental exercise to exhaustion using gas analysis

VO2 max is the highest rate of oxygen uptake reached during graded maximal exercise, measured with expired gas analysis on a treadmill or cycle ergometer. Sport-specific modes give the most relevant values.
The usual entry point for a lumbar pedicle screw is at the junction of the:
Transverse process midline and the lateral edge of the superior articular process (pars)

The Magerl or Roy-Camille landmark lies where a line through the middle of the transverse process meets the lateral border of the superior articular facet. The screw converges medially more at lower lumbar levels.
A patient has saddle anaesthesia but normal motor function and reflexes in the legs. The lesion most likely involves the:
Conus medullaris or lower sacral roots (S3–S5)

S3–S5 supply the perineum, bladder and anal sphincter but no leg muscles, so an isolated low sacral lesion causes saddle anaesthesia and sphincter dysfunction without leg weakness. Urgent MRI is needed.
In a sagittally balanced adult spine, the C7 plumb line normally falls:
Through the anterior part of the L3 body
Within about 5 cm of the posterosuperior corner of S1

A sagittal vertical axis over 5 cm anteriorly indicates positive sagittal imbalance, which correlates with disability in adult deformity. Pelvic incidence–lumbar lordosis mismatch and pelvic tilt are also assessed.
Vertebral bodies form by resegmentation, in which each vertebra arises from:
The caudal half of one sclerotome fused with the cranial half of the next
Resegmentation lets the segmental muscles span adjacent vertebrae and the spinal nerves pass between them. The notochord persists as the nucleus pulposus.
Baastrup disease (kissing spines) is pain from contact between adjacent:
Spinous processes, often with an interspinous bursa
It is most common at L4–L5 in older people with lordosis and disc degeneration. Pain is worse on extension; injections help, and spinous process resection is occasionally used.
Persistent femoral anteversion in a child causes in-toeing and typically shows:
External rotation greater than internal rotation
Increased internal hip rotation (often over 70°) with reduced external rotation

Most resolve by about 8–10 years. Derotational osteotomy is considered only for severe anteversion (over about 45–50°) with functional problems in an older child. Shoe modifications and braces do not help.
A young rugby player cannot flex the DIP joint of the ring finger after grabbing a jersey; the FDP tendon has retracted into the palm. This Leddy–Packer type 1 injury should be repaired within about:

In type 1 both vincula are torn and the tendon loses blood supply and shortens quickly. Type 2 retracts to the PIP level, held by the long vinculum, and type 3 has a large bony fragment caught at the A4 pulley.
After syndactyly release, 'web creep' is best prevented by:
A dorsal rectangular or trapezoidal flap to reconstruct the commissure, with skin grafts for raw areas
Leaving the web open to heal secondarily
A well-designed dorsal commissural flap creates a sloping web that resists migration. Release is usually done around 12–18 months, earlier for border digits of unequal length.
Which is NOT typically seen in amniotic band syndrome (constriction band syndrome)?
Bands produce asymmetrical, random lesions distal to the constriction, with lymphoedema and acrosyndactyly. Tight bands threatening circulation need urgent Z-plasty release.
Central deficiency of the hand (typical cleft hand) differs from symbrachydactyly because it:
Often occurs bilaterally with cleft feet and is frequently inherited
Has nubbins at the ends of the digits

Typical cleft hand has a V-shaped central defect, is often bilateral and autosomal dominant, and may involve the feet. Symbrachydactyly is unilateral, sporadic and has small nubbins. Surgery addresses the thumb web and closes the cleft.
Gantzer's muscle, an accessory head of FPL, can compress the:

It lies behind the median nerve and AIN in the forearm. AIN syndrome causes weakness of FPL, FDP to the index (and middle) and pronator quadratus without sensory loss, and a pinch test gives a flat 'OK' sign.
The deep (motor) branch of the ulnar nerve leaves Guyon's canal passing:
Around the hook of hamate, between abductor and flexor digiti minimi, through opponens digiti minimi

Hook of hamate fractures and ganglia can compress it, producing intrinsic weakness without sensory loss. The superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis and the skin of the little and half the ring finger.
In established CRPS type 1, plain radiographs may show:
Rapid patchy demineralisation develops after several weeks; a triple-phase bone scan shows increased periarticular uptake in the delayed phase. Diagnosis is clinical using the Budapest criteria.
Which amino acid group is preferentially oxidised by skeletal muscle during prolonged endurance exercise?

Muscle can oxidise branched-chain amino acids directly, so protein contributes a few percent of energy in long events, more when glycogen is depleted. Leucine also triggers muscle protein synthesis via mTOR.
In the modified Tokuhashi score for spinal metastases, which primary tumour carries the best prognosis?

Thyroid, breast and prostate cancers score highest (longest expected survival); lung, gastric and liver cancers score lowest. The score also includes general condition, the number of bone and visceral metastases and paralysis.
A patient has 3/5 deltoid power, weak biceps and numbness over the lateral upper arm, with a reduced biceps reflex. The most likely root is:
C5 supplies deltoid and contributes to biceps, with sensation over the regimental badge and lateral arm. C5 palsy is also a recognised complication after cervical decompression.
Rising from a standard chair without using the arms needs roughly how much knee flexion?
Daily tasks need about 65–70° for swing phase of walking, 85–90° for stairs and about 90–105° for rising from a chair. Patients with less than about 90° after TKA struggle with these activities.
During TKA, the extension gap is tight while the flexion gap is loose. Which single step corrects this?
Removing more distal femur opens only the extension gap, so a thicker insert can then fill the loose flexion gap. Releasing the posterior capsule also opens extension.
During routine aseptic revision TKA, 3 of 5 intraoperative tissue cultures later grow coagulase-negative staphylococcus of the same type. This should be treated as:
Periprosthetic joint infection, with a course of targeted antibiotics
A reason to repeat surgery the next day
Two or more positive cultures of the same organism meet a major criterion for PJI. Unexpected positive cultures after presumed aseptic revision are usually treated with a prolonged antibiotic course.
Using an extensively porous-coated cobalt–chromium stem in a patient with osteoporotic bone is most likely to cause:

A stiff, distally fixed stem bypasses the proximal femur, causing calcar and greater trochanter bone loss; thigh pain is also more common. These stems still give reliable fixation in revision with poor proximal bone.
Which proximal femoral shape (Dorr type) is best suited to a cemented stem?
Type C bone gives poor press-fit stability, so cement gives immediate fixation. Type A suits uncemented stems.
When planning TKA in a knee with two old parallel longitudinal scars, the general rule is to use:
The skin's blood supply comes mainly from the medial side, so using the lateral scar avoids leaving a lateral flap with poor perfusion. Narrow skin bridges (under about 5–6 cm) should be avoided.
When reaming the acetabulum for THA in protrusio acetabuli, the key precaution is to:
Ream medially to the true floor
Ream peripherally only, avoid further medialisation and fill the medial defect with graft
Use a cemented cup without graft
Place the cup in the medialised position
The aim is to restore the hip centre to its normal position by lateralising the cup on the rim, grafting the medial defect. Dislocating the hip can be difficult; an in-situ neck cut avoids fracture.
A patient with hip pain cups the hand around the front and side of the hip in a C shape when asked where it hurts. This 'C sign' most suggests:
Intra-articular hip pathology such as labral tear or FAI
The C sign points to an intra-articular source. Provocation tests such as FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) and the FABER test support it, and MR arthrography shows labral tears.
Lateral epicondylitis mainly involves microtears and degeneration at the origin of:
Angiofibroblastic hyperplasia of the ECRB origin is the hallmark. Resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley test) and Cozen test reproduce pain.
Which statement about the ACL is FALSE?
The anteromedial bundle is tight in flexion and the posterolateral bundle in extension
Its main blood supply is the middle genicular artery
It is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation
The PCL resists posterior translation; the ACL resists anterior translation and internal rotation. The middle genicular artery supplies both cruciates.
A patient has an ACL tear plus a high-grade tear of the LCL, popliteus and biceps femoris, with an intact PCL. The best surgical plan is:
ACL reconstruction with posterolateral corner reconstruction (or repair), ideally in the same stage within about 2–3 weeks

An unaddressed posterolateral corner injury puts excess varus and rotational stress on the ACL graft, a leading cause of graft failure. Early repair with augmentation or reconstruction gives better results than late reconstruction.
A young patient has anterior shoulder pain, cannot keep the hand off the lower back (positive lift-off test), and has increased passive external rotation. The tendon injured is:
The lift-off and belly-press tests assess subscapularis. Increased passive external rotation and medial subluxation of the biceps tendon support a complete tear, which is repaired early.
The strongest ligament of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis is the:
Posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (including the deep transverse ligament)

The PITFL is the strongest component; the AITFL is usually injured first in external rotation injuries. Posterior malleolar fractures often carry the intact PITFL, so fixing them restores much syndesmotic stability.
A 10-year-old footballer has heel pain with activity that settles with rest, and tenderness on squeezing the posterior calcaneus. Diagnosis:

Sever disease is traction apophysitis during growth spurts. It is self-limiting and treated with heel cups, calf stretching and activity modification. Radiographs are only needed for atypical features.
The 'unhappy triad' of O'Donoghue classically involves which three structures?
The triad follows valgus and external rotation with a planted foot. Later studies found the lateral meniscus is actually torn more often than the medial in acute injuries.
The point during incremental exercise at which ventilation rises disproportionately to oxygen uptake is the:
Above this threshold, lactate accumulates and bicarbonate buffering produces extra CO2, driving ventilation. Training raises the threshold as a fraction of VO2 max, improving endurance performance.
An anteromedialising tibial tubercle (Fulkerson) osteotomy is mainly indicated for:
Lateral patellar instability or maltracking with lateral or distal patellar cartilage wear
Anteriorisation unloads the patellofemoral joint, and medialisation corrects a raised TT–TG distance. It is avoided with proximal or medial patellar facet lesions, which it would overload.

A baseball pitcher has medial elbow pain and loss of velocity. MRI shows a complete midsubstance tear of the anterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament. For a high-level thrower, the usual treatment is:
UCL reconstruction with a tendon graft (Tommy John surgery)

The anterior bundle is the primary restraint to valgus stress in throwing. Reconstruction (for example with palmaris longus) allows most elite throwers to return, after about a year of rehabilitation. Non-throwers often do well without surgery.
On sagittal knee MRI, a meniscus that is present on peripheral slices but 'missing' on the central slices where the posterior horn should be (ghost meniscus) indicates:
Meniscal root tear or radial tear
A full-thickness radial or root tear produces a fluid gap, so the posterior horn is not visible on one or more sagittal images. Meniscal extrusion on coronal images is often associated.
The most common source of loose bodies in an adult knee is:
Degenerative fragments are the commonest loose bodies in adults, while OCD is a common cause in adolescents. Symptomatic loose bodies cause locking and are removed arthroscopically.
A footballer has an obvious ankle fracture-dislocation with the skin tented over the medial malleolus. After the primary survey, the next step on the field is:
Prompt gentle reduction by longitudinal traction and splinting, with neurovascular check
Apply ice and walk off the pitch
Early reduction relieves skin tension and vascular compromise, preventing skin necrosis. Splint, check pulses and sensation before and after, then arrange radiographs and definitive fixation.
Which statement about scapholunate dissociation is FALSE?
The scaphoid flexes and the lunate extends
A gap over about 3 mm on the PA view suggests it
The scapholunate angle is increased above 60°
Scapholunate injury gives DISI (dorsal intercalated segment instability); VISI follows lunotriquetral injury. Signs include a widened SL gap and the scaphoid 'ring sign' from foreshortening.
A 4-year-old obese child has infantile Blount disease with a metaphyseal–diaphyseal angle of 18° and depression of the medial tibial plateau (Langenskiöld stage III–IV). The best treatment is:
Proximal tibial valgus derotation osteotomy, with or without medial plateau elevation

Bracing is reserved for younger children with early stages. Progressive or advanced disease at this age needs osteotomy, overcorrecting slightly into valgus, and medial plateau elevation if it is depressed. Physeal bars need resection.
During treatment of osteoarticular tuberculosis, the first radiological sign of healing is:
Remineralisation and sharpening of cortical and articular margins
Return of bone density and sharpening of eroded margins indicate healing, and MRI shows resolution of marrow oedema. Clinical improvement often precedes radiological change.
Symmetrical ascending paralysis with sensory loss
Asymmetrical flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation

The virus destroys anterior horn cells, causing asymmetric lower motor neuron paralysis with normal sensation. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes symmetrical ascending weakness, often with sensory symptoms.
The direct anterior (Smith-Petersen/Hueter) approach to the hip uses the internervous plane between:
Sartorius (femoral nerve) and tensor fasciae latae (superior gluteal nerve)

Superficially the plane is between sartorius and TFL; deeper, between rectus femoris (femoral) and gluteus medius (superior gluteal). The ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery crosses the field and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is at risk.
A cook cuts the volar wrist. He has clawing of the ring and little fingers, cannot abduct the fingers, and has numbness of the little finger. The nerve injured is:
A low ulnar nerve lesion spares FDP to the ring and little fingers, so clawing is more marked than in a high lesion (the 'ulnar paradox'). Early primary repair gives the best result.
A man who uses his palm as a hammer has ring and little finger numbness and cold intolerance. Angiography shows ulnar artery occlusion near the hook of hamate. Diagnosis:

Repetitive blunt trauma damages the ulnar artery in Guyon's canal, causing thrombosis or aneurysm with distal emboli. Treatment ranges from stopping the activity to resection and vein graft reconstruction.
Conventional high-frequency TENS relieves pain mainly by:
Activating large A-beta fibres that inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn (gate control)
Gate control explains high-frequency TENS; low-frequency acupuncture-like TENS also releases endogenous opioids. Effects are short-lived and best used alongside exercise.
In a child aged about 4–8 years, the femoral head receives its blood supply mainly from:
Lateral epiphyseal vessels from the medial femoral circumflex artery

The physis blocks metaphyseal supply, and the ligamentum teres contributes little until later, so the head depends on the lateral epiphyseal (retinacular) vessels, which helps explain Perthes disease at this age.
Degeneration of the proximal stump back to the cell body
Breakdown of the axon and myelin distal to a nerve injury
Regeneration of axons at 1 mm per day

Schwann cells and macrophages clear debris within days to weeks, forming bands of Büngner that guide regeneration. It explains why distal nerve conduction stays normal for several days after transection.
In a non-ambulant child with severe cerebral palsy and a chronically dislocated, painful hip with a deformed femoral head, the preferred procedure is often:
Proximal femoral resection (Castle) or valgus osteotomy with head resection

Reconstruction is preferred when the femoral head is salvageable; when the head is severely deformed and painful in a non-walker, salvage resection or a valgus (McHale) osteotomy improves sitting and hygiene.
The functional (safe) position for immobilising the hand is:
Wrist flexed, MCPs extended, IPs flexed
Wrist extended about 20–30°, MCPs flexed about 70–90°, IP joints straight
In this 'intrinsic plus' position the collateral ligaments of the MCP joints are taut and the IP volar plates stretched, so they do not contract during immobilisation.
Within 30 minutes of injury, an awake, cooperative patient has a C4–C5 bilateral facet dislocation with incomplete cord injury. The usual next step is:
Closed reduction with skull tong traction and serial neurological checks, followed by surgical stabilisation

Early closed reduction in an awake patient who can report neurological change is widely practised. MRI before reduction is advised in patients who cannot be examined or when reduction fails, because of disc herniation.
After ACDF through a right-sided approach, a patient has hoarseness and unilateral vocal cord palsy. The most likely cause is:
Recurrent laryngeal nerve traction or compression

Retractor pressure and endotracheal tube cuff pressure are common causes; most recover in weeks to months. The right RLN runs a less predictable course, though injury rates are similar from either side.

A diabetic man has bilateral saddle anaesthesia, bladder and bowel dysfunction and absent bulbocavernosus reflex, with relatively mild leg weakness and preserved ankle reflexes. The likely level is the:

Conus lesions cause early, symmetrical sphincter and sacral sensory loss, with mild or no root pain and may mix upper and lower motor neuron signs. Cauda equina lesions are more often asymmetrical, painful and radicular.
Axial CT of a young man's spine shows a small lucent nidus with dense surrounding sclerosis in the pedicle–lamina junction of L2, with painful scoliosis relieved by aspirin. Diagnosis:

Spinal osteoid osteomas favour the posterior elements, especially the lamina and pedicle, and produce painful scoliosis with the lesion on the concave side. Excision or ablation usually relieves pain and allows the curve to resolve if treated early.
A patient with a cardiac pacemaker needs imaging for suspected cauda equina compression. The best alternative if MRI is not safe is:
Many modern pacemakers are MRI-conditional, so check with cardiology first. If MRI is contraindicated, CT myelography shows the thecal sac and nerve root compression.
Two weeks after lumbar discectomy, a patient has severe back pain and muscle spasm without fever. CRP is rising and MRI shows disc space enhancement with end-plate oedema. Diagnosis:
Severe pain out of proportion and a rising CRP after the normal early postoperative peak suggest infection, usually staphylococcal. CT-guided biopsy or surgical sampling guides antibiotics.
In the Wiltse classification, isthmic spondylolisthesis (type II) includes:
A pars defect from a stress fracture, an elongated intact pars, or an acute pars fracture

Type I is dysplastic, II isthmic (IIA lytic, IIB elongated pars, IIC acute fracture), III degenerative, IV traumatic, V pathological and VI postsurgical. Isthmic L5–S1 slips are most common in young people.
In the buffy-coat method of preparing platelet-rich plasma, after the first spin the platelets are concentrated in:
The red cell layer at the bottom
The buffy coat between the red cells and plasma
The thin buffy coat contains platelets and leucocytes; leucocyte-rich PRP is made from it. The plasma-based method collects mainly the upper plasma, giving leucocyte-poor PRP.
A 9-month-old has short stature like his brother, frontal bossing and short proximal limbs. The pelvis radiograph shows a 'champagne glass' pelvic inlet. Diagnosis:

Achondroplasia (FGFR3) shows rhizomelia, frontal bossing, trident hands, squared iliac wings, flat acetabula and a narrowing interpedicular distance in the lumbar spine. Foramen magnum stenosis needs monitoring in infancy.
On a lateral radiograph of the calcaneus, a dense ring-like sclerotic outline around a central fatty lucency within the bone suggests:

Intraosseous lipomas commonly occur in the calcaneal neutral triangle and often contain central calcification ('cockade' or target appearance). Fat density on CT or MRI confirms them, and most need no treatment.
The C8 nerve root exits the spinal canal between:
There are eight cervical nerves but seven vertebrae, so C8 exits below C7 and each thoracic nerve then exits below its own vertebra. A C7–T1 disc herniation affects C8.
When reducing a cervical facet dislocation with Gardner-Wells tongs, traction typically starts at about:
About 4.5 kg (10 lb), adding about 2–5 kg per level
Weight is added in increments with radiographs and neurological checks after each, up to about a third of body weight in some protocols. Overdistraction must be avoided.
The Bunnell–Littler test distinguishes intrinsic tightness from PIP capsular tightness by:
Comparing PIP flexion with the MCP held in extension and in flexion
If PIP flexion is limited with the MCP extended but improves with the MCP flexed, the intrinsics are tight. If it is limited in both positions, the PIP capsule or joint is the cause.
After an acute high-grade posterolateral corner injury, delaying surgery beyond about 3 weeks is a concern mainly because:
Primary repair becomes difficult, so reconstruction is needed, with poorer results
Scarring and retraction make anatomical repair hard after about 2–3 weeks; delayed reconstruction has higher failure rates. Chronic varus malalignment may also need high tibial osteotomy first.
The anterior cruciate ligament receives most of its blood supply from the:
Popliteal artery directly through the menisci
Branches of the middle genicular artery and synovial vessels supply the ACL; the bony attachments contribute little, which partly explains poor healing of midsubstance tears.
The deep deltoid ligament mainly resists:
Lateral translation and external rotation of the talus
The deep deltoid (anterior and posterior tibiotalar fibres) is the primary medial restraint to talar shift. Its rupture with a fibular fracture makes the injury unstable, functionally bimalleolar.
After a first-time lateral patellar dislocation without an osteochondral fragment, the usual treatment is:
Short immobilisation then physiotherapy focusing on quadriceps and hip strengthening

Most first-time dislocations are managed non-operatively. Surgery is considered for osteochondral fractures, recurrent instability, or high-risk anatomy such as severe trochlear dysplasia and patella alta.
In the normal lumbar spine, the interpedicular distance on an AP radiograph:
Widens progressively from L1 to L5
Is the same at all levels
Progressive widening is normal. In achondroplasia it narrows caudally, which predisposes to spinal stenosis; abnormal widening suggests an intraspinal mass.
The most important lateral stabiliser of the elbow against posterolateral rotatory instability is the:
The LUCL runs from the lateral epicondyle to the supinator crest of the ulna. Its deficiency causes PLRI, shown by the lateral pivot-shift test and chair push-up test.
Which is NOT a usual indication for reverse total shoulder arthroplasty?
Massive irreparable cuff tear with pseudoparalysis
Comminuted proximal humerus fracture in an older patient
Primary osteoarthritis in a 45-year-old manual worker with an intact cuff and deltoid paralysis

A non-functioning deltoid is a contraindication, and young patients with intact cuffs are better served by anatomic arthroplasty. Reverse arthroplasty is used for cuff deficiency, fractures in older patients and some revisions.
To best assess and palpate the lateral collateral ligament of the knee, the knee is placed in:
Figure-of-four position (hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, knee flexed)

In the figure-of-four position the LCL becomes a palpable taut cord between the lateral epicondyle and fibular head. Varus stress at 30° flexion isolates the LCL; laxity at 0° suggests added cruciate injury.
The best predictor of final knee range of motion after TKA is:

Preoperative flexion strongly predicts postoperative flexion. Stiff knees need extensile exposure and careful balancing; manipulation under anaesthesia is considered if progress stalls in the first few months.
Flexor hallucis longus arises mainly from the:
Lower two-thirds of the posterior fibula

FHL runs behind the talus between the posterior tubercles and under the sustentaculum tali. Tibialis posterior arises from tibia, fibula and the interosseous membrane, and FDL from the posterior tibia.
On biopsy, myositis ossificans shows a 'zonal' pattern with:
Immature cells at the periphery and mature bone in the centre
Mature lamellar bone at the periphery and immature proliferating cells in the centre
Peripheral maturation distinguishes it from osteosarcoma, which is most immature at the periphery. Lesions mature over 6–8 weeks; excision, if needed, waits until maturity.
Which is a marker of bone resorption rather than formation?
CTX (C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen)
CTX, NTX, deoxypyridinoline and TRAP-5b reflect resorption. Bone-specific ALP, osteocalcin and P1NP reflect formation. CTX and P1NP are the reference markers for monitoring osteoporosis treatment.
Fewer than two consecutive sagittal MRI slices showing the 'bow-tie' appearance of the meniscal body suggests:
Bucket-handle tear with a displaced fragment

A normal meniscal body (about 10 mm wide) appears as a bow-tie on two adjacent 4–5 mm slices. Loss of it suggests a displaced bucket-handle fragment, often with a double PCL or flipped meniscus sign. More than two bow-ties suggests a discoid meniscus.
The 'lethal triad' that prompts damage-control orthopaedics in polytrauma is:
These feed on each other and predict death. Temporary external fixation and resuscitation come first, with definitive fixation once the patient is stabilised.
Adductor pollicis is supplied by the:
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Superficial branch of the ulnar nerve
Its weakness causes Froment's sign. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles except adductor pollicis and the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.
Loss of thumb opposition with thenar wasting (ape-thumb deformity) indicates injury to the:
Median nerve (or its recurrent motor branch)
Opponens pollicis and abductor pollicis brevis are median-innervated. Opponensplasty (for example with FDS of the ring finger or EIP) restores opposition when recovery fails.
In ankylosing spondylitis, the occiput-to-wall distance measures:
Thoracic kyphosis and cervical flexion deformity

With heels and back against a wall, the patient tries to touch the wall with the back of the head; any gap reflects fixed thoracic and cervical kyphosis. The modified Schober test assesses lumbar flexion.
Supracondylar periprosthetic femoral fractures above a TKA, by fracture level

Type I is proximal to the femoral component, type II starts at the proximal edge of the component and extends upwards, and type III is entirely distal to the upper edge of the component. Location determines whether a nail, plate or distal femoral replacement suits best.
Which statement about the cruciate ligaments is true?
The PCL is twice as weak as the ACL
Both are covered by a synovial fold, so a torn ACL bleeds into the joint. The PCL is broader and roughly twice as strong as the ACL.
Which is NOT part of the 'biceps pulley' (rotator interval) stabilising the long head of biceps in the bicipital groove?
Transverse humeral ligament as a primary stabiliser
Supraspinatus and subscapularis fibres bordering the interval

The pulley sling is formed by the coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments with fibres of subscapularis and supraspinatus. The transverse humeral ligament contributes little. Pulley lesions cause biceps instability and anterior shoulder pain.
Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease most commonly presents at:
Boys are affected about four to five times as often as girls. Onset after 8 years and lateral pillar collapse predict worse outcomes.
Primary aneurysmal bone cysts of long bones most commonly arise in the:

They are eccentric, expansile and contain fluid–fluid levels. Treatment options include curettage with adjuvants and grafting, sclerotherapy (for example polidocanol) and denosumab for unresectable lesions.
A volar rim fracture of the distal radius
An oblique radial styloid fracture from a direct blow or force transmitted through the scaphoid
The styloid carries the radioscaphocapitate ligament, so the fracture may accompany scapholunate or perilunate injury. Displaced fractures are fixed with screws.
The fabella is usually found in the tendon of the:
It articulates with the posterior lateral femoral condyle and anchors the fabellofibular ligament. Fabella syndrome causes posterolateral pain and can irritate the common peroneal nerve.
Which statement about the menisci is FALSE?
The medial meniscus is C-shaped and more firmly attached
The lateral meniscus is more mobile
The menisci carry about half of the load in extension
The menisci are fully vascular throughout their width
Only the peripheral 10–30% is vascular. The lateral meniscus covers more of its plateau and carries a greater share of lateral compartment load than the medial meniscus does medially.
A young cricketer has a displaced (more than 2 mm) bony avulsion of the PCL from its tibial attachment. Best management:
Open reduction and screw or suture fixation through a posterior approach
Bony avulsions heal well after anatomical fixation, giving better results than ligament reconstruction. The posteromedial Burks–Schaffer approach exposes the tibial attachment.
The female athlete triad consists of:
Low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density
It now sits within the broader concept of relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S), which also affects men. Stress fractures, especially in trabecular-rich sites, are a common presentation.
Which is a contraindication to negative pressure wound therapy?
Exposed major blood vessels or untreated osteomyelitis

Placing NPWT directly over exposed vessels, organs or anastomoses risks bleeding; malignancy in the wound and untreated infection are also contraindications. It is useful as a temporary dressing until definitive cover.
A child has recurrent fractures with minor trauma, blue sclerae and conductive hearing loss in the family. The most likely diagnosis is:
Classic OI is a type I collagen defect. Hearing loss often starts in adolescence or early adulthood. Bisphosphonates reduce fractures; telescopic rods treat recurrent long-bone deformity.
The recommended screening test for protective sensation in a diabetic foot is:
Joint position sense of the toes
Inability to feel the 10 g monofilament at specified sites indicates loss of protective sensation and high ulcer risk. A 128 Hz tuning fork and ankle reflexes add information.
Chondrocalcinosis of the knee menisci on radiographs is most typical of:

CPPD causes linear calcification of fibrocartilage (menisci, TFCC, symphysis) and hyaline cartilage. Associations include haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia, which should be looked for in younger patients.
Which is NOT a red flag in a patient with low back pain?
Night pain and unexplained weight loss
Pain worse on prolonged sitting that eases with walking

Red flags (cancer, infection, fracture, cauda equina) include age over 50 with new pain, cancer history, fever, immunosuppression, weight loss, night pain, trauma or osteoporosis, and neurological deficit. Mechanical pain without these features rarely needs early imaging.
The strongest known risk factor for symptomatic lumbar disc degeneration is:
Twin studies show heredity explains most of the variance in disc degeneration, more than occupational loading. Smoking and obesity contribute smaller effects.
A 6-year-old has painful torticollis for 3 weeks after a throat infection. CT shows rotatory subluxation of C1 on C2. Diagnosis:
Inflammation spreading from the pharynx loosens the C1–C2 ligaments. Early cases respond to antibiotics, a collar or halter traction; chronic fixed subluxation may need fusion.
During spinal shock after a high cervical cord injury, which combination is typical?
Bradycardia, hypotension and absent reflexes including the bulbocavernosus reflex
Tachycardia with absent bulbocavernosus reflex only
Loss of sympathetic tone with unopposed vagal activity causes neurogenic shock (bradycardia, hypotension). Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex marks the end of spinal shock.
A trauma patient with hip pain has normal pelvic and hip radiographs, but an occult femoral neck fracture is suspected. The best next investigation is:

MRI is highly sensitive and specific within hours of injury and shows other injuries such as pubic rami fractures. CT is an alternative if MRI is unavailable but can miss undisplaced fractures in osteoporotic bone.
Sciatic nerve injury during THA is most likely in:
Revision THA, developmental dysplasia with lengthening over about 4 cm, and posterior approaches
Excessive lengthening, retractor placement, cement extrusion and haematoma increase the risk. The peroneal division is affected most. Shortening osteotomy is used when large lengthening is needed.
A complication specific to computer-navigated TKA is:
Fracture through the tracker pin sites in the femur or tibia
Bicortical pins near the diaphysis create stress risers; using small unicortical pins in metaphyseal bone or within the incision reduces the risk.
Which is NOT a knee outcome score?
The Harris Hip Score is used for hip arthroplasty. Knee scores include the Oxford Knee Score, Knee Society Score, KOOS and WOMAC.
In patients with a severe IgE-mediated penicillin allergy having orthopaedic surgery, the usual prophylactic antibiotic is:

Most penicillin-allergic patients can safely receive cefazolin because cross-reactivity is low, but those with anaphylaxis are given clindamycin or vancomycin. Vancomycin should start 60–120 minutes before incision because of its slow infusion.
Which statement about synovial sarcoma is FALSE?
It carries the SS18–SSX fusion, t(X;18)
It commonly occurs near large joints in young adults
Calcification is seen in about a third
It arises from synovial lining inside joints in most cases
Despite its name, synovial sarcoma rarely arises within a joint and does not derive from synovium. It often grows slowly and may be mistaken for a benign lesion. It is relatively chemosensitive.
Which treatment for knee osteoarthritis does the AAOS guideline recommend against?
Hyaluronic acid injections as routine treatment
Total knee arthroplasty for end-stage disease

The AAOS guideline does not recommend routine use of hyaluronic acid because of a lack of meaningful benefit, and is against arthroscopic lavage and debridement for primary knee OA. Exercise, weight loss, NSAIDs and education are strongly supported.
Madura foot (mycetoma) is characterised by the triad of a painless swelling, multiple discharging sinuses and:

Grain colour helps identify the organism: black grains suggest fungal Madurella, while white, yellow or red grains are usually actinomycetes. Actinomycetoma responds to prolonged antibiotic combinations; eumycetoma needs antifungals with surgery.
Which statement about Ponseti treatment of clubfoot is FALSE?
The first cast corrects cavus by supinating the forefoot
The talar head is the fulcrum for abduction
Pronation of the forefoot is used early to correct deformity
A tenotomy is often needed for residual equinus
Pronating the forefoot early worsens the cavus. The forefoot is supinated first to align it with the hindfoot, then the foot is abducted around the talar head.
A 6-month-old has anterolateral bowing of the tibia with cystic change at the apex. The child has several café-au-lait spots. The most important management principle is:
Protect the leg with a brace to prevent fracture, avoiding osteotomy

Anterolateral bowing with NF1 risks congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia; osteotomy for cosmesis can precipitate non-union. Established pseudarthrosis is treated with resection and intramedullary fixation, graft, Ilizarov techniques or vascularised fibula.
Which is NOT a usual component of infantile Blount disease?

Infantile Blount disease combines varus, procurvatum and internal tibial torsion of the proximal tibia. Adolescent Blount disease is more often seen in obese teenagers and may include distal femoral varus.
Under WADA rules, intravenous infusions or injections without a therapeutic use exemption are prohibited if they exceed:

Infusions over 100 mL per 12 hours are banned (except in hospital treatment, surgery or clinical investigation) because they can mask doping or alter blood values. Dehydrated athletes should be rehydrated orally when possible.
Daily calcium intake usually recommended for athletes at risk of bone stress injury is about:
Adequate calcium and vitamin D, together with sufficient energy intake, reduce stress fracture risk, particularly in female athletes and military recruits.
When were gene and cell doping first added to WADA's Prohibited List?
Gene doping was added in 2003, early in WADA's history, to cover the non-therapeutic use of genes, genetic elements or cells to enhance performance.
Osteoblastoma most commonly occurs in the:
About a third or more arise in the spinal posterior elements. Unlike osteoid osteoma, the lesion is over 2 cm, NSAIDs help less and it can behave aggressively, so excision or curettage is needed.
ALVAL (aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesion) around a hip arthroplasty is mainly a:
Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to metal ions
ALVAL is a T-cell–mediated response to cobalt and chromium, seen mainly with metal-on-metal bearings and taper corrosion. It can occur at modest wear rates and destroy soft tissues.
Brodie abscess is a form of:

It is a localised abscess walled off by sclerotic reactive bone, typically in the tibial metaphysis of children and young adults, often with mild symptoms and normal blood tests. Curettage and antibiotics are curative.
Which spinal instrumentation system is applied anteriorly rather than posteriorly?

Dwyer used vertebral body screws connected by a cable on the convex side, compressing it to correct scoliosis; Zielke later added a solid rod. Harrington, Luque and Cotrel–Dubousset are posterior systems.
With the arm abducted to 90° and externally rotated, the main static restraint against anterior shoulder dislocation is the:
Anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament

The IGHL complex tightens anteriorly in abduction and external rotation; the Bankart lesion detaches it with the labrum. The SGHL and coracohumeral ligament resist inferior translation with the arm at the side.
A 70-year-old has numbness only in the dorsal first web space of the foot. The nerve affected is the:

The deep peroneal nerve supplies the first web space after passing under the extensor retinaculum (anterior tarsal tunnel). The superficial peroneal nerve supplies most of the dorsum, the sural nerve the lateral border and the saphenous nerve the medial side.
In adults, cells of the nucleus pulposus receive nutrition mainly by:
Diffusion through the vertebral end plates
The adult disc is the largest avascular structure in the body. End-plate calcification with age reduces diffusion, contributing to cell death and degeneration.
With ageing, the nucleus pulposus shows:
Loss of proteoglycans and a rise in the keratan sulphate to chondroitin sulphate ratio

Proteoglycan and water content fall, collagen becomes more fibrous (more type I) and the keratan sulphate to chondroitin sulphate ratio rises. The disc loses height and its ability to distribute load.
An 'engaging' Hill–Sachs lesion is a defect of the:
Posterosuperolateral humeral head that engages the anterior glenoid rim in abduction and external rotation
Large posterolateral defects that drop over the glenoid rim cause recurrent instability. Remplissage (infraspinatus capsulotenodesis into the defect) or bony procedures address them.
High-level disinfection of heat-sensitive arthroscopes with 2% glutaraldehyde needs immersion for about:
20 minutes (for high-level disinfection); about 10 hours for sterilisation

Glutaraldehyde achieves high-level disinfection in about 20 minutes but needs about 10 hours to be sporicidal. Low-temperature methods such as hydrogen peroxide plasma or ethylene oxide sterilise heat-sensitive instruments more reliably.
In the Spaulding classification, items that enter sterile tissue, such as implants and arthroscopic instruments, are classed as:
Critical items need sterilisation; semi-critical items (contacting mucous membranes) need high-level disinfection; non-critical items (contacting intact skin) need cleaning or low-level disinfection.
During an anterior approach to the cervical spine, which statement is correct?
The plane is between the carotid sheath laterally and the trachea and oesophagus medially
The approach goes lateral to the carotid sheath
The vertebral artery is routinely exposed
The thoracic duct is at risk at C3

The Smith–Robinson approach develops the interval between the carotid sheath and the visceral column. The recurrent laryngeal nerve, superior laryngeal nerve, oesophagus and sympathetic chain are at risk; the thoracic duct is at risk low on the left.
In the lumbar spine, the motion that facet orientation allows most freely is:
Lateral bending in the upper lumbar spine only
Sagittally oriented lumbar facets permit flexion–extension and restrict rotation. Thoracic facets in the coronal plane allow rotation, limited by the rib cage.
After a lateral patellar dislocation, the most consistent soft-tissue injury is:

The MPFL, the main restraint to lateral translation in early flexion, tears in nearly all dislocations, usually at its femoral attachment or patellar side. Bone bruising of the medial patella and lateral femoral condyle is typical on MRI.
An Ogden-type construct for periprosthetic femoral fractures around a hip stem combines:
A plate secured with cerclage wires or cables around the stem proximally and screws distally
Where screws cannot pass the stem, cables provide proximal fixation; locking attachment plates and unicortical screws are modern alternatives. It is used for Vancouver B1 and C fractures.
During elbow arthroscopy, which step does NOT help avoid nerve injury?
Distending the joint with fluid before portal placement
Making only skin incisions and spreading bluntly
Placing the anteromedial portal without knowing whether the ulnar nerve subluxes
The ulnar nerve may subluxate anteriorly over the medial epicondyle, so it must be palpated before medial portals. Distension and flexion move the anterior nerves away from the capsule.
MRI of a vertebral body shows a lesion that is bright on T1 and T2 with a 'polka-dot' appearance on axial CT. Diagnosis:

Fat within a typical haemangioma gives high T1 signal, and thickened vertical trabeculae give the polka-dot and corduroy signs. Aggressive haemangiomas with low T1 signal and soft-tissue extension may need embolisation, vertebroplasty or surgery.
Which tumour is often treated with stereotactic radiosurgery (such as CyberKnife) when complete resection would be too morbid?
Chordoma of the sacrum or clivus
Chordoma resists conventional radiotherapy, so high-dose techniques such as stereotactic radiosurgery or proton/carbon-ion therapy are used, especially for upper sacral and skull-base tumours.
For a below-knee amputation in a patient with peripheral vascular disease, the preferred flap is:
The posterior calf skin and gastrocnemius have a better blood supply than the anterior skin. The tibia is bevelled anteriorly and the fibula cut about 1 cm shorter.
Three weeks after lumbar discectomy, the original leg pain has returned after an initial pain-free period. The most likely cause is:

Early recurrence after a pain-free interval suggests reherniation at the same level; MRI with contrast distinguishes disc (non-enhancing) from scar (enhancing). Wrong-level surgery causes pain that never improves.
Overall, the most frequent complication after knee arthroscopy is:
Haemarthrosis is the most common early complication, especially after lateral release or synovectomy. Infection and DVT are uncommon but serious.
A professional wrestler has had about 20 anterior shoulder dislocations. CT shows 25% anterior glenoid bone loss. The best procedure is:
Contact athletes with recurrent dislocations and significant glenoid loss have high failure rates after soft-tissue repair. The Latarjet adds bone and the sling effect of the conjoint tendon.
A patient has leg pain worse on standing and walking, a positive Trendelenburg sign and weak EHL and ankle dorsiflexion. The root most likely involved is:

L5 supplies gluteus medius, EHL and tibialis anterior partly, so L5 radiculopathy causes a Trendelenburg gait and foot drop. L4 involves the quadriceps and knee reflex; S1 plantarflexion and the ankle reflex.

A 65-year-old has progressive cervical myelopathy. Radiographs show flowing ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament and bridging osteophytes on the right side of the thoracic spine with preserved discs and normal sacroiliac joints. The most likely condition is:

DISH requires flowing ossification across at least four contiguous vertebrae with preserved disc height and no SI joint ankylosis. It is associated with diabetes and obesity, and with OPLL in some patients, which can cause myelopathy.
The most common spinal ependymoma is the myxopapillary type, which typically arises in the:
Myxopapillary ependymomas are slow-growing tumours of young adults causing back pain and sciatica. Complete en bloc removal is curative; piecemeal removal risks CSF seeding.
Which statement about the reamer–irrigator–aspirator (RIA) is FALSE?
It harvests large volumes of autograft from the femoral canal
Graft quality is comparable to iliac crest
It causes less donor-site pain than iliac crest harvest
It carries no risk of femoral fracture
Eccentric reaming can thin the cortex and cause fracture, and blood loss can be significant. It is useful for large defects such as the Masquelet technique.
At 3 years of age, the normal tibiofemoral angle is about:
Children pass from varus at birth, to neutral at about 18–24 months, to maximum valgus at 3–4 years, then settle to about 5–7° adult valgus by about 7 years.
A 'herringbone' pattern of spindle cells on histology is classically associated with:

Fascicles of spindle cells arranged in a herringbone pattern are typical of adult fibrosarcoma, which is now a diagnosis of exclusion. Biphasic spindle and epithelial patterns suggest synovial sarcoma.
Which is NOT a recognised cause of hallux varus after bunion surgery?
Excessive resection of the medial eminence

Overcorrection (over-release laterally, fibular sesamoid excision, excess medial eminence resection, overtightened medial capsule, over-correction of the IMA) causes hallux varus. Undercorrection leads to recurrent valgus.
A 44-year-old with long-standing hip pain walks with a lurch towards the affected side in stance. This gait mainly reduces:
The abductor force needed by moving the centre of gravity over the hip

An antalgic or compensated Trendelenburg gait shifts the trunk over the painful hip, shortening the body-weight lever arm and lowering joint reaction force. A stick in the opposite hand has a similar effect.
After TKA for a severe valgus knee, a complication to watch for particularly is:

Correcting valgus with flexion contracture stretches the peroneal nerve; treatment is to remove compressive dressings and flex the knee. Lateral release, instability and patellar maltracking are other issues.
A runner has tibial pain with normal radiographs. The best investigation for a suspected stress fracture is:
MRI detects early marrow oedema and grades bone stress injuries, guiding return to sport. Bone scans are sensitive but non-specific and involve radiation. Radiographs may stay normal for weeks.
A 19-year-old gymnast has back pain on extension for 3 months, relieved by rest. Single-leg hyperextension reproduces it. The most likely diagnosis is:
Repeated extension and rotation load the pars interarticularis. MRI (or SPECT/CT) detects early stress reaction; most heal or settle with rest and bracing.
Which statement about paediatric cervical spine injury is FALSE?
Upper cervical injuries are more common in young children because of a large head and lax ligaments
SCIWORA can occur because the spine stretches more than the cord
Pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3 can be normal
Injuries most commonly affect the lower cervical spine in children under 8

In children under about 8, injuries cluster at C1–C3 because the fulcrum of motion is higher; after that, the pattern becomes adult-like. A cut-out board or occipital padding avoids forced flexion during immobilisation.
A 5-year-old has a painful limp for 2 days, fever of 38.2 °C, ESR 25 mm/h and a normal white cell count but can bear weight. The most likely diagnosis is:
With one of the Kocher criteria (fever) the probability of septic arthritis is low. CRP above about 20 mg/L adds weight. Children who fail to improve or worsen need aspiration.
The anteromedial portal in ankle arthroscopy is placed:
Just medial to the tibialis anterior tendon at the joint line
It lies medial to tibialis anterior, away from the saphenous nerve and vein. The anterolateral portal is lateral to peroneus tertius, where branches of the superficial peroneal nerve are at risk.
A young cricketer cannot fully extend his knee after a twisting injury, and MRI shows a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear. The best treatment is:
Arthroscopic reduction with repair where possible, otherwise partial meniscectomy
A locked knee needs prompt arthroscopy. Repair is favoured in young patients with peripheral (red-red or red-white) tears, especially with concurrent ACL reconstruction.
After PCL reconstruction, the most common problem is:

Some posterior laxity often persists because of graft stretching and the 'killer turn' at the tibial tunnel. Early prone rehabilitation and bracing that supports the tibia reduce this. Popliteal artery injury is the most feared but rare complication.
The Andrews lesion seen in throwing athletes is:
A tear of the anterosuperior glenoid labrum near the biceps origin

Andrews described anterosuperior labral tears near the long head of biceps in throwers, attributed to biceps traction during deceleration. They were early descriptions before SLAP lesions were classified.
For fixation of a scaphoid waist fracture, the volar approach is often preferred over the dorsal approach because it:
Gives better access to the proximal pole
Avoids the dorsal ridge vessels that supply most of the scaphoid

The main blood supply enters through the dorsal ridge, so a dorsal approach for waist fractures risks it. Proximal pole fractures are usually fixed dorsally because the screw must start in the small proximal fragment.
In a Schenck KD III-L knee dislocation, the injured structures are:
ACL and PCL with the MCL
ACL and PCL with the LCL/posterolateral corner

KD I involves one cruciate, KD II both cruciates with intact collaterals, KD III both cruciates with one side (M or L), KD IV both cruciates and both sides, and KD V adds a periarticular fracture. KD III-L carries a high rate of peroneal nerve injury.
The most common site of clavicle fracture is the:
About 80% are midshaft. Lateral third fractures medial to the coracoclavicular ligaments (Neer type II) have a high non-union rate because the medial fragment is pulled up.
In Mirels scoring of an impending pathological fracture, which combination scores the maximum of 3 points each?
Upper limb, mild pain, blastic, under one-third of the cortex
Peritrochanteric site, functional pain, lytic lesion, over two-thirds of the cortex
Lower limb, moderate pain, mixed, one-third to two-thirds
Upper limb, functional pain, blastic, over two-thirds
Site (upper limb 1, lower limb 2, peritrochanteric 3), pain, lesion type (blastic 1, mixed 2, lytic 3) and size are scored. A total of 9 or more favours prophylactic fixation.
After an acute Achilles tendon rupture, which is NOT a technique for acute repair?
V–Y advancement as the standard acute repair
V–Y advancement and flexor hallucis longus transfer are used for chronic ruptures with a gap. Acute ruptures are repaired open, mini-open or percutaneously, or treated with functional rehabilitation.
Which structure is NOT part of the posteromedial (semimembranosus) corner of the knee?

The posteromedial corner comprises the posterior oblique ligament, semimembranosus and its expansions, the oblique popliteal ligament, the posteromedial capsule and the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. The popliteofibular ligament belongs to the posterolateral corner.
A Perthes lesion of the shoulder is:
An anteroinferior labral avulsion with the scapular periosteum stripped but intact, so the labrum may look undisplaced
Humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament

Because the periosteal sleeve stays attached, the labrum may sit in a near-normal position and be missed on MRI; ABER positioning helps. An ALPSA lesion is the same sleeve healed medially down the glenoid neck.
At shoulder arthroscopy, a Buford complex is:
A normal variant with an absent anterosuperior labrum and a thick, cord-like middle glenohumeral ligament
It must not be repaired: sewing the cord-like MGHL to the glenoid causes severe loss of external rotation. A sublabral foramen is another normal anterosuperior variant.
Which is NOT a recognised factor contributing to the higher ACL tear rate in female athletes?
Greater dynamic knee valgus on landing
Quadriceps-dominant landing with less hamstring activation

Females tend to have a lower hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, which reduces protection. Neuromuscular training programmes that improve landing mechanics lower ACL injury rates. Hormonal effects on ligament laxity have also been suggested.
A force platform in a gait or sports laboratory measures:
Ground reaction forces and centre of pressure
Combined with motion capture, ground reaction forces allow joint moments and powers to be calculated (inverse dynamics). They are used to study landing, jumping and running mechanics.
Which is NOT a proposed benefit of compression garments for athletes?
A large increase in maximal strength
Evidence shows modest benefits in perceived soreness and recovery. They do not meaningfully increase maximal strength or power.
In knees with chronic ACL deficiency, the meniscal tear most commonly found is in the:
Posterior horn of the medial meniscus
The posterior horn of the medial meniscus acts as a secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation and fails with repeated instability. Acute ACL tears more often involve the lateral meniscus.
Which statement about the Ganga Hospital open injury score is FALSE?
It separately scores bone, covering tissues and the functional tissues (muscles and tendons)
A total of 14 or more favours amputation
It was designed for open fractures of the forearm only

The score was designed for open tibial fractures and helps decide between salvage and amputation and plan reconstruction. Scores of 17–20 are strongly associated with amputation, and 14 or more suggests a poor salvage prognosis.
The knee joint is best classified as a:
Modified hinge (bicondylar) synovial joint with rotation
It combines flexion–extension with rolling, gliding and rotation, including the screw-home mechanism. The patellofemoral joint is a separate plane-type articulation within the same capsule.
A positive Galeazzi (Allis) sign, with one knee lower than the other when the child lies with hips and knees flexed, indicates:
Leg-length or apparent femoral length difference, as in unilateral hip dislocation
It is unreliable in bilateral DDH, where both sides appear equal. Tibial shortening also gives a positive sign, so the source must be identified.
Paralysis of gluteus maximus mainly causes:
A backward lurch of the trunk at heel strike (gluteus maximus lurch)
The trunk is thrown backwards to keep the hip extended in early stance. Gluteus medius weakness causes the Trendelenburg gait, and ankle dorsiflexor weakness causes a high-stepping gait.
A Gustilo–Anderson type IIIC open fracture is defined by:
An arterial injury requiring repair, regardless of wound size
IIIC refers to vascular injury needing repair, which carries the highest amputation rate. Restoring perfusion (shunt, then repair) comes before definitive fixation, with fasciotomy.
Which statement about congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia is FALSE?
It is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1
Treatment often uses intramedullary rods with graft or circular frames

The hamartomatous tissue at the pseudarthrosis heals poorly, so casting alone rarely succeeds. Bracing protects before fracture; established cases need resection, grafting and stable fixation, sometimes a vascularised fibula.
External snapping hip is caused by:
The iliopsoas tendon over the iliopectineal eminence
The iliotibial band or gluteus maximus slipping over the greater trochanter
External snapping is often visible and common in dancers and runners. Internal snapping involves the iliopsoas tendon; intra-articular snapping suggests a labral tear or loose body.
The definitive test for chronic exertional compartment syndrome is:
Compartment pressure measurement before and after exercise
Exercise-related pressures (such as the Pedowitz criteria) confirm the diagnosis. MRI helps exclude stress fractures and other causes of exertional leg pain.
Is the most commonly symptomatic plica
Runs from the infrapatellar fat pad to the intercondylar notch, anterior to the ACL, and rarely causes symptoms
Is attached to the medial meniscus
It may be mistaken for the ACL at arthroscopy. The medial plica is the one most often symptomatic.
With the knee flexed 90° and the tibia internally rotated, the knee is extended; pain appears at about 30° and is relieved by external rotation. This Wilson test suggests:
Osteochondritis dissecans of the lateral part of the medial femoral condyle
Internal rotation brings the tibial spine against the classic OCD site. The test has limited sensitivity; MRI confirms and stages the lesion.
In the Outerbridge classification, grade IV cartilage damage is:
Full-thickness loss with exposed subchondral bone

Grade I is softening, II partial-thickness fissuring under 1.5 cm, III fissuring over 1.5 cm reaching deep layers, and IV exposed bone. Arthroscopy remains the reference standard for grading cartilage damage.
Occur only without a meniscal tear
Arise from horizontal cleavage tears and present as a joint-line swelling
Are best treated by excising the cyst alone
Synovial fluid is pumped through a horizontal tear into the parameniscal tissue. Treating the tear arthroscopically with cyst decompression reduces recurrence; excision alone often fails.
The Gillquist portal in knee arthroscopy is a:
Central transpatellar tendon portal used to reach the posterior compartment through the notch
Placed through the patellar tendon about 1 cm below the patella, it allows the arthroscope to pass between the cruciates into the posterior compartment.
During inside-out repair of the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, the structure at greatest risk is the:
A posterolateral incision with a retractor placed anterior to the biceps femoris and lateral head of gastrocnemius protects the peroneal nerve. Medial repairs endanger the saphenous nerve.
To limit wear and fatigue failure, tibial polyethylene inserts in TKA should be at least about:

Thin inserts (below about 6–8 mm of polyethylene) have high contact stresses and fail by delamination and pitting, especially with older non-crosslinked material. Excessive bone resection should not be compensated by very thick inserts.
In an inversion ankle sprain, the lateral ligaments usually fail in which order?
The ATFL is weakest and taut in plantarflexion, so it fails first. The PTFL is strongest and injured only with severe injuries or dislocation.
In the Lauge-Hansen supination–external rotation pattern, the first structure to fail is the:
SER stages are: I AITFL, II spiral fibular fracture, III posterior malleolus or PITFL, IV medial malleolus or deltoid. A vertical medial malleolar fracture suggests supination–adduction instead.
Which structure passes through the greater sciatic notch below piriformis?

Below piriformis lie the sciatic, inferior gluteal and posterior femoral cutaneous nerves, the pudendal nerve and vessels, and the nerves to obturator internus and quadratus femoris. Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above it.
Compared with first-generation autologous chondrocyte implantation, second-generation ACI:
Uses a periosteal flap to cover the cells
Uses a collagen membrane instead of periosteum, reducing graft hypertrophy
Is done in a single stage without biopsy
Periosteal patches often hypertrophied, needing revision. Collagen membranes (and third-generation matrix-seeded techniques) reduce this and simplify surgery.
In combined ACL and PCL reconstruction, which graft is usually tensioned and fixed first?
PCL, to restore the normal tibial step-off before fixing the ACL

Fixing the PCL first, with an anterior drawer, re-establishes the neutral tibial position; fixing the ACL first can lock the tibia in posterior subluxation. Collateral reconstructions are tensioned after the cruciates.
In articular cartilage, the tidemark separates:
The tidemark marks the mineralisation front; the cement line lies between calcified cartilage and subchondral bone. Microfracture must penetrate both to allow marrow cells to fill the defect.
Which is NOT a typical feature of fibrous dysplasia?
Shepherd's crook deformity of the femur
Fibrous dysplasia shows woven bone trabeculae without osteoblastic rimming. Osteoblastic rimming is typical of osteofibrous dysplasia and ossifying fibroma.
Protrusio acetabuli is defined radiographically when:
The femoral head lies medial to the ilioischial line (Köhler's line)

Medial displacement of the femoral head past Köhler's line, often with a centre-edge angle over 40°, defines protrusio. Causes include rheumatoid arthritis, Paget's disease, osteomalacia and Marfan syndrome.
Which antihypertensive class is prohibited at all times by WADA, because it can mask other drugs and cause rapid weight loss?
Diuretics are listed as masking agents and are banned in and out of competition. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are permitted; beta-blockers are banned only in certain precision sports.
Which knee condition is MRI LEAST reliable for?
Early chondromalacia (cartilage softening without surface defect)
MRI shows menisci, cruciates and bone oedema well, but softening without a surface defect (Outerbridge I) is often missed; arthroscopy remains more sensitive for early cartilage change.
Erb's point in the brachial plexus is formed where the:
C5 and C6 roots join to form the upper trunk

Six nerves meet there: the C5 and C6 roots, the upper trunk's anterior and posterior divisions, the suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius. Traction here causes Erb palsy, with the arm adducted and internally rotated ('waiter's tip').
During the 'screw-home' mechanism in the last degrees of knee extension:
The tibia internally rotates on the femur
The tibia externally rotates on the femur, locking the knee
The femur externally rotates on the fixed tibia

Because the medial femoral condyle is longer, the tibia externally rotates (or the femur internally rotates in weight-bearing) at terminal extension. Popliteus unlocks the knee by internally rotating the tibia.
When drilling the femoral tunnel for ACL reconstruction through an anteromedial portal (rather than transtibially), the main advantage is:
More anatomical, lower femoral tunnel placement independent of the tibial tunnel
Less risk to the peroneal nerve

Transtibial drilling tends to produce a vertical ('high noon') tunnel that leaves rotational instability. Anteromedial drilling needs knee hyperflexion to avoid a short tunnel and posterior wall blow-out.
Which statement about Achilles tendon rupture is FALSE?
It is common in middle-aged weekend athletes
Fluoroquinolones and steroid injections increase risk
A positive Thompson test shows absent plantarflexion on calf squeeze
Active plantarflexion is always lost, so it is never missed

Patients can often still plantarflex using tibialis posterior, the peroneals and long toe flexors, so ruptures are missed in a significant proportion. The Thompson test and a palpable gap are more reliable.
In Bigliani's classification, a type III acromion is:
Type III is most associated with rotator cuff tears and external impingement, although acromial shape may partly be acquired with age (spur formation).
The most commonly fractured carpal bone is the:
Scaphoid fractures are most common, followed by triquetral dorsal chip fractures. Waist fractures are most frequent, and proximal pole fractures carry the highest risk of non-union and AVN.
Mallet finger results from disruption of the extensor mechanism at its insertion into the:

The terminal tendon (or a bony fragment) is avulsed from the dorsal base of the distal phalanx. Continuous extension splinting of the DIP for 6–8 weeks treats most; volar subluxation of the distal phalanx needs fixation.
Which statement about jumper's knee (patellar tendinopathy) is FALSE?
It most often affects the proximal tendon at the inferior pole of the patella
It is common in basketball and volleyball
Eccentric decline squats are an effective treatment
It is primarily an acute inflammatory condition best treated with repeated steroid injections
It is a degenerative tendinopathy with failed healing rather than inflammation. Load management and progressive loading programmes are first-line; repeated steroid injections risk rupture.
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome of the leg most commonly affects the:
The anterior compartment is most often involved, followed by the lateral compartment. Symptoms appear at a predictable point in exercise and settle with rest.
Tilts the head to the same side and rotates the face to the opposite side
Tilts the head to the opposite side
Rotates the face to the same side
Both muscles together flex the neck. In congenital muscular torticollis, the tight muscle tilts the head towards the affected side with the chin turned away.
Bone is weakest when loaded in:
Cortical bone is strongest in compression, weaker in tension and weakest in shear. Spiral fractures from torsion fail initially in shear, then in tension.
Which radiographic view best shows an impacted femoral neck fracture?
AP pelvis with the hip externally rotated
AP with the hip in about 15° internal rotation, plus a cross-table lateral

Internal rotation brings the neck parallel to the film, showing its full length. External rotation foreshortens the neck and can hide an undisplaced fracture. MRI is used when radiographs are negative.
Which is NOT one of the classic '5 Ps' of compartment syndrome?
The classic signs are pain, paraesthesia, pallor, paralysis and pulselessness; pain on passive stretch is the earliest. Pulselessness and paralysis are late findings.
Gas within the intervertebral disc (vacuum phenomenon) on imaging is typical of:

Nitrogen collects in degenerative fissures and makes infection much less likely. Gas within a collapsed vertebral body (intravertebral cleft) suggests osteonecrosis (Kümmell disease) rather than malignancy.
In the Allen test of the hand, a positive (abnormal) result for the ulnar artery is:
Immediate flushing when the ulnar artery is released
Delayed or absent flushing of the palm after releasing the ulnar artery while the radial artery is still compressed
Loss of pulse with neck rotation

Both arteries are occluded, the patient opens and closes the fist, then one artery is released; flushing within about 5–7 seconds shows that artery fills the arch. The test is used before radial artery cannulation or harvest.
A fast bowler has radial-sided wrist pain; ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb held in the palm reproduces sharp pain over the radial styloid. The affected compartment contains:

De Quervain tenosynovitis involves the first dorsal compartment. Splinting and a steroid injection help most; surgical release must look for a separate EPB subcompartment and protect the superficial radial nerve.
A 'jailhouse' or corduroy pattern of vertical striations in a vertebral body on radiographs is typical of:
Thickened vertical trabeculae among fatty marrow cause the striated appearance; on axial CT they appear as dots. Paget's disease gives an enlarged vertebra with a thick cortical 'picture frame'.
Which is NOT a recommended treatment for a simple bone cyst?
Curettage and grafting with or without flexible nails
Simple cysts are benign and often heal after fracture or with minimally invasive treatment. Wide resection is never indicated.
In a 10-year-old with a radial neck fracture, angulation is generally acceptable without reduction up to about:

Up to about 30° of angulation (with some translation) remodels well in children under 10. Greater angulation needs closed reduction, percutaneous joystick manipulation or flexible nail (Métaizeau) reduction.
In paediatric forearm shaft fractures, which deformity most limits forearm rotation?
Malrotation and loss of the interosseous space from mid-shaft angulation
Translation of 50% in the distal third
Rotational malalignment does not remodel, and mid-shaft angulation narrows the interosseous space. Distal-third angulation in young children remodels well.
In children's hip fractures (Delbet classification), the type with the highest risk of avascular necrosis is:
Type I separations carry the highest AVN risk, approaching 100% when associated with dislocation, followed by type II. Early reduction, capsular decompression and stable fixation lower the risk.

Pressing the palm into the abdomen with the elbow forward requires internal rotation by subscapularis; a weak muscle makes the elbow drop back and the wrist flex. It is useful when pain prevents the lift-off position.
Which statement about the knee ligaments is true?
The MCL has superficial and deep layers, with the deep layer attached to the medial meniscus
The LCL is attached to the lateral meniscus
The PCL is weaker than the ACL
The ACL is extrasynovial and extra-articular

The deep MCL (meniscofemoral and meniscotibial ligaments) attaches to the medial meniscus, partly explaining combined injuries. The LCL is separate from the lateral meniscus, with the popliteus tendon between them.
For single-level cervical spondylotic myelopathy caused by an anterior disc–osteophyte complex, the usual operation is:
Anterior compression at one or two levels is best addressed directly from the front. Multilevel compression with preserved lordosis suits laminoplasty or posterior decompression and fusion.
Symptomatic thoracic disc herniations most commonly occur at:
The lower thoracic segments have more motion. Thoracic discs are often calcified and central, so posterior laminectomy alone is unsafe; anterior, lateral or posterolateral approaches are used.
The most widely used technique for thoracolumbar pedicle screw insertion is:
Fluoroscopy-free freehand technique using anatomical landmarks, with tactile feedback and fluoroscopic confirmation
The freehand technique, guided by landmarks and a pedicle probe, is used most worldwide, with fluoroscopy or navigation increasingly added to improve accuracy, especially in deformity.
The earliest clinical feature of tuberculosis of the spine is usually:
Back pain and paraspinal muscle spasm
Pain and spasm, with constitutional symptoms, precede deformity. Night cries in children result from relaxation of spasm during sleep.
Which statement about ACL grafts is FALSE?
Hamstring grafts cause less anterior knee pain
Quadriceps tendon grafts are an option
Allografts have the lowest failure rates in young athletes
Allografts have higher failure rates in young, active patients, partly due to slower incorporation and processing (such as irradiation). Autografts are preferred in this group.
The filum terminale extends from the conus medullaris to attach at the:
The internal filum lies within the dural sac to about S2; the external part continues to the coccyx. A tight, thickened filum causes tethered cord syndrome.
The earliest MRI finding of a bone stress injury is:
Periosteal oedema, then marrow oedema on fluid-sensitive sequences
Fredericson grading of tibial stress injury progresses from periosteal oedema (grade 1), to marrow oedema on T2 then T1, to a visible fracture line (grade 4).
Traction apophysitis of the fifth metatarsal base
Osteonecrosis of the second metatarsal head
It occurs in active adolescents at the peroneus brevis insertion. The apophysis lies parallel to the shaft, unlike a fracture, which is transverse. Treatment is rest and offloading.
Compartment syndrome of the foot most often follows:
The calcaneal compartment, containing quadratus plantae, is commonly involved. Untreated, it leads to claw toes and chronic pain. The foot has about nine compartments.
A triple-phase bone scan with increased uptake in all three phases (flow, blood pool and delayed) suggests:
Osteomyelitis is active in all phases; cellulitis is active only in early phases. Fractures, Charcot arthropathy and CRPS can also be positive in all phases, so clinical correlation is needed.
Which medial meniscal tear is LEAST suitable for repair?
Peripheral longitudinal tear in a young patient
Complex degenerative tear in the white–white zone in an older patient
Root tear in a young patient
Repair suits vertical tears in vascular zones in young patients, especially with ACL reconstruction. Complex degenerative avascular tears do poorly.
A patient has an ACL tear with a grade I–II MCL injury. Usual management is:
Brace and rehabilitation to let the MCL heal, then ACL reconstruction once motion is restored
The MCL heals reliably; early ACL surgery with an acute MCL injury raises stiffness risk. Persistent valgus laxity after healing may need MCL repair or reconstruction at the time of ACL surgery.
Which is a contraindication to high tibial osteotomy for medial compartment arthritis?

Contraindications include lateral or patellofemoral arthritis, inflammatory arthritis, flexion contracture over about 15°, flexion under about 90° and significant instability. Smoking and obesity reduce success.
On an AP ankle radiograph, the 'ball sign' refers to:
A loose body in the joint
A rounded lateral talar dome outline seen when there is a fibular shortening or malreduction, showing an abnormal talocrural angle
An ossicle below the medial malleolus

The continuous curve between the distal fibula and the lateral talus is lost when the fibula is short, producing a 'ball' at the lateral talar shoulder. Restoring fibular length and rotation restores the mortise.
In a haematoma block for distal radius fracture reduction, local anaesthetic is injected:
Into the fracture haematoma from the dorsal side
Aspiration of blood confirms the needle is in the haematoma. Bier block (IV regional anaesthesia) and nerve blocks give better relaxation and may allow better reduction.
Weakness of extensor hallucis longus without other deficit most commonly reflects compression of which root?
EHL is the most reliable L5 muscle. Peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular neck also weakens EHL, but with ankle eversion weakness and sparing of hip abduction and tibialis posterior.
Müller–Weiss syndrome is spontaneous osteonecrosis and collapse of the:
It typically affects women in their 40s–60s, often bilaterally, with a comma-shaped lateral collapse and paradoxical pes planovarus. Advanced cases need talonavicular-cuneiform fusion.
A 'rugger-jersey' spine on a lateral radiograph is typical of:
Dense bands at the end plates alternate with lucent central bone. Osteopetrosis gives a 'sandwich' vertebra with sharper margins.
Which type of juvenile idiopathic arthritis carries the highest risk of chronic anterior uveitis?
Oligoarticular JIA in a young ANA-positive girl
Uveitis is often silent, so regular slit-lamp screening is essential. Systemic JIA has spiking fevers and rash but little uveitis.
Horizontal sclerotic 'zebra' lines in the metaphyses of a child with osteogenesis imperfecta result from:
Each pamidronate or zoledronate cycle leaves a dense band as the physis grows. Lead poisoning gives broad dense metaphyseal bands without a cyclical pattern.
Regarding incidental dural tears during spinal surgery, which is true?
