Primary watertight repair, with or without sealant, at the time of surgery usually succeeds
Recognised tears are repaired primarily; persistent CSF leaks can cause positional headache, pseudomeningocele and wound problems, and may need lumbar drainage or revision.
Internal snapping hip is caused by the:
Iliotibial band over the greater trochanter
Iliopsoas tendon over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head
It produces an audible snap as the hip moves from flexion, abduction and external rotation into extension. Most respond to stretching; endoscopic release is used for refractory cases.
The medial clavicular physis is notable because it:
Is the last physis in the body to fuse, at about 23–25 years
Apparent sternoclavicular dislocations in young adults are often physeal separations, which remodel well. Posterior injuries still need careful assessment of the mediastinum.
The normal adult prevertebral soft-tissue thickness at C6–C7 (retrotracheal) is up to about:
Normal values are about 7 mm at C2 and 22 mm at C6. Widening suggests haematoma or abscess.
Lytic bone destruction in spinal metastases is driven mainly by:
Osteoclast activation via tumour-induced RANKL and PTHrP

Tumour cells secrete PTHrP and other factors that increase RANKL, recruiting osteoclasts; bone resorption releases growth factors that feed the tumour (the 'vicious cycle'). Bisphosphonates and denosumab interrupt it.
The main principle of minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis (MIPO) is:
Absolute stability with anatomical reduction of every fragment
Preserving the fracture biology by bridging the zone of comminution through small incisions with indirect reduction

MIPO aims for relative stability, restoring length, alignment and rotation without stripping fragments. It suits metaphyseal and comminuted diaphyseal fractures, such as distal tibia and distal femur.
A horizontal-beam lateral knee radiograph shows a fat–fluid level in the suprapatellar pouch. This indicates:
An intra-articular fracture releasing marrow fat
Lipohaemarthrosis indicates an intra-articular fracture, most often of the tibial plateau. CT then defines the fracture.
Normal resting intracompartmental pressure in the leg is about:
Pressures approaching diastolic pressure (delta pressure under 30 mmHg) impair perfusion. After casting, split the cast and padding if compartment syndrome is suspected.
After ACL reconstruction, which exercise is usually avoided in the early phase because it strains the graft?
Open-chain resisted knee extension in the 0–45° range
Open-chain extension near full extension puts high anterior shear on the graft. Closed-chain exercises with co-contraction are preferred early; open-chain work is added later in safer ranges.
The Slocum test with the tibia externally rotated about 15° assesses:
Anteromedial rotatory instability (MCL and posteromedial structures)
Anterior drawer with external rotation tightens the medial structures; increased translation indicates anteromedial instability. With internal rotation, it assesses anterolateral instability.
Malrotation after intramedullary nailing of the femur is most likely with:
Comminuted fractures, where cortical landmarks are lost
Fractures nailed on a traction table only
Without cortical keys, rotation must be judged with the lesser trochanter profile, cortical thickness and comparison with the other side. Clinical rotation should be checked before leaving theatre.
Stage II posterior tibial tendon dysfunction is characterised by:
Flexible flatfoot with inability to do a single heel rise

Stage I is tenosynovitis with normal alignment, stage III a rigid deformity and stage IV adds ankle valgus. Stage II is typically treated with medial calcaneal osteotomy and FDL transfer if non-operative treatment fails.
In degenerative lumbar canal stenosis, the main source of neural compression is usually:
Hypertrophied ligamentum flavum and facet joints, with disc bulge
Ligamentum flavum thickening and buckling, facet hypertrophy and disc bulge combine to narrow the canal and lateral recesses. Decompression removes the hypertrophied ligament and the medial facets.
A 4-year-old has a short forearm with the hand deviated radially and a hypoplastic thumb. Which investigation should be considered because of a life-threatening association?
Blood count and chromosomal breakage test for Fanconi anaemia
Radial longitudinal deficiency is associated with Fanconi anaemia, TAR syndrome, Holt–Oram syndrome and VACTERL association. Echocardiography and renal ultrasound are also recommended.
Which is NOT a recognised cause of vertebra plana?

Vertebra plana means uniform flattening of a vertebral body with preserved discs; in children LCH is the classic cause, with leukaemia, Ewing sarcoma, infection and osteogenesis imperfecta as differentials. Spondylolysis is a pars defect without body collapse.
After a distal tibial shaft fracture, a patient's great toe clawing worsens when the ankle is dorsiflexed and eases when it is plantarflexed. This checkrein deformity results from:
Tethering of flexor hallucis longus in scar or callus at the fracture

FHL becomes adherent near the fracture or in the posterior compartment, so ankle dorsiflexion pulls the toe into flexion. Treatment is release or lengthening of FHL, sometimes at the level of the foot.
Catterall's classification of Perthes disease is based on:
The extent of femoral head involvement on radiographs (groups I–IV)
Group I involves the anterior head only and group IV the whole head. Interobserver reliability is poorer than for the Herring lateral pillar classification, which is now preferred for prognosis.
In the Ficat–Arlet classification of femoral head osteonecrosis, stage IV is:
Collapse with joint space narrowing and acetabular arthritis

Stage I has normal radiographs, stage II sclerosis or cysts, stage III collapse (crescent sign), and stage IV secondary arthritis. Core decompression is used before collapse; THA is usual for stage IV.
Which statement about the subvastus approach for TKA is FALSE?
It preserves the quadriceps tendon and extensor mechanism
Exposure can be difficult in obese patients or stiff knees
It may allow faster early recovery of quadriceps function
It splits the vastus medialis obliquus muscle fibres

The subvastus approach elevates VMO from the intermuscular septum without cutting muscle. The midvastus approach splits VMO fibres in line with them, and the medial parapatellar approach goes through the quadriceps tendon.
In a child with chronic lead poisoning, dense transverse bands are seen at the:
Metaphyses of fast-growing bones such as the distal femur and proximal tibia

Lead deposits in the zone of provisional calcification. Unlike normal growth density, lead lines involve the proximal fibula too. Other causes of dense metaphyseal bands include healing rickets, bisphosphonates and leukaemia (lucent bands).
A woman develops burning and numbness over the dorsoradial hand and thumb after wearing a tight watch strap, worse on forearm pronation with wrist ulnar flexion. Diagnosis:
The superficial radial nerve is compressed where it emerges between brachioradialis and ECRL. There is no motor weakness. Removing the compressing cause usually helps; release is rarely needed.
On an AP lumbosacral radiograph, an 'inverted Napoleon's hat' sign suggests:
The forward-slipped and tilted L5 body projects over the sacrum like an upturned hat. Lateral standing films grade the slip and measure the slip angle and pelvic incidence.
The most common site of skeletal metastasis is the:
Spine (especially thoracic and lumbar vertebral bodies)
Red marrow-rich axial bones are the main sites, then the pelvis, proximal femur and humerus. Distal (acral) metastases are rare and most often from lung cancer.
During full arm elevation, the overall ratio of glenohumeral to scapulothoracic movement is about:
Of about 180° of elevation, roughly 120° occurs at the glenohumeral joint and 60° at the scapulothoracic joint. Scapular dyskinesis disturbs this rhythm and contributes to impingement.
The Achilles tendon is most vulnerable to rupture about 2–6 cm above its insertion because:
Blood supply is poorest in this watershed zone

The tendon's mid-portion has the fewest vessels, which is where most degenerative ruptures and midportion tendinopathy occur. Supply comes from the paratenon and the musculotendinous and osteotendinous junctions.
A simple ganglion of the palm
Tuberculous tenosynovitis of the flexor sheaths, distended above and below the flexor retinaculum, often with 'melon-seed' bodies
Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath

The hourglass swelling fluctuates across the flexor retinaculum (cross-fluctuation). Treatment is antitubercular therapy with synovectomy if needed. Rheumatoid tenosynovitis can also produce rice bodies.
After a wrist injury, pressing the prominent distal ulna downward makes it spring back up when released. This 'piano key' sign indicates:
Distal radioulnar joint instability, as with a TFCC tear or Galeazzi injury
The ballottement and piano key tests assess the DRUJ in pronation and supination. Foveal TFCC detachment is the key lesion; repair or reconstruction restores stability.
During overarm throwing or fast bowling, maximum valgus stress at the elbow occurs during:

As the shoulder reaches maximum external rotation and the arm begins to accelerate, the medial elbow is loaded close to the failure strength of the UCL. Deceleration stresses the posterior cuff and posterior capsule.
During coracoid surgery (such as Latarjet), vigorous retraction of the conjoint tendon can injure the musculocutaneous nerve, which enters the coracobrachialis about how far below the coracoid tip?
The nerve can enter the muscle as close as 2–3 cm in some people, so retraction should be gentle. Injury causes weak elbow flexion and lateral forearm numbness.
Recent perfusion studies suggest the main blood supply to the humeral head comes from the:

The arcuate artery (ascending branch of the anterior circumflex) was classically considered dominant, but studies show the posterior circumflex supplies most of the head. Preserving the posteromedial metaphyseal 'hinge' protects perfusion after fractures.
A boxer's fracture is a fracture of the:

Striking with a closed fist angulates the neck volarly. Considerable angulation (often 40–70°) is tolerated in the little finger, but any rotational deformity causing scissoring needs correction. A wound over the knuckle suggests a fight bite.
Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur is classically seen in:
Marrow expansion or failure of metaphyseal remodelling flares the distal femur. Other causes include osteopetrosis, thalassaemia, Pyle disease and lead poisoning.
Looser zones (pseudofractures) are NOT typically seen in:

Looser zones are bands of unmineralised osteoid in osteomalacia and hypophosphataemic states; similar insufficiency fractures appear on the convex side of bowed pagetic bones. Simple osteoporosis does not produce them.
Which statement about Paget's disease of bone is FALSE?
It begins with an osteoclastic (lytic) phase
It can cause deafness and high-output cardiac failure
Calcium and phosphate are usually normal unless the patient is immobilised. Bisphosphonates (especially zoledronic acid) treat pain and activity.
The Stryker notch view of the shoulder is designed to show:
A Hill–Sachs lesion of the posterolateral humeral head
The patient lies supine with the hand on the head and the beam angled 10° cephalad. The West Point view shows the anteroinferior glenoid rim for bony Bankart lesions; CT is the best overall test.
Among the following, the most specific marker of periprosthetic joint infection after THA is:
Serum markers are sensitive but not specific. Synovial alpha-defensin and leukocyte esterase are highly specific, and synovial fluid cell count and neutrophil percentage remain central.
A Pellegrini–Stieda lesion on a knee radiograph is:
Calcification near the medial femoral epicondyle at the MCL origin after an old injury
Avulsion of the lateral tibial plateau
It indicates a previous MCL injury with post-traumatic ossification at the femoral attachment and may be painful. A Segond fracture is a lateral capsular avulsion linked to ACL tears.
Which is NOT a cause of aseptic loosening after THA?
Low-grade infection causes septic loosening, which must be excluded before any revision for presumed aseptic loosening. Particle-induced osteolysis is the main aseptic cause.
Which statement about cauda equina syndrome is FALSE?
Saddle anaesthesia is a key sign
It is a lower motor neuron lesion
Delaying decompression beyond several days does not affect bladder outcome
Outcomes, especially bladder function, are better with decompression before retention develops (incomplete CES), ideally within 48 hours or sooner. Urgent MRI and surgery are standard.
Axial rotation and lateral bending of the head on C1–C2
They run from the dens to the occipital condyles. The transverse ligament holds the dens against C1 and is the main stabiliser against anterior C1 translation.
The best indication for meniscal repair is:
A degenerative complex tear in a 60-year-old
An acute longitudinal peripheral (red–red zone) tear in a young patient, ideally with ACL reconstruction
A radial tear in the white–white zone
A tear associated with grade IV arthritis
Healing is best in vascular zones in young knees, and the haemarthrosis from ACL reconstruction supplies growth factors that improve healing.
In lumbar canal stenosis, the space in the central canal is greatest in:
Flexion stretches the ligamentum flavum and opens the canal and foramina, so patients lean forward or sit for relief ('shopping cart sign'). Extension narrows the canal.
The valgus stress test for the elbow's ulnar collateral ligament is done with the elbow in about:
20–30° of flexion, to unlock the olecranon from its fossa
Slight flexion removes bony stability so the ligament is isolated. The moving valgus stress test (flexion from 120° to 70° under valgus load) is sensitive in throwers.
The rotator interval is bordered superiorly by supraspinatus and inferiorly by:

Its base is the coracoid and its apex the transverse humeral ligament. It contains the coracohumeral ligament, superior glenohumeral ligament and long head of biceps; contracture here causes frozen shoulder.
Fanconi syndrome causes rickets or osteomalacia mainly because of impaired reabsorption in the:
Proximal renal tubule, causing phosphate, glucose, amino acid and bicarbonate wasting
Phosphate wasting and acidosis impair mineralisation. Causes include cystinosis, drugs such as tenofovir, and myeloma light chains in adults.
Compared with a cancellous screw, a cortical screw has:
A larger thread depth and wider pitch
A smaller thread depth, finer pitch and larger core diameter relative to the outer diameter
Cortical screws suit dense diaphyseal bone; cancellous screws, with deeper threads and wider pitch, grip soft metaphyseal bone. Pull-out strength depends on outer diameter and bone quality.
A PASTA lesion of the shoulder is a:
Partial articular-sided tears are more common than bursal-side tears. Tears involving more than about 50% of tendon thickness are often repaired (transtendon or completed and repaired).
The ulnar bursa of the hand typically communicates with the:
Little finger flexor sheath, and often with the radial bursa via Parona's space

The ulnar bursa encloses the finger flexors in the carpal tunnel and is continuous with the little finger sheath. Infection can spread to the radial bursa (FPL) through Parona's space, causing a horseshoe abscess.
In Pott's spine with developing cord compression, the earliest neurological sign is usually:
Exaggerated tendon reflexes and ankle clonus (upper motor neuron signs)

Motor tracts are affected before sensory ones, so spasticity, brisk reflexes and clonus come first, then weakness, then sensory and sphincter loss. Most patients recover with ATT, with surgery for poor response.
The bone most often affected by a march (stress) fracture in military recruits is the:
The long, relatively fixed second metatarsal bears high loads in push-off. Most heal with a stiff-soled shoe and reduced activity.
Which spinal finding is NOT typical of neurofibromatosis type 1?

NF1 causes dystrophic short, sharp kyphoscoliosis with rib pencilling, dural ectasia, scalloping and foraminal widening. Dystrophic curves progress rapidly and need early fusion with careful planning.
Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) is characteristic of:
TRAP is used as an osteoclast marker in histology and as a serum marker of resorption (TRAP-5b). Alkaline phosphatase is the osteoblast marker.
McCune–Albright syndrome results from an activating mutation of:
GNAS (Gs alpha, increasing cyclic AMP signalling)
Postzygotic GNAS mutations cause polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots and endocrine hyperfunction. The same mutation in a single bone causes monostotic fibrous dysplasia.
The posterior interosseous nerve enters the forearm by passing:
Between the two heads of pronator teres
Between the superficial and deep layers of supinator
It enters under the arcade of Frohse at the proximal edge of supinator. The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres.
Ranked from lowest to highest elastic modulus, the correct order is:
Cortical bone, PMMA, titanium, stainless steel, cobalt–chromium
PMMA, cortical bone, titanium alloy, stainless steel, cobalt–chromium

Approximate values: polyethylene about 1 GPa, PMMA about 2–3 GPa, cortical bone about 15–20 GPa, titanium alloy about 110 GPa, stainless steel about 200 GPa and cobalt–chromium about 220 GPa; ceramics are higher still.
Prophylactic cefazolin should ideally be given:
After the tourniquet is released only
Giving it within the hour before incision achieves tissue levels at incision; redose for long cases or major blood loss. Vancomycin needs to start 60–120 minutes before because of its infusion time.
Developmental dysplasia of the hip is more common in:
Girls, first-born, breech presentation, with a family history

Risk factors include female sex, breech, first pregnancy, family history and oligohydramnios, with the left hip affected most. Neonatal clinical screening with selective or universal ultrasound is standard.
Proteoglycans are stored in greatest quantity in which zone of the physis?
The reserve zone stores lipids, glycogen and proteoglycan aggregates and is affected in some storage disorders. The hypertrophic zone is involved in rickets and SCFE.
The posteromedial approach to the tibial plateau uses the interval between:
Gastrocnemius medial head and pes anserinus or semimembranosus
Tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus

Medial gastrocnemius is retracted laterally to protect the popliteal neurovascular bundle while exposing the posteromedial plateau. It is used for posteromedial shear fragments that lateral plates cannot buttress.
After ORIF of a distal humerus fracture, routine anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve:
Clearly lowers the risk of ulnar neuropathy in all trials
Has not been shown to reduce neuropathy and may increase it; practice varies
Evidence is mixed; some studies show more ulnar neuritis after routine transposition. Many surgeons identify and protect the nerve and transpose it only if it lies on or near hardware or is unstable.
When templating a THA on a standard AP pelvic radiograph, image magnification is usually about:
A calibration ball at the level of the greater trochanter allows correction; uncorrected magnification leads to oversized components. Templating also plans leg length and offset.
'Melon-seed' (rice) bodies within a joint or tendon sheath are classically associated with:
Tuberculous synovitis and also rheumatoid arthritis
They form from fibrin and synovial debris in chronic synovitis. A compound palmar ganglion with rice bodies is a classic presentation of TB tenosynovitis.
The Watson-Jones (anterolateral) approach to the hip develops the interval between:
Tensor fasciae latae and gluteus medius
It is not a true internervous plane because both muscles are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, which is at risk if the interval is developed too far proximally.
The main cell responsible for contraction in Dupuytren disease is the:
Myofibroblasts express alpha-smooth muscle actin and contract the cords. Nodules contain abundant myofibroblasts and represent the active proliferative phase.
A soldier has anterior mid-tibial pain; the lateral radiograph shows a horizontal lucent line in the anterior cortex (the 'dreaded black line'). This indicates:
A tension-side tibial stress fracture at high risk of non-union and completion
Anterior cortical stress fractures heal poorly and can progress to complete fracture. Prolonged rest is often unsuccessful, so intramedullary nailing is commonly recommended for athletes.
Rises with knee flexion and quadriceps force, peaking around 60–90° in activities like squatting

Forces reach several times body weight during deep squats and stair climbing. Open-chain extension loads the patellofemoral joint most near full extension, and closed-chain exercises most in deep flexion.
A 45-year-old diabetic has a painless, warm, swollen ankle with crepitus and joint destruction on radiographs, but normal inflammatory markers. Most likely diagnosis:

Loss of protective sensation and autonomic changes allow repeated microtrauma and bone destruction. A temperature difference over 2 °C compared with the other side indicates activity; offloading is the mainstay.
After final component implantation in TKA, the patella tracks laterally. Which component positioning error most commonly causes this?
External rotation of the femoral component
Internal rotation of the femoral or tibial component
Lateral placement of the femoral component
Medial placement of the patellar button

Internal rotation brings the trochlea medially and effectively lateralises the tubercle. The patellar button should be medialised and the femoral component lateralised and externally rotated to improve tracking.
A Kim lesion of the shoulder is:
A concealed, incomplete avulsion of the posteroinferior labrum (a marginal crack)

It is a cause of posterior instability and pain that may look intact on the surface. The Kim test (axial load with the arm elevated and adducted) and jerk test help diagnose posteroinferior labral lesions.
The swimmer's view is used to visualise the:
The shoulders often obscure C7–T1 on the lateral view; raising one arm above the head while the other is lowered shows it. CT is now used in most trauma settings.
Which is NOT a poor prognostic factor in synovial sarcoma?
Extensive calcification is associated with a better prognosis. Large size, older age, positive margins and poorly differentiated subtype predict worse outcomes.
Training the same way all year
Planned variation of training volume and intensity across cycles to optimise performance and avoid overtraining
Training is divided into macrocycles, mesocycles and microcycles, with tapering before competition. It reduces staleness and injury risk.
Cycles of isometric contraction and relaxation of the stretched muscle (contract–relax) to increase range
Contraction followed by relaxation (autogenic inhibition) allows a greater stretch. PNF generally produces larger short-term gains in range than static stretching.
A newborn has a single, fixed, painless shoulder and the shoulders can be brought together in front of the chest. The X-ray shows absence of both clavicles with a widened symphysis pubis. Diagnosis:
Cleidocranial dysplasia (RUNX2) also causes delayed fontanelle closure, wormian bones and dental anomalies. Clavicular absence rarely needs treatment.
In mucopolysaccharidoses, which statement about treatment is FALSE?
Enzyme replacement is available for several types
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation helps Hurler syndrome if done early
Enzyme replacement fully corrects established skeletal dysplasia
Atlantoaxial instability may need surgical stabilisation
Enzyme replacement does not cross the blood–brain barrier well and has limited effect on established bone and cartilage changes. Spinal cord compression and hip dysplasia often still need surgery.
The most common forearm deformity in hereditary multiple exostoses is:
Ulnar shortening with radial bowing and ulnar deviation of the wrist (possible radial head dislocation)
Exostoses at the distal ulna tether its growth, so the radius bows and the wrist deviates towards the ulna, sometimes dislocating the radial head. Excision and ulnar lengthening are options.
A 1.5-year-old has symmetric moderate bowing of the legs, normal height and a metaphyseal–diaphyseal angle of 8°. Best management:
Physiological bowing peaks around 1 year and corrects by 2 years. Angles under about 10° are reassuring; asymmetry, short stature, progression or angles over 16° warrant further assessment.
Which is NOT a common indication for adding anterolateral ligament reconstruction or lateral extra-articular tenodesis to ACL reconstruction?
Isolated partial ACL tear in a sedentary older patient
Lateral extra-articular procedures reduce graft failure and rotational laxity in high-risk patients. They are not needed for low-demand patients.
Which statement about tourniquet palsy is FALSE?
It is more common in the upper limb
Excessive pressure and prolonged inflation increase the risk
The radial nerve is the most commonly affected in the arm
Most tourniquet palsies are neuropraxias that recover over weeks to months. Using the lowest effective pressure (based on limb occlusion pressure), wide cuffs and limiting time reduce the risk.
In anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty, a radial mismatch between the glenoid and humeral head (glenoid radius larger) of about how much reduces rim loading and loosening?
Some mismatch allows translation without edge loading; too little leads to rim stresses, too much to point contact and polyethylene wear.
Tumour-induced (oncogenic) osteomalacia results from tumour secretion of:

Small, often hidden mesenchymal tumours (phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours) secrete FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting and low calcitriol. Removal of the tumour, found by functional imaging such as Ga-68 DOTATATE PET, cures the condition.
If femoral offset is not restored during THA (offset too small), the most likely consequence is:
Abductor weakness, limp and a higher dislocation risk from soft-tissue laxity and impingement
Reduced offset shortens the abductor lever arm, increasing joint reaction force and polyethylene wear, and slackens the soft tissues. Excess offset can cause trochanteric pain.
A hip shows a positive crossover sign on a well-centred AP pelvic radiograph. This means:
Focal anterior over-coverage from acetabular retroversion

The anterior rim line crosses the posterior rim line before reaching the lateral sourcil. Combined with the posterior wall and ischial spine signs, it suggests retroversion, a cause of pincer impingement.
Charnley's original low-friction arthroplasty was performed through a:
Trochanteric osteotomy gave excellent exposure and allowed the trochanter to be advanced to tension the abductors, at the cost of trochanteric non-union and wire breakage.
Which THA approach carries the lowest risk of sciatic nerve injury?

Anterior and anterolateral approaches keep away from the sciatic nerve; the posterior approach has a higher risk. The femoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves are more at risk with anterior approaches.
Primary (idiopathic) protrusio, often in women, is called Otto pelvis. Secondary causes include rheumatoid arthritis, osteomalacia and Marfan syndrome.
Initial stability of an uncemented press-fit acetabular cup comes mainly from:
Peripheral rim press-fit from under-reaming by about 1–2 mm
Bone ingrowth in the first week
Under-reaming creates hoop stresses at the rim. Screws add stability in poor bone. Ingrowth over weeks gives long-term (secondary) fixation.
In a well-positioned acetabular liner, polyethylene wear is usually greatest in the:
Superolateral (superior) region, the direction of the joint reaction force
The femoral head penetrates superiorly and slightly posteriorly with gait loading. Steep cups move contact towards the rim, increasing edge loading and wear.
In a posterior-cruciate–retaining TKA, paradoxical anterior femoral sliding in flexion is mainly due to:

Without the ACL, the femur slides forward on the tibia instead of rolling back in flexion, reducing flexion and quadriceps efficiency. Medial-pivot and ultracongruent designs try to reproduce normal kinematics.
In a child with cerebral palsy, knee hyperextension (recurvatum) during stance is most often driven by:
Spasticity or contracture of the calf (ankle plantarflexor–knee extension couple)
A tight or overactive gastrocnemius–soleus holds the tibia back in stance, forcing the knee into hyperextension. Over-lengthened hamstrings and rectus femoris spasticity also contribute.
Klein's line on an AP pelvic radiograph is drawn along the:
Superior border of the femoral neck, and should intersect the lateral femoral epiphysis
Inferior border of the femoral neck
In SCFE the line fails to cut the epiphysis or cuts less of it than on the normal side. A frog-lateral view is more sensitive for early slips.
When measuring a Cobb angle in scoliosis, you identify the:
Upper and lower end vertebrae most tilted into the curve

Lines along the superior end plate of the upper end vertebra and inferior end plate of the lower end vertebra give the Cobb angle. Measurement error is about 5°, so smaller changes are not significant.
During wrist arthroscopy, the tendon most often injured by the 3–4 portal is the:

The 3–4 portal lies between EPL and EDC, just distal to Lister's tubercle. The 6R portal risks ECU and the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve, and the 1–2 portal the superficial radial nerve and radial artery.
An extra-articular base of thumb metacarpal fracture
A comminuted intra-articular fracture of the thumb metacarpal base (Y or T shaped)
A fracture of the fifth metacarpal base
Rolando fractures have a worse prognosis than Bennett fractures. Large fragments are fixed; severe comminution may need external fixation or traction.
Spontaneous EPL rupture in a drummer ('drummer's palsy') typically occurs at:
Lister's tubercle in the third compartment
Repetitive wrist movement causes attrition where EPL turns around Lister's tubercle. Treatment is EIP transfer.
Which is NOT part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex?
The TFCC includes the articular disc, radioulnar ligaments, meniscal homologue, ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligaments, ulnar collateral ligament and ECU subsheath.
The 'killer turn' in transtibial PCL reconstruction can be reduced by all EXCEPT:
Smoothing the posterior tibial tunnel exit
A more anterolateral, flatter tibial tunnel
A sharper, more vertical tunnel angle
The graft bends sharply where it exits the posterior tibia, causing abrasion and stretching. Inlay fixation, a flatter tunnel and chamfering the exit reduce this.
Most infections after open fractures are caused by:
Organisms present in the wound at the time of injury
Many infections are caused by hospital-acquired organisms rather than the initial contaminants, which is why early antibiotics, debridement and early wound cover are crucial.
Which is a recognised risk factor for recurrence of Dupuytren disease (Dupuytren diathesis)?
Positive family history, bilateral disease, ectopic lesions (Garrod's pads, Ledderhose, Peyronie) and onset before 50
Diathesis features predict aggressive disease and recurrence. Dermofasciectomy with skin grafting lowers recurrence in high-risk patients.
Longitudinal split tears of peroneus brevis most often occur because the tendon is compressed between:
Peroneus longus and the posterior fibula in the retromalleolar groove

Brevis lies closer to the bone and is pressed by longus against a shallow groove or edge of the fibula, especially with superior peroneal retinaculum laxity. Brevis tears are more common than longus tears.
Pelvic incidence (PI) is related to pelvic tilt (PT) and sacral slope (SS) by:
PI is a fixed anatomical parameter after growth, while PT and SS change with posture. High PI needs more lumbar lordosis and is associated with spondylolisthesis.
The CPAK (Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee) classification uses:
Arithmetic HKA (MPTA − LDFA) and joint line obliquity (MPTA + LDFA)
CPAK describes nine phenotypes; varus aHKA with apex distal joint line (type I) is common in arthritic knees. It supports 'kinematic' or restricted alignment strategies in TKA.
Which osteotomy around the knee tends to cause patella baja rather than alta?
Medial opening-wedge HTO with proximal tibial tubercle

Opening the wedge above the tubercle lifts the joint line away from the tubercle, effectively lowering the patella. A biplanar cut with the tubercle on the proximal fragment avoids this. Closing-wedge HTO tends to raise the patella slightly.
Autologous conditioned plasma (ACP), a single-spin PRP product, is:
Leucocyte-poor PRP with a modest (about 2–3 times) platelet concentration
Single-spin plasma-based systems collect the upper plasma, giving leucocyte-poor PRP; buffy-coat systems give leucocyte-rich PRP with higher platelet counts.
Which is NOT a radiographic method for measuring acetabular cup anteversion on an AP film?
Widmer, Lewinnek, Liaw and Pradhan methods use the ellipse of the cup opening. Dorr's classification describes proximal femoral shape, not cup version. CT is the most accurate measure.
Which is an absolute contraindication to total ankle arthroplasty?
Active or recent infection, Charcot arthropathy or severe peripheral neuropathy
Relative contraindications include young high-demand patients, severe deformity, poor bone stock, AVN of the talus and smoking. Ankle fusion remains the alternative.
The 'grand piano' sign on an axial (skyline) view of the distal femur in TKA indicates:
Correct femoral component rotation, with the anterior lateral cut larger than the medial
Internal rotation of the femoral component
Correct external rotation removes more anterior bone laterally than medially, giving a resected surface shaped like a grand piano. A symmetrical 'butterfly' shape suggests internal rotation.
McPherson's rule for TKA with extra-articular deformity helps decide whether a femoral deformity can be corrected by intra-articular bone cuts based on:
The magnitude of deformity and its distance from the joint
Deformities close to the joint have a greater effect on the bone cut and may compromise the collateral ligament attachments; larger or nearer deformities need corrective osteotomy before or with TKA.
More clawing in a high ulnar nerve lesion
Less clawing in a high (elbow) ulnar lesion than in a low (wrist) lesion because FDP to the ring and little fingers is also paralysed
With FDP intact (low lesion), unopposed long flexors flex the IP joints strongly, so clawing is worse. As a high lesion recovers, clawing can paradoxically increase.
After an anterior approach for THA, a patient has numbness over the anterolateral thigh. The nerve affected is the:
The LFCN crosses near the interval between sartorius and TFL. Most symptoms improve; a more lateral incision over the TFL reduces risk.
Symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumour not amenable to surgery
It inhibits the CSF1 receptor that drives TGCT. Hepatotoxicity requires liver function monitoring.
